■

Though judgments in G. McKenzie and Punjab National Bank Ltd. supra at the first glance indicate that the jurisdiction under section 33(2)(b) is limited to consider prima facie aspects and not adjudicatory, on consideration of the factual background in which those judgments are rendered one cannot but conclude that jurisdiction exercised while refusing or granting approval under section 33(2)(b), is adjudicatory on few aspects namely, "Whether the domestic enquiry is fair and proper, which in its fold may include few aspects like, compliance of principles of natural justice, compliance of requirements of the Standing Orders governing domestic enquiry or compliance of any other binding contract of employment, payment of wages as provided under section 33(2)(b)?" [Para 33]

■

After considering the above aspects, if the Authority takes a final call approving the punishment imposed, then the order granting approval for the punishment is neither an adjudication on the merits of the finding in the domestic enquiry nor on the proportionality of the punishment. It is in this context, it has been held that the scope of enquiry under section 33(2)(b) is limited to lifting the ban on the punishment. [Para 34]

■

The interpretation that the scope of enquiry under section 33(2)(b) is limited cannot be stretched to contend that the finding as to whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper is not on adjudication. For the reasons recorded above, it is held that the finding on the issue relating to fairness of domestic enquiry is adjudicatory. And said question cannot be revisited in an industrial dispute challenging the penalty. [Para 35]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 276C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Offences and prosecution - Wilful attempt to evade tax, etc. - Respondents applied for stay of criminal proceedings in cases filed for offences punishable under the Income-tax Act on ground that appeals against assessments were pending before appellate authorities and Tribunal - Magistrate allowed work of recording evidence to proceed but stayed passing of order about framing of charges, discharge or acquittal of accused during pendency of appeals before income-tax authorities - High Court passed interim order staying proceedings in criminal cases - Whether since ultimate result of proceedings before appellate authorities would have a definite bearing on cases alleged against respondents, High Court was justified in passing interim order and its order called for no interference - Held, yes

FACT: Several cases were filed against the respondents in the Magistrate Court for offences punishable under the Act. As appeals were pending before the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal, the respondents filed applications for the stay of criminal proceedings. The Magistrate, after examining the position in law as to whether the findings of appellate authorities were relevant for the purpose of criminal proceedings and to avoid conflicting decisions of Criminal Court and appellate authorities, allowed the work of recording evidence to proceed but stayed the passing of order about framing of charges, discharge or acquittal of accused during pendency of appeals before income-tax authorities. Revision petitions were dismissed by the sessions court. The High Court granted an interim order staying the proceedings in the criminal cases.

On special leave petition :

HELD: The prosecution in criminal law and proceedings arising under the Act are undoubtedly independent proceedings and, therefore, there is no impediment in law for the criminal proceedings to proceed even during the pendency of the proceedings under the Act. However, a wholesome rule will have to be adopted in matters of this nature where courts have taken the view that when the conclusions arrived at by the appellate authorities have a relevance and bearing upon the conclusions to be reached in the case, necessarily one authority will have to await the outcome of the other authority.

In the present case, there was no claim of quashing of the proceedings. When ultimately the result to come out of the proceedings before the appellate authorities would have a definite bearing on the cases alleged against the respondents, the High Court was justified in granting the interim order it did and such an interim order did not call for interference.

The petitions were, therefore, dismissed.

a lesser penalty - Held, yes - Whether since dismissal order was wholly disproportionate, same was to be set aside, while leaving finding of misconduct undisturbed - Held, yes - Whether competent authority was to be directed to consider any punishment other than ultimate penalty of dismissal from service, after considering appellant’s long service, past record, age, nature of misconduct, absence or presence of financial loss, and other relevant circumstances - Held, yes [Paras 111.2 and 111.7] FACT: ■

The appellant, a clerical employee of the respondent–company, was appointed in 1985 and later promoted. Earlier service disputes included a transfer to Warora that was set aside. On 04.09.2006, she was suspended pending enquiry on allegations of indiscipline, insubordination, disobedience, tampering with official documents, negligence and misuse of company property. The suspension order recorded entitlement to subsistence allowance as per rules and required weekly reporting at Warora. A charge-sheet was issued on 19.09.2006. The domestic enquiry commenced in March 2008; on 25.03.2008, her request for time was declined, the enquiry proceeded ex parte, five witnesses were examined, and the Enquiry Officer submitted a report on 25.04.2008. A show-cause notice proposing dismissal was also issued on 25.04.2008.

■

The appellant challenged the show-cause notice by Complaint (ULP) No. 34 of 2008. On 29.11.2014, the Labour Court held that the enquiry was not fair and the finding was perverse. In Revision (ULP) No. 4 of 2015, the Industrial Court on 14.08.2015 set aside the Labour Court’s order and remanded the matter, permitting the respondent–management to establish misconduct by leading evidence before the Labour Court, as the domestic enquiry was found defective.

■

After remand, the respondent–management led evidence before the Labour Court. The appellant’s request to respond to the charge-sheet at that stage was declined. By judgment dated 27.06.2017, the Labour Court held the misconduct proved on the evidence led post-remand and also held the earlier show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008 legal and proper, dismissing Complaint (ULP) No. 34 of 2008.

■

On 12.07.2017, the respondent issued the dismissal order removing the appellant from service and directing that the suspension period be treated as punishment. The order recorded that no explanation was submitted to the show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008. No fresh show-cause notice on punishment was issued after the post-remand findings. The appellant’s Revision (ULP) No. 37 of 2017 against the Labour Court’s judgment dated 27.06.2017 was dismissed by the Industrial Court on 08.06.2018, and was not carried further.

■

Separately, the appellant challenged the dismissal order by Complaint (ULP) No. 28 of 2017, inter alia, on the grounds that the Executive Engineer lacked competence since she was appointed by the Superintending Engineer, that a fresh notice under Regulation 88(j) was required after the de novo proof of misconduct before the Labour Court, that subsistence allowance was not paid during the entire suspension, that treating the suspension period as punishment was illegal, and that the dismissal was disproportionate. By judgment dated 08.08.2019, the Labour Court dismissed Complaint (ULP) No. 28 of 2017, holding that misconduct could not be reopened; the Executive Engineer was competent to impose dismissal; no fresh show-cause notice was required; the treatment of the suspension period as punishment was valid; and the penalty was not shockingly disproportionate. In Revision (ULP) No. 14 of 2019, the Industrial Court on 18.01.2023 dismissed the revision and affirmed the Labour Court’s judgment.

■

The appellant’s writ petition (No. 1200 of 2023) before the High Court was dismissed on 05.04.2024, upholding the concurrent findings on competency of the disciplinary authority, form of the dismissal order, show-cause notice, treatment of the suspension period, and proportionality; her review application was also dismissed on 11.11.2024.

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court.

HELD: ■

WHETHER THE DISMISSAL ORDER DATED 12.07.2017 WAS PASSED BY THE COMPETENT AUTHORITY ?

■

The Appellant has laid considerable emphasis on the fact that she was appointed by the Superintending Engineer but dismissed by the Executive Engineer. According to her, the dismissal order is invalid because it was passed by an authority lower than the appointing authority. [Para 30]

■

The courts below examined the applicable MSEDCL Employees Service Regulations and found that the Appellant was a Pay Grade-III employee. They further held that, under the relevant regulations and schedules governing disciplinary action, the Executive Engineer was competent to impose punishment on an employee belonging to that category. The High Court also considered the Appellant's reliance on the schedule relating to transfers and held that the said schedule did not govern dismissal from service. [Para 31]

■

Magistrate had yet not taken cognizance of the offences alleged to have been committed by the accused named therein but merely had referred the complaint to the police for investigation and to file a challan/charge sheet if there was evidence. From the above, it was clear that there was no criminal proceeding pending so as to tantamount to a parallel proceeding as contended by the respondents. The application for stay was liable to be dismissed on that ground alone. [Paras 14 and 15] The pleadings in the instant case were complete and no further disclosure was required to be made by the respondents against whom the criminal case was filed. Therefore, the arguments advanced by the respondents/applicants that they would be prejudiced by the continuance of the instant proceedings were without any basis and were not tenable. No prejudice was likely to affect them. Moreover, the CLB has consistently taken a view that if both the parties on similar grounds have filed another civil case, the CLB would not encourage parallel proceedings. There was nothing to prevent the CLB to proceed with the instant case when the criminal complaint filed was only at stage of investigation by the police. Relying on the judgment of the Supreme Court in Karamchand Ganga Pershad v. Union of India [1970] 3 SCC 694, it can be said that the proceedings before the CLB can continue even when criminal case is pending which may have been filed by either parties against each other. The matters before the CLB are to be decided in summary proceedings on the basis of evidence by way of affidavits filed by the parties. The overall assessment of the case led to the conclusion that the CLB could proceed with the case when criminal proceedings were pending. However, there was no need to proceed in the instant case for the reasons that the whole issue was evolving around the question of 55,005 shares held by the petitioner which had been fraudulently and by tampering certain documents allegedly were reduced to 405 shares. The question of tampering the documents fraudulently or otherwise had to be decided by the Criminal Court. That being the sole basis of the petition, the case was to be adjourned sine-die with certain directions to be followed. [Para 21]

2010] 13 SCC 255, also identified various exceptions to this general rule by observing that disclosure of evidential material which may inflict serious harm on a person directly concerned or other persons or where disclosure would be breach of confidence or might be injurious to the public interest as it would involve the revelation of official secrets, inhibit frankness of comment and the detection of crime, might make it impossible to obtain certain clauses of essential information at all, in the future. [Para 41]

■ The concept of fairness may require the Adjudicating Authority to furnish the copies of the documents upon which reliance has been placed by him to issue show cause notice requiring a notice to explain why an inquiry under section 16 of the Act, should not be initiated. To this extent, the principles of natural justice and concept of fairness are required to be read into rule 4(1) of the rules. The noticee is always entitled to satisfy the Adjudicating Authority that those very documents upon which reliance has been placed, do not make out even a prima facie case requiring any further inquiry. Therefore, all such documents relied on by the Authority are required to be furnished to the notice enabling him to show a proper cause as to why an inquiry should not be held against him. [Para 42]

■

Therefore, it was held in the case of Natwar Singh (supra), that the documents and the evidence relied upon by the Adjudicatory Authority, must be made available to the accused, to ensure reasonable opportunity of being heard and also to ensure the fairness of the procedure. The duty of adequate disclosure is only an additional procedural safeguard in order to ensure the attainment of the fairness. A distinction was drawn between the stage of enquiry under rule 4(1) and the final adjudication and it was observed that at the stage of show cause notice, it is sufficient that only documents that are relied upon are disclosed. [Para 43]

■

The logic behind such disclosure is the likelihood of being influenced by the documents referred in the enquiry whether relied or not. It was observed in the case of Khudiram Das v. State of West Bengal, (1960) 1 SCR 820 in the context of preventive detection, that it can hardly be disputed that if there was before the District Magistrate material against the detenu, which is of a highly damaging character and has nexus and relevancy with the object of detention, and proximity with the time when the subjective satisfaction forming part of the detention order was arrived at, it would be legitimate for the Court to infer that such material must have influenced the District Magistrate in arriving at the subjective satisfaction and the Court would refuse to accept the bald statement of the District Magistrate that he did not take any material into account and excluded it from consideration. The human mind does not function in compartments. [Para 44]

■

When it receives impressions from different sources, it is the totality of the impressions, which goes into the making of the decision. It is not possible to analyse and dissect the impressions and predicate which impressions went into the making of the decision. Nor is it any easy exercise to erase the impression created by particular circumstances so as to exclude the influence of such impression in the decision-making process. [Para 45]

■

Therefore, where there is material before the District Magistrate, which is of the character as would have reasonable probability to influence the decision of a reasonable man, the Court would be reluctant to accept the ipse dixit of the District Magistrate that he was not so influenced and a fortiori, if such material is not disclosed to the detenu, the order of detention would be vitiated. [Para 46]

■

The principle that the material that may influence the decision of a quasi-judicial authority to award a penalty, must be disclosed to the delinquent, was affirmed by the Apex Court in the case of Union of India v. Mohd. Ramzan Khan, (1991) 1 SCC 588. [Para 47]

■

This principle was again reaffirmed by the Constitution Bench of the Apex Court in the case of ECIL v. B. Karunakar, (1993) 4 SCC 727. It was held that the reason why the right to receive the report of the enquiry officer is considered as an essential part of the reasonable opportunity at the first stage and also a principle of natural justice, is that the findings recorded by the enquiry officer forms an important material before the disciplinary authority, which along with the evidence, is taken into consideration by it to come to the conclusion. The principles of natural justice require that the employee should have a fair opportunity to meet, explain and controvert it before he is condemned. It is negation of the tenets of justice and a denial of fair opportunity to the employee, to consider the findings recorded by a third party like an enquiry officer, without giving an opportunity to reply. [Para 48]

■

Although the disciplinary authority is required to arrive at its own findings on the basis of the evidence, but it is equally true that the disciplinary authority takes into consideration the findings recorded by the enquiry officer along with the evidence on record. In the circumstances, the findings of the enquiry officer do constitute an important material, which is likely to influence the conclusions of the disciplinary authority and therefore, the same must be made available to the employee. [Para 49]

■

ions, particularly concerning the lack of evidence and the illegality of the proceedings before the Court of Inquiry. Although some discussion was undertaken regarding the permissibility of initiating disciplinary proceedings after the appellant's discharge by a criminal court, even that aspect, in the Court's view, remains doubtful. While adverting to the appellant's reply, the authority merely noted their dissatisfaction in respect thereof, at paragraph 15 of the proceeding note dated 5-6-1992. [Para 32]

■ While courts ordinarily refrain from examining the sufficiency or adequacy of evidence in disciplinary matters, such restraint operates only where the finding of guilt is preceded by a duly conducted inquiry. In cases such as the present, where no regular inquiry was conducted and the delinquent was deprived of the opportunity to test the evidence through cross-examination, the scope of judicial review necessarily becomes a bit more intrusive. In such circumstances, the show cause notice, the reply thereto and the final order assume critical importance as the primary safeguards of natural justice. Consequently, where the delinquent furnishes a detailed explanation which is not ex facie frivolous or untenable, the competent/disciplinary authority is under a legal obligation to consider the same and pass a reasoned order demonstrating due application of mind as to why the defence raised was perceived to be unacceptable. A cryptic or mechanical rejection, particularly one which does not even advert to the specific contentions raised, falls foul of the principles of natural justice and renders the decision arbitrary and unsustainable in law. [Para 33]

■

In the instant case, where the appellant was not privy to the proceedings preceding his dismissal, any irregularity in the proceedings, if at all, can only be raised at the time of judicial proceedings. Keeping this in view, the Court has examined and reproduced the relevant notes from the original file in detail. [Para 34]

Arbitrariness in punishment

■

Even assuming, for the sake of argument, that the decision to take disciplinary action was otherwise proper, the punishment imposed upon the appellant is manifestly unreasonable. [Para 35]

■

What the Government missed is that the appellant was caught between the devil and the deep sea. Had he disobeyed the instruction of the Wg. Cmdr. by not removing the driver from the camp, he would risk being proceeded against for insubordination and indiscipline. On the other hand, the appellant has been punished for relocating the driver to desolate surroundings; this, he did while acting on the instructions of his superior. Though there is no definite material, it would be assumed that the corpse found was of the driver who, having been left to fend for himself, did not survive the harsh climate of the Thar; but , at the same time, there is also no definite material to suggest that such relocation was made by the appellant with any motive of harming him. Indeed, it is revealed from the records that to keep the driver away from the next day's anticipated visit of the AOC-i-C (so that the driver does not create any ruckus) was the real object intended to be achieved. It is also evident that the Wg. Cmdr. had given specific instructions, which later were even viewed as encouraging his subordinates to suppress the truth. Possibly, the appellant had no other option but to obey the orders of his superior. Non-consideration of these circumstances in course of the decision-making process being writ large together with the absence of reasoning in the order punishing the appellant, renders the same arbitrary and unsustainable in law sufficient to vitiate the entire proceedings against the appellant. [Para 36]

■

HEADNOTE: Section  33,  read with section  20,  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Conditions of service to remain unchanged under certain circumstances during pendency of proceedings - Whether proceedings before Tribunal are deemed to continue until date on which award becomes enforceable under Section 17A - Held, yes - Whether where award recording settlement, disposal or other closure has been made, legal pendency under Section 20(3) does not vanish because parties may feel that dispute has ended - Held, yes - Whether once it is held that proceedings were pending in eye of law on relevant date, compliance with Section 33(2)(b) became obligatory if employer intended to dismiss workman for misconduct not connected with dispute - Held, yes - Whether where termination of workman was effected during pendency of References and was in contravention of Section 33(2)(b), workman was to be reinstated in service to his original post, or to an equivalent post carrying same pay scale, status and service benefits, with continuity of service for all purposes including seniority, increments and retiral benefits, subject to applicable rules - Held, yes - Whether workman was to be entitled to full back wages from date of termination till commencement of grocery shop in 2016, fifty percent back wages for period from 2016 till closure of grocery shop during Covid period and full back wages thereafter till date of reinstatement - Held, yes [Paras 27, 28, 30, 39 and 40]

FACT: ■

A charge-sheet dated 12 October 2012 was issued to the workman alleging misconduct under various Standing Orders. A domestic enquiry was conducted, and on 31 July 2014 the Enquiry Officer held the workman guilty; the report was forwarded on 6 October 2014. The workman submitted an apology on 16 October 2014, and the recognised Union also requested a sympathetic view. An industrial dispute was pending between the company and the recognised Union, and during its subsistence an MoU dated 14 August 2014 was executed stating that 13 of 18 suspended workmen would be taken back subject to conditions at the management’s discretion, while enquiries against the remaining five, including the workman, would continue. After considering the apology and the Union’s request, management decided to dismiss the workman, and he was terminated on 17 October 2014.

■

It was pleaded that he remained unemployed for about two years, then started a grocery business, and that the business suffered losses and was closed on 28 November 2021, after which he remained without gainful employment.

■

The workman filed a complaint under Section 33A challenging the dismissal as arbitrary and illegal and sought reinstatement with back wages, also alleging discriminatory treatment vis-à-vis 13 similarly situated workmen who were given minor punishment. By order dated 27 September 2019 on preliminary issues, the Tribunal held the domestic enquiry fair and proper and the findings not perverse.

■

By final Award dated 18 January 2024, the Tribunal declined reinstatement with back wages and awarded compensation of Rs. 7 lakhs, while recording that the termination occurred during pendency of References and thus amounted to breach of Section 33(2)(b).

■

On writ petitions before the High Court.

HELD: ■

Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is enacted as a provision of protection, made by Legislature with intention to preserve industrial peace during time when conciliation proceedings or adjudication proceedings are pending before competent authority. The object behind such provision is that when dispute between employer and workmen has reached legal forum, atmosphere between parties remains strained. At such stage, if employer is permitted to alter service conditions against workers, then pending proceedings may get influenced by pressure. Therefore, law intervenes and places temporary restraint upon employer's powers. In that sense, Section 33 is a statutory device for maintaining fairness. It keeps pending proceedings free from coercion. [Para 23]

■

Sub-section (1) of Section 33 deals with matters which are connected with pending industrial dispute. In such matters, Act requires prior permission in writing from authority before whom proceeding is pending. This shows that where subject matter of proposed action touches the dispute under consideration, employer cannot act and then justify later. Sub-section (2), however, addresses another category, namely matters not connected with pending dispute. There Act gives wider liberty to employer to proceed according to standing orders or contractual terms. Yet even there, if employer proposes discharge or dismissal of workman concerned in dispute, proviso imposes two mandatory pre-conditions. One month wages must be paid, and application for approval must be made before competent authority. Hence, even where misconduct is outside dispute, disciplinary power is not uncontrolled. [Para 24]

■

paragraphs were duly considered and relied upon by the Division Bench while passing the impugned order, on the basis of which it was held that the disciplinary action against the appellant were not time-barred. The Court quite agrees with this part of the impugned order. [Para 22]

■

However, significantly, another crucial aspect of the very same decision - one that squarely operates against the armed forces - appears to have escaped the attention of the Division Bench. [Para 23]

■ In Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra), while examining sections 19 and 125 of the Army Act and Rule 14 of the Army Rules, which are pari materia sections 19 and 124 of the AF Act and Rule 6 of the 1969 Rules, respectively, this Court observed that where the commanding officer, exercising discretion vested in him to choose between a trial by a criminal court and a court-martial, opts for trial before a criminal court, an acquittal of the accused by such court brings finality to the matter. In such circumstances, the initiation or continuation of disciplinary action would not be sustainable. [Para 24]

■

Though the law laid down in Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra) is on consideration of the provisions of the Army Act and the Army Rules, there is no reason why it would not squarely apply to a case covered by pari materia provisions of the AF Act and the AF Rules. [Para 25]

■

True though, as per Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra), initiation of administrative proceedings is barred when an accused is 'acquitted'; however, the Court finds no reason for the ratio of the decision to not apply in a case where the accused is 'discharged' (which stands on a better footing than acquittal, as discussed supra). Once the appellant has been discharged by the criminal court, that should mark the end of the matter. [Para 26]

■

Thus, the Air Force upon electing to have the alleged offence tried by the criminal court, it is clear (in view of the discussion above) that they then cannot fall back on either a court martial or any disciplinary action. Once the road is chosen, the traveller must walk it to the end. [Para 27]

■

Initiation of administrative proceedings for disciplinary action against the appellant is unhesitatingly held to be bad in law and non-est. [Para 28]

■

This reason alone is sufficient to allow the present appeal. However, the decision is not proposed to rest on this sole reason; the discussion is taken forward as to why, independent of the aforesaid discussion, the disciplinary action is also otherwise considered to be flawed. It is solely for the reason that the decision in Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra) is subsequent to the appellant's dismissal from service and the Court wishes to test whether, even in view of the law prevailing prior thereto, disciplinary action which had been taken was justified on facts and in the circumstances. [Para 29]

Reasons given in proceeding note dated 5-6-1992

■

The reasoning given in the proceeding note dated 5-6-1992 has been noted above. From the same, there is absolutely no discussion on the merits of the case. [Para 30]

■

What is found is that there was sufficient 'morally convincing evidence' against the appellant. Such an expression, vague and indeterminate in nature, falls far short of the standard required for recording findings in disciplinary proceedings. It neither discloses the material relied upon nor indicates the process of reasoning by which the authority arrived at its conclusion. [Para 31]

■

Further, as noted above at paragraph 2(l), the appellant, in his reply to the show cause notice, had raised various contentions which required due consideration by the competent authority. However, it is a matter of surprise that there is a complete absence of any discussion on such contentions, particularly concerning the lack of evidence and the illegality of the proceedings before the Court of Inquiry. Although some discussion was undertaken regarding the permissibility of initiating disciplinary proceedings after the appellant's discharge by a criminal court, even that aspect, in the Court's view, remains doubtful. While adverting to the appellant's reply, the authority merely noted their dissatisfaction in respect thereof, at paragraph 15 of the proceeding note dated 5-6-1992. [Para 32]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 276C/277 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Offence and prosecution - Wilful attempt to evade tax, etc. - Petitioner sought to quash prosecution for offence under sections 276C and 277 on ground that departmental appeals were pending - Whether criminal prosecution cannot be quashed merely because proceedings under tax law were pending - Held, yes - Whether, however, petitioner was free to request Magistrate not to pronounce judgment till departmental proceedings were over - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner filed the instant petition to have the prosecution for offence under sections 276 and 277 quashed on the ground that departmental appeals were pending.

HELD: The Supreme Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal [1984] 149 ITR 696 had made it clear that no criminal prosecution can be quashed merely because proceedings under the tax laws are pending. The criminal court is to decide the case on the evidence before it, no doubt giving due weight to findings which could have been rendered by the departmental tribunals and, if need be and if a request is made, to postpone its decision by a short period.

The criminal proceedings, therefore, could not be quashed

If, after the conclusion of the trial and before the pronouncement of the judgment, the petitioner feels that he should make such a request to the trial court not to pronounce the judgment till the departmental proceedings were over, he was free to do so and the Magistrate would deal with that request according to law.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the Revenue.

HEADNOTE: Article 311 of the Constitution of India, read with Section 25 of the MSEDCL Employees Service Regulations - Dismissal, removal or reduction in rank of persons employed in civil capacities under the Union or a State - Appellant was appointed as Lower Division Clerk in 1985 and later promoted as Upper Division Clerk - She was suspended on 04.09.2006, charge-sheeted on 19.09.2006, and issued a show-cause notice on 25.04.2008 pursuant to a domestic enquiry - Domestic enquiry was later found not fair; in revision, Industrial Court remanded matter permitting employer to prove misconduct before Labour Court, which, by judgment dated 27.06.2017, held misconduct proved - Employer then issued dismissal order dated 12.07.2017 and directed suspension period to be treated as punishment - Appellant challenged dismissal in Complaint ULP No. 28 of 2017, contending that Executive Engineer lacked competence as she had been appointed by Superintending Engineer - Labour Court (08.08.2019) held that for a Pay Grade-III employee Executive Engineer was competent under Service Regulations and dismissed complaint; Industrial Court affirmed Labour court's order - High Court upheld these findings and review was dismissed - Whether since appellant was a Pay Grade-III employee, Executive Engineer was competent under applicable MSEDCL Employees Service Regulations to pass an order of punishment against appellant - Held, yes - Whether since appellant had not established that she held a civil post under Union or State, she was not entitled to protection as envisaged in Article 311 of Constitution - Held, yes - Whether thus, challenge to dismissal order on ground of lack of competence was to be rejected - Held, yes [Paras 31, 36 and 111.5]LABOUR LAWS: Where an employee charged with misconduct and dismissed by Executive Engineer challenged competence of disciplinary authority, it was found she was a Pay Grade-III employee under MSEDCL Service Regulations and Executive Engineer was competent to issue dismissal, and since she did not hold a civil post, Article 311 protection was not available, so challenge to dismissal for lack of competence was rejected  LABOUR LAWS: Where employer, after a defective domestic enquiry, was allowed to prove misconduct before Labour Court with employee participating, non-service of a fresh show-cause notice did not invalidate misconduct finding, but disciplinary authority was required to independently consider punishment and issue a fresh notice based on Labour Court’s findings, so dismissal order proceeding on previous defective notice was unsustainable, and matter required remittance for fresh consideration on punishment  LABOUR LAWS: Where appellant remained suspended for nearly eleven years without mandatory review after initial six-month period as per Regulation 88(a)(ii), continued suspension on strength of original order was invalid, and original reporting condition could be considered only for subsistence allowance entitlement during first six months, but for subsequent period appellant was entitled to subsistence allowance, as Regulations prohibit indefinite suspension without periodic review.  LABOUR LAWS: Where appellant was dismissed after proven misconduct and disciplinary authority treated entire prior suspension period as independent punishment in addition to dismissal, such dual penalties for same misconduct were impermissible since service rules did not authorize them, and subsistence allowance rights under relevant regulations remained protected, so imposition of second penalty was set aside and authority was directed to decide service and monetary consequences separately under governing rule  LABOUR LAWS : Where an employee with long service was dismissed for misconduct after proven charges, failure by disciplinary authority to consider gravity of offence, long service, past record, age, and absence of financial loss rendered dismissal grossly disproportionate, resulting in setting aside of dismissal while finding of misconduct was left undisturbed, and remand to authority for consideration of lesser punishment was warranted

headnotes.text: Domestic enquiry—Pendency of Criminal case or appeal—Employer need not wait for its decision—Enquiry may be proceeded with.
The principles of natural justice do not require that the employer must wait for the decision of a criminal case or an appeal before proceeding with a domestic enquiry. 1960(1) L.L.J. 520, Approved.

Held, that it was desirable that when the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry was being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending final disposal of the criminal case. In view of the accepted principles of law, in the event thepetitioner was convicted in the criminal trial, he would automatically be dismissed and/or removed from service, without taking recourse to formalities of departmental proceedings and, in the atternative, if the criminal case failed for want of evidence, by an order of discharge and not acquittal, in that event also, the departmental authorities would be entitled to proceed with the departmental enquiry, even after passing of such order of discharge by the criminal court. Therefore, during the pendency of the criminal trial, the employer would be restrained from proceeding further with the departmental enquiry against the petitioner.

It is desirable that if the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry is being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending the final disposal of the criminal case. It would be particularly appropriate to adopt such a course where the charge against the workman is of a grave character, because in such a case, it would be unfair to compel the workman to disclose the defence which he may take before the criminal court. But to say that domestic enquiries may be stayed pending criminal trial is very different from anything that if an employer proceeds with the domestic enquiry in spite of the fact that the criminal trial is pending, the enquiry for that reason alone is vitiated and the conclusion reached in such an enquiry is either bad in law or mala fide.

The decision to hold or not to hold a domestic enquiry, during the pendency of a criminal trial in respect of the same allegation, against a workman, is that of the employer to be taken at his discretion and if the employer decides to hold such enquiry, he cannot be prevented from doing so by the issue of a writ of prohibition.

Domestic enquiry—Criminal case and disciplinary proceedings based on same set of facts—Proceedings simultaneously conducted—Defence in the criminal case would be affected—Disciplinary proceedings to be stayed—On facts held that no justification to stay disciplinary proceedings.

Domestic enquiry—Alleged misconduct by employee—Simultaneous criminal proceedings and disciplinary action—Should not be permitted when both are based on same grounds—Disciplinary proceedings should be stayed—That criminal proceedings had not yet commenced or that accused employee had already put in his defence in disciplinary proceedings not relevant.

It is well-settled that a domestic enquiry and a criminal trial can proceed simultaneously and the decision in the criminal case would not materially affect the outcome of the domestic enquiry. The nature of both the proceedings and the test applied to reach a final conclusion in the matter, are entirely different. The charge-memo dated 17.8.1987 records charges of grave indiscipline, misconduct, dereliction of duty and involvement in the criminal case. Obviously, the charges in the domestic enquiry and before the criminal Court were not similar.

It is not necessary to examine the question as to whether the domestic enquiry was vitiated in law when simultaneous criminal proceedings were pending against the petitioner on the same charge and as such in consequence the order of dismissal becomes bad in law.

There is no legal bar for both criminal proceedings and disciplinary proceedings going on simultaneously against a Government servant. But, in certain situations, it may not be “desirable”, “advisable” or “appropriate” to proceed with the disciplinary enquiry when a criminal case is pending on identical charges. The staying of disciplinary proceedings is a matter to be determined taking into consideration all the facts and circumstances of the particular case and no hard and fast rule can be enunciated in that behalf. The only ground constituting a valid ground for staying the disciplinary proceedings is that the defence of the employee in the criminal case with charges of a grave nature and involving complicated questions of fact and law may not be prejudiced.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Criminal case pending on same matter—Employer can decide whether to hold domestic enquiry or not—Employer cannot be prevented by writ of prohibition from proceeding with enquiry.

It cannot be held as a general rule that whenever a person is acquitted by a criminal court, no further disciplinary action can be taken as the scope, purpose and object of the two enquiries are different and the standards of proof are also different and all depends upon the facts of each case. Where a criminal offence is committed, it is for the management to charge-sheet the employee and conduct a domestic enquiry and if the misconducts are proved, to punish the employee. The management is also free not to conduct the enquiry but to wait for the criminal court judgment.

It is now a settled legal principle that the domestic enquiry under the standing order and/or disciplinary proceeding under the service rule qua criminal proceeding on the identical fact situation, there is no embargo of simultaneous proceeding of both the two matters. It is also settled legal position now that the domestic enquiry and/or departmental proceeding relates to adjudication of the conduct of the workman and/or employee concerned upon being charged for misconduct on issue of factual matrix as mentioned in the article of charge, whereas in a criminal proceeding on the identical fact situation, determination and decision of the Court is to find the guilt of the person concerned in terms of the criminal offence either relating to Indian Penal Code or any other penal statute. Furthermore, it is a settled legal principle that proof of fact and the degree of such proof varies in respect of the two proceedings. In a criminal proceeding, charge is required to be proved without any doubt and strictly following the Evidence Act, whereas in a domestic enquiry and/or departmental proceed­ing preponderance of probability would suffice for determining the conduct of the delinquent. Even if in identical fact situation, it is now settled that even after acquittal of an accused from a criminal proceeding, domestic enquiry can be completed and punishment can be imposed. Hence, pendency of a criminal proceeding or adjudication of a criminal proceeding on the identical fact ipso facto will not destroy the findings of the domestic enquiry. Judgments of all these legal propositions are based on: Union of India v. Sardar Bahadur. 1972 Lab IC 627 Nelson Motis v. Union of Indiaand another. 1992 (65) FLR 853 (SC) State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Meena, 1996 (74) FLR 2550 (SC) and Depot Manager, Andhra State RoadTransportCorpn. v. Mohd.Yusuf Miya. 1997 (77) FLR 9 (SC)

There is no legal prohibition which prevents the holding of a domestic enquiry into an act of misconduct by a workman just because a criminal case is pending against the workman. The domestic enquiry in which the workman is answerable to his master and which may end in a departmental penalty is entirely different from the criminal proceeding in which the same person in respect of the same act is prosecuted for violation of the penal law of the land, which may end in conviction and sentence.

The law is well settled that the inquiry officer can come to a different conclusion than arrived at by a Criminal Court and that it is immaterial whether the charges were identical or the witnesses were the same, as long as the power exercised by the Criminal Court and the inquiry under the relevant law and the service law was distinct and separate. There is no bar for holding a disciplinary proceeding during the pendency of the trial though the basis may be one and the same. It is for the disciplinary authority to decide as to whether in a given case it should keep the domestic inquiry pending till the outcome of the criminal trial or not.

The petitioners have no legal right to insist that the enquiry proceedings against them are to be stayed till such time the Criminal Court concludes its trial. Possible prejudice to the interest of the employer also might have to be noticed, as it cannot be a one way traffic, and they are not expected to silently suffer in the bargain.
Domestic enquiry—Stay of domestic enquiry pending disposal of criminal case—Desirability—Inference of mala fide where enquiry not stayed

Where an employee is alleged to have committed an offence in assaulting an officer, in the proceedings taken by the employer taking disciplinary action against the employee, it is the duty of the employer to accept and treat as conclusive the finding of the Criminal Court which tried the offence. The employer, in such case, of course, need not wait for the decision before taking action; except in grave cases. In simple cases, he can proceed with his own domestic enquiry and decide on the disciplinary action to be taken against the employee. In a case of acquittal of the employee by the Criminal Court, the management must accept the same, otherwise his bona fides will be questioned. In such a case the Industrial Tribunal would be justified in interfering with the order of the employer terminating the services of the employee.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Domestic enquiry started by employer against employee—Simultaneously criminal proceedings initiated by CBI on same charges—Principles of law—Employer should stay domestic enquiry pending final disposal of criminal case

Where an employee is placed under suspension pending domestic enquiry into alleged misconduct in accordance with the conditions of his service, the fact that the employee is acquitted by a criminal court before the domestic enquiry ends will not result in the termination of the order of suspension ds the suspension was pending the domestic enquiry and not pending the criminal trial. Hence it cannot be contended that once he is acquitted in the criminal case, he should be reinstated in service. The suspension order will continue till the domestic enquiry is over unless it is terminated by another order of the authority concerned.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Criminal proceedings pending on same charges—Is no bar to domestic enquiry being held by employer—No right in employee to obtain temporary injunction against continuation of domestic enquiry.

Service Jurisprudence—Dismissal of petitioner-appellant from service—On basis of a Domestic Enquiry—On charges that a criminal case under section 376 of IPC was filed and pending against petitioner—And that petitioner has been sent to jail in connection with said criminal case—Held, charges framed against the appellant—Did not relate to dereliction of duty—And could only be tried and decided by Criminal Court on the basis of evidence adduced in Trial—Respondents-departmental authorities had misdirected themselves in making the charges a subject matter of Departmental Enquiry—And passing an order of dismissal from service—While the Criminal Trial was still pending—Impugned orders of the Departmental Authorities, as upheld by the Single Judge, set aside—Along with the order of dismissal from service—Appellant to be re-instated in service forthwith—Respondents given liberty to proceed against the appellant departmentally in case of his conviction by Criminal Court—Appeal allowed.

Domestic Inquiry—Delinquent subjected to criminal trial—Domestic inquiry also instituted simultaneously on same misconduct—Delinquent found guilty of misconduct alleged in domestic inquiry—Order of dismissal from service passed on basis of domestic inquiry proceedings—Delinquent subsequently acquitted in criminal case but appeal against order of acquittal pending—Delinquent not entitled to judgment/order of acquittal as the same is not final. [Paras 35 and 36]

It is well settled that criminal and disciplinary proceedings by the department are different and they are not inter-connected. Therefore, in this case it has been rightly held by the second respondent that the pendency of the criminal case was no ground to bar the domestic enquiry and also the Labour Court has clearly found that the Manager was entitled to hold the enquiry and award the punishment in the terms of Standing Order. Therefore, in the above circumstances it is the categoric contentions of the respondent that merely because the petitioner and the other two workmen were acquitted by this Court, it cannot be said the domestic enquiry was vitiated or the findings of the enquiry officer were not justified. Further in this case it is significant to note that the petitioners herein and other were charged for misconduct under Standing Orders 23.11 riotous and disorderly behaviour, 23.12 acts subversive of discipline, 23.25 causing danger to the security of the life of the co-worker whereas the criminal case was for the offence of murder. Therefore, I see every force in the various contentions raised by the respondents. In the above circumstances of these cases, I am of the clear view that the impugned award of the second respondent does not suffer from any error of law or jurisdiction calling for interference by this Court.

There is no legal prohibition for the holding of disciplinary proceedings just because a criminal case is pending. It is also well settled that a writ in the nature of prohibition preventing the holding of a domestic enquiry can issue only when there is total lack of jurisdiction and no such infirmity exists in this case.
Domestic Enquiry—And criminal trial—Can proceed simultaneously—Decision in criminal case would not materially affect the outcome of domestic enquiry. [Para 5]

The petitioner, an employee who had been charged by the employer, with alleged offences, was informed by the disciplinary authority that it had been decided to hold a “domestic enquiry” in respect of the charges against him and that he would be given an opportunity to inspect the documents on the basis of which the charge-sheet had been framed, when the proceedings would be started by the appropriate enquiring officer. In the meantime, the petitioner was arrested in July, 1987, by the officers of the Central Bureau of Investigation on the same charges under section 409, Indian Penal Code, read with sections 5(2) and 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. Subsequently, the petitioner was released on bail and on 21st September, 1987, while the proceedings before the CBI were going on, the disciplinary authority of the employer placed the petitioner “under suspension” with retrospective effect from 15th July, 1987, under section 12(1)(b) of UCO Bank Officer Employees’ (Discipline and Appeal) Regulations, 1976. On a writ petition filed by the petitioner challenging the continuance of departmental proceedings simultaneouly with the criminal trial :

The law as enunciated by the Supreme Court leaves no scope for doubt that all said and done, there is no bar for simultaneous proceedings being taken against the delinquent in the form of criminal action and also disciplinary proceedings unless the charges are extremely serious and grave requiring the judicial determination in preference to the verdict in the domestic inquiry proceedings. In the instant case, even though the criminal action and disciplinary proceedings are grounded upon the same sets of fact, in my view, there is no provision of law empowering the Court to stay the departmental proceedings merely because criminal prosecution is pending in the Criminal Court.

The departmental enquiry is to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of public service. It would, therefore, be expedient that the disciplinary proceedings are conducted and completed as expeditiously as possible. It is not, therefore, desirable to lay down any guidelines as inflexible rules in which the departmental proceedings may or any not be stayed pending trial in criminal case against the delinquent officer. Each case requires to be considered in the backdrop of its own facts and circumstances. There would be no bar to proceed simultaneously with departmental enquiry and trial of a criminal case unless the charge in the criminal trial is of grave nature involving complicated questions of fact and law.

Departmental Enquiry—Criminal Proceedings—Staying of departmental enquiry—Charge-sheet in domestic enquiry founded upon same facts on which a criminal case pending—Petitioner had not chosen to file any petition to stop department from proceeding with departmental enquiry—Petitioner did not file any petition for restraining employer to proceed in departmental enquiry on alleged ground—Not fit case where petitioner fulfills litmus test laid down by Supreme Court in case of Capt. M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd., 1999 (82) FLR 627 (SC) as requirement—No complicated questions of fact and law involved—Department not under obligation to stay domestic enquiry. [Para 12]

Departmental Proceedings—And criminal proceedings—Mere pendency of criminal proceedings—Does not automatically warrant stay of departmental proceedings—Superior Courts, while exercising their discretionary jurisdiction, must take into consideration whether the charges as also the evidence in both the proceedings are common—And whether any complicated question of law is involved in the matter—Court should also take into consideration whether prejudice will be caused to the delinquent employee in the criminal case if departmental proceedings are not stayed—Leading Apex Court judgments starting from the case of Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd. v. Kushal Bhan, AIR 1960 SC 806 referred—In facts of instant case, where respondents 1 to 4, employees of the appellant-Bank, apart from being charged for criminal offences under sections 341, 323, 324, 427, 307 and 506 (ii) of IPC, were also departmentally proceeded with misconduct on charges of highly unruly conduct within the premises of the Bank and causing damage to Bank’s property—In such facts of case, specially in view of the revocation of the suspension order against the respondents on their undertaking that they will co-operate in the departmental enquiry, High Court, held, was not justified in staying the departmental proceedings pending criminal trial—Impugned order of the High Court set aside—Appeal allowed with observations. [Paras 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 15, 16, 22, 27 and 28]

Held, that while there could be no legal bar for simultaneous proceedings being taken, yet, there may be cases where it would be appropriate to defer disciplinary proceedings awaiting disposal of the criminal case. In the latter class of cases it would be open to the delinquent employee to seek such an order of stay or injunction from the court. Whether, in the facts and circumstances of a particular case, there should or should not be such simultaneity of the proceedings would then receive judicial consideration and the court will decide in the given circumstances of a particular case as to whether the disciplinary proceedings should be interdicted, pending criminal trial. It is neither possible nor advisable to evolve a hard and fast, strait-jacket formula valid for all cases and of general application without regard to the peculiarities of the individual situation.

Domestic enquiry—Acquittal of employee by Court—Similar charges forming subject matter of domestic enquiry—Dismissal of employee from service as result of finding of guilt by enquiry officer—Binding effect—Labour Court erred in the holding that enquiry officer cannot come to different conclusion from one recorded by criminal Court—Domestic enquiry can be proceeded with despite acquittal order—Appeal allowed.

Mere pendency of a criminal case against the employee is not a bar to the initiation of disciplinary action against him and the answer to the question whether or not the disciplinary proceedings should remain stayed pending disposal of the criminal case would depend upon the facts of each case and in particular on whether the case involves complex questions of law and fact as make it desirable to await the result of the criminal case pending against the employee.

By the court : (i) Disciplinary enquiry cannot be, and should not be, delayed unduly. If a criminal case is unduly delayed that may itself be a good ground for going ahead with the disciplinary enquiry even when the disciplinary proceedings are held over at an earlier stage. The interests of administration and good Government demand that these proceedings are concluded expeditiously. The interests of administration demand that undesirable elements are thrown out and any charge of misdemeanour is enquired into promptly. The disciplinary proceedings are meant not really to punish the guilty but to keep the administrative machinery unsullied by getting rid of bad elements. The interest of the delinquent officer also lies in a prompt conclusion of the disciplinary proceedings. If he is not guilty of the charges, his honour should be vindicated at the earliest possible moment and, if he is guilty, he should be dealt with promptly according to law. It is not also in the interest of administration that persons accused of serious misdemeanour should be continued in office indefinitely, i.e., for long periods awaiting the result of criminal proceedings. Stay of disciplinary proceedings cannot be, and should not be, a matter of course. All the relevant facts, for and against, should be weighed and a decision taken. The possibilities that not all disciplinary proceedings are based on true charges or that charges might be levelled for oblique reasons do not detract from the desirability of early conclusion of disciplinary proceedings. Delay in such cases really works against the employee.

Domestic enquiry—Commencement of criminal proceedings on same set of facts—Whether both proceedings can be continued simultaneously—Depends on facts of each case though there is no legal bar—No hard and fast rule can be laid down.

Government servant—Disciplinary proceedings—Disciplinary enquiry and criminal proceedings going on simultaneously—Stay of disciplinary enquiry—To be made only where criminal charges are of grave nature and case involves complicated questions of fact and law—Stay granted at one stage may have to be reconsidered where criminal proceedings unduly delayed—Objects of criminal proceedings and disciplinary proceedings are different—Necessity for expeditious conclusion of disciplinary enquiry.

Normally, a court, in a petition under article 226 of the Constitution of India, will not interfere with a charge-memo issued to an employee or an order of ad interim suspension. In such cases the only relief which could be granted to the employee would be to direct the employer to hold up the departmental enquiry till the criminal proceedings are over, where the employee has been charged on the same set of charges before the criminal court. Whether, in the facts and circumstances of a particular case, there should or should not be such simultaneity of proceedings would have to receive judicial consideration and the court will decide in the given circumstances of a particular case as to whether the disciplinary proceedings should be interdicted.

Sometimes both the criminal trial and departmental enquiry go on. There is no bar against that. But, if a departmental enquiry is withheld till the decision of the criminal trial, then that decision should be taken into account and cannot be overridden by continuing the departmental enquiry thereafter on the identical charges. Furthermore, if a departmental enquiry is not at all launched but a criminal case is instituted and that ends in acquittal of the accused, it will not be proper for the department again to proceed on the same charges.

Disciplinary proceedings—Stay pending disposal of prosecution—Whether to be granted—Factors to be considered—Prejudice to employee—Drain on employer’s resources by payment of subsistence allowance—Witnesses necessary for enquiry may not be available—On facts, stay of disciplinary proceedings granted with liberty to seek expeditious disposal of prosecution.

In the instant case it was held that the Industrial Tribunal was in error when it characterised the result of the domestic enquiry as mala fide partly because the enquiry was not stayed pending the criminal proceedings against the concerned workman.

A writ in the nature of prohibition preventing the holding of a domestic enquiry by an employer into alleged acts of misconduct by a workman can be issued only if there was total lack of jurisdiction in the authority holding the enquiry. No such writ can be issued preventing an authority having jurisdiction to hold the enquiry, even if criminal proceedings are pending in respect of the same matter.

Held, reversing the decision of the High Court, that the criminal proceedings were launched for an offence of or violation of a duty which the offender owed to the society for the breach of which law had provided that the offender shall make satisfaction to the public. The departmental enquiry was to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of public service. It was, therefore, expedient that the disciplinary proceedings were conducted as expeditiously as possible. There would be no bar to proceeding simultaneously with the departmental enquiry and the trial of the criminal case unless the charge in the criminal trial was of a grave nature involving complicated questions of fact and law. When a trial for a criminal offence was conducted it should be in accordance with proof of the offence as per the evidence defined under the Evidence Act. Converse is the case of departmental enquiry : the enquiry in departmental proceedings related to conduct orbreach of duty of the delinquent officer to punish him for his misconduct defined under the relevant statutory rules or law. The strict proof or applicability of the Evidence Act stood excluded. The enquiry in the departmental proceedings related to the conduct of the delinquent officer and proof in that behalf was not as high as in an offence in a criminal charge. Invariably the departmental enquiry had to be conducted expeditiously so as to effectuate efficiency in public administration and the criminal trial would take its own course. What was required to be seen in departmental enquiry was whether the departmental enquiry would seriously prejudice the delinquent in his defence at the trial in the criminal case. This was always a question of fact to be considered in each case depending on its own facts and circumstances. Since the charge, in this case, was failure to anticipate the accident and prevent it and this had nothing to do with the culpability of the offence under section 304-A and 338 of the Indian Penal Code, the High Court was not right in staying the departmental proceedings.

Disciplinary Proceedings—Permanent injunction against the employer and the Enquiry Officer restraining them from proceeding with the enquiry—Disciplinary proceedings initiated by the appellant company against respondent-employees for their alleged misconduct—Matter reported to police also and criminal case registered against the employees under sections 143, 147, 323, 324, 356, 427, 504, 506 and 114/149 I.P.C.—Offences alleged not ordinary—But case does not involve complicated questions of law and fact—Defence of respondents already disclosed—Disciplinary proceedings cannot remain stayed for an indefinitely long period—Number of accused large—All the three Courts exercised their discretion in favour of staying ongoing disciplinary proceedings—Not proper to vacate the stay straight away—Court dealing with the criminal charges against the respondents directed to conclude the trial as early as possible and in any case within one year. [Paras 14 and 15]

(ii) That the authorities need not hold a detailed departmental enquiry to find whether the employee was guilty of the charge or not or whether he was a fit person to be Continued in service or not. Once a person is convicted by a criminal court, the person concerned loses his right to the job and can be terminated without detailed domestic enquiry proceedings. The Tribunal was wrong in refusing approval to the dismissal on the ground that appeals against the conviction were pending before the Sessions Judge.

It would, therefore, be expedient that the disciplinary proceedings are conducted and completed as expeditiously as possible. It is not, therefore, desirable to lay down any guidelines as inflexible rules in which the departmental proceedings may or may not be stayed pending trial in criminal case against the delinquent officer. Each case requires to be considered in the backdrop of its own facts and circumstances. There would be no bar to proceed simultaneously with departmental enquiry and trial of a criminal case unless the charge in the criminal trial is of grave nature involving complicated questions of fact and law. Offence generally implies infringement of public duty, as distinguished from mere private rights punishable under criminal law. When trial for criminal offence is conducted it should be in accordance with proof of the offence as per the evidence defined under the provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (in short the ‘Evidence Act’). Converse is the case of departmental enquiry. The enquiry in a departmental proceedings relates to conduct or breach of duty of the delinquent officer to punish him for his misconduct defined under the relevant statutory rules or law. That the strict standard of proof or applicability of the Evidence Act stands excluded is a settled legal position. Under these circumstances, what is required to be seen is whether the departmental enquiry would seriously prejudice the delinquent in his defence at the trial in a criminal case. It is always a question of fact to be considered in each case depending on its own facts and circumstances.

Departmental Proceedings—And criminal trial—Not necessary to stay departmental enquiry on account of pendency of criminal trial relating to the same incident involving the delinquent—Departmental enquiry to be stayed only if it would seriously prejudice the defence of the delinquent in his criminal trial. [Paras 1 to 6]

(b) If the criminal case against the delinquent em­ployee is of a grave nature which involves complicated questions of law and fact, then it would be desirable to stay the departmental proceedings till the conclusion of the criminal case.

Disciplinary Proceedings and Criminal Trial—Whether disciplinary proceedings can be stayed pending conclusion of the Trial—No legal bar for conducting of the disciplinary proceedings and a criminal Trial simultaneously—Stay of disciplinary proceeding an advisable course in cases where criminal charge against the employee is grave and continuance of disciplinary proceedings is likely to prejudice his defence before the Criminal Court—Gravity of charge not enough to determine the question unless charge involves complicated questions of law and fact. [Para 13]

It is held by the Supreme Court in Noida Entrepreneurs Association v. Noida and others, 2007 (112) FLR 1139 (SC) that mere acquittal in criminal case would not affect outcome of the enquiry proceeding which is based on the evidence recorded during the domestic enquiry.

facts.text: 'P', a chartered accountants firm, was statutory auditor of 'Satyam' and petitioner was working with 'P'. On 7-1-2009, the then Chairman of Satyam, 'R' informed the board of directors of Satyam of the systematic fudging of accounts of the said company by him. This disclosure, which was widely publicized, was acted upon as information against the petitioner under section 21. The CID, Hyderabad registered a criminal case under section 120B, read with sections 406, 420, 467, 471 and 477A IPC against the Chairman and directors of Satyam and other accused persons, including the petitioner. The petitioner was arrested by the police. Thereafter, the case was transferred to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) for investigation, and R.C. was registered against the petitioner and eight others by the CBI, Hyderabad. The Director (Discipline) acted on the information which came to him. The Director (Discipline) arrived at a prima facie opinion, dated 17-9-2009 on the occurrence of alleged misconduct falling under the Second Schedule to the Act against the petitioner. Consequently, the Council of the ICAI constituted a Disciplinary Committee in terms of section 21B. The procedure to be adopted by the Disciplinary Committee is prescribed in rule 18 of the Chartered Accountants (Procedure of Investigations of Professional and Other Misconduct and Conduct of Cases) Rules, 2007. The Disciplinary Committee after considering the prima facie opinion dated 17-9-2009, decided to proceed further in the matter under Chapter V of the Rules. The respondent sent a letter to the petitioner, calling upon him to submit his written statement along with supporting documents, if any, and a list of witnesses, if any, that the petitioner might desire to examine under rule 18(4) of the Rules. The petitioner did not respond to the said communication, presumably because he was still behind bars, and was granted bail by the Supreme Court only on 4-2-2010. After the petitioner was released on bail, as aforesaid, he was served with a letter, directing him to appear before the Disciplinary Committee. The petitioner preferred a writ petition before the Court against the holding of the disciplinary enquiry, primarily on the ground that on the same subject-matter the petitioner could not be simultaneously proceeded with in criminal proceedings and in disciplinary proceedings. He claimed that the same would be violative of his fundamental rights under the Constitution of India. The Court vide order dated 16-4-2010 stayed the aforesaid disciplinary proceedings. During the pendency of the aforesaid writ petition, the Supreme Court directed that the trial in the criminal proceedings be conducted on a day-to-day basis. The petitioner's writ petition was eventually dismissed by the Single judge later on, the respondent issued a notice to the petitioner requiring him to appear before the Disciplinary Committee. In the meantime, the petitioner preferred a Letters Patent Appeal. The Division Bench issued notice on the said appeal to the respondent, and directed the petitioner to appear before the Disciplinary Committee, and to accept, or deny the charges. The petitioner appeared before the Disciplinary Committee at Hyderabad, and denied the charges read out by the Disciplinary Committee. Subsequently, the petitioners LPA was dismissed. However, the Division Bench directed that the respondent would proceed with the disciplinary enquiry keeping in view the convenience of the petitioner and affording him adequate opportunity to put forth his case. The petitioner was again issued notice by the respondent requiring him to appear before the Disciplinary Committee. The petitioner, vide letter dated 11-6-2011, sought an adjournment on the ground that the criminal trial was at a crucial stage and he was facing genuine difficulty in appearing before the Disciplinary Committee, as he required adequate time and opportunity to face the enquiry. The request for adjournment was accepted by the respondent. The petitioner sought repeated deferment of the proceedings finally on 31-7-2011 the Disciplinary Committee rejected petitioner's request for deferment and recorded the deposition of one witness, 'K' D.I.G., CBI who was produced to prove the charges against the petitioner. The petitioner's representative was thereafter given the opportunity to cross-examine the said witness. However, he refused to do so. The Supreme Court disposed of the petitioner's Special Leave Petition, directing the respondent-Institute to commence the disciplinary proceedings. The respondent issued notice requiring the petitioner to appear before the Disciplinary Committee. The petitioner sent his preliminary reply to the respondent. The petitioner also sought the documents which formed part of the SEBI investigation report, the main CBI chargesheet and the two supplementary charge sheets, relied upon by the Director (Discipline) for forming the prima facie opinion. The respondent rejected petitioner's request for cross examination as it considered that adequate opportunities had been given to the petitioner, which were not availed of by him

■

The respondent, a typist-cum-clerk of the petitioner–bank, faced disciplinary proceedings. The inquiry officer, after conducting a domestic inquiry, held that the charges were proved, and the bank discharged the respondent from service with effect from 16.06.2004.

■

The industrial dispute was referred to the Central Government Industrial Tribunal-cum-Labour Court to adjudicate the legality and justification of the discharge. The Tribunal held that the domestic inquiry was fair, just and proper and recorded that the charges stood proved on the evidence, including the respondent’s involvement in a transaction in which his wife and brother were involved. Despite these findings, it interfered with the punishment and directed the bank to pay 80% of the back wages from 16.06.2004 till the respondent attained the age of superannuation, noting inter alia the High Court’s modification of punishment in the connected Manager’s matter and the respondent’s acquittal in a criminal case.

■

On writ petition before the High Court.

On the basis of a complaint filed by the ITO, a case was instituted against the petitioner and other partners of a firm on the allegations that they wilfully attempted to evade payment of tax, penalty or interest, chargeable or imposable under the Act, by suppressing and/or concealing their assessable income, thereby rendering them liable to be prosecuted under section 276C, and that the accused persons made false statements during verification by knowingly delivering statements and/or accounts which were false, thereby committing an offence under section 277. After appearance in Court the accused persons filed an application to defer hearing of the case till disposal of the appeal filed before the Commissioner (Appeals). The prayer was rejected on the ground that pendency of the appeal could not stand as a bar to the criminal court’s proceeding in the matter and to launching prosecution, and there was no necessary to stay the proceeding.

On writ :

■

The petitioner, an ex-lekhpal (revenue staff), was proceeded against departmentally on the allegation that he accepted a bribe of Rs. 500 from a village chak holder. A criminal case under the Prevention of Corruption Act was also registered on the same allegation, in which he was later acquitted by the Special Judge. In his written explanation, he stated that the complainant bore enmity with him owing to his official action under Section 122-B (U.P.Z.A. & L.R. Act) concerning a chak road, and that the complainant attempted to thrust Rs. 500 into his pocket/hand despite his refusal; the currency fell on the ground, was picked up by another person who again tried to put it in his hand; he refused, and vigilance personnel then took him to the police station. In the oral enquiry he consistently denied taking any money.

■

The enquiry officer held the charge proved, treating the petitioner’s explanation as an admission that the complainant had put Rs. 500 in his pocket, and the disciplinary authority imposed the major penalty of dismissal from service.

■

On departmental appeal, the appellate authority upheld the dismissal, observing that the petitioner’s criminal acquittal resulted because the main witnesses turned hostile and was a case of benefit of doubt, and further noting that in departmental proceedings the standard is preponderance of probabilities.

■

On writ petition before the High Court.

’T’, an employee of the petitioner-company, failed to vacate the company’s flat after retirement, in spite of demand, and a complaint was filed against him under section 630. While the criminal proceedings were in progress, the company also filed a civil suit for recovery of possession of the flat for damages. ’T’ filed an application before the Trial Court for staying the criminal proceedings on the ground of the pendency of the civil suit. When this was rejected, he filed a revisional application. The Sessions Judge ordered that the judgment in the case under section 630 should not be delivered till the disposal of the civil suit.

On revision petition :

The appellant, a chartered accountant and a member of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), was a partner of PW, a firm of Chartered Accountants registered with ICAI. In the year 2000, the firm was appointed as the statutory auditors of SCSL. The statutory audits of SCSL for the years 2001 to March, 2007 were conducted and the reports were signed by the appellant. Subsequently, ‘R’ the Chairman of SCSL, in a communication sent to the Board of Directors, disclosed that the balance sheet of SCSL carried inflated (non-existent) cash and bank balances and the liability was understated. The ICAI corresponded with PW, referring to the letters of ‘R’ the Chairman of SCSL, that the said firm had failed to carry out necessary checks which were required while undertaking the audit of the financial statements and certifying the quarterly results of the company. The ICAI alleged that the firm had violated the accounting principles while auditing and certifying the accounts/quarterly results of SCSL for the aforementioned years and quarters and did not give a true and fair view of the accounts and further did not exercise due diligence and were negligent in their professional duties as statutory auditors. The ICAI treated the newspaper report as information within the meaning of section 21(2) of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 [as amended by the Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2006. Thus, PW was called upon to disclose the name or names of the member or members who was/were answerable to the allegation/s and send a copy of the aforesaid information letter along with its enclosures to the said member/members.
