IAC4, they are mutually exclusive remedies and under the 1961 Act, both the proceedings are available, though under the 1922 Act, penalty proceedings would have been a bar on the launching of a prosecution. This does not make a difference to the distinction drawn. These are concurrent remedies and the invocation of one does not necessarily dispense with, obviate or oust the other. The imposition of penalties under the Act by the authorities, and the conviction in a Court of law for an offence created by the Act, do not attract the principle of double jeopardy either. Ordinarily, the decision to prosecute an assessee or a person, who may be deemed to be an assessee under the various penal provisions of the Act, is a decision taken by the officer empowered to initiate action on being satisfied on the objective material before him that there is a case for prosecution without judicial determination under the Act, as to taxability, quantification of liability, or liability to any penalty, etc.

The view that the proceedings entailing penalty under the Income-tax Act are to be equated to the prosecution attracting the punishments is not correct as no conviction for any offence is involved in the imposition of penalty. From a reading of the provision of article 20(1) of the Constitution, it is evident that the first limit and the second limit are interlinked and have to be read together, and that while the first limit refers to a conviction for an offence, the second limit refers to the punishment that has to be inflicted with regard to an offence. Penalty is, on the other hand, levied for an act or omission of the assessee, not because it is an offence but because it is an attempt at evasion in the payment of the tax. In such a situation, article 20(1) of the Constitution is not attracted.1

There are a large number of cases where criminal law and civil law can run side by side. The object of the criminal law is to punish an offender who commits an offence against a person, property or the State for which the accused, on proof of the offence, is deprived of his liberty and in some cases even his life. This does not, however, affect the civil remedies at all for suing the wrongdoer in cases like arson, accident, etc. It is an anathema to suppose that when a civil remedy is available, criminal prosecution is completely barred. The two types of actions are quite different in content, scope and import.2

Article 20 and constitutional validity of criminal prosecution and levy of penalty for the same offence

3.8 Article 20 of the Constitution states that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of commission of the offence, and no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

The Supreme Court in Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay1 observed:

“Article 20(2) incorporates within its scope the plea of ‘autrefois convict’ as known to the British Jurisprudence or the plea of double jeopardy as known to the American Constitution, but circumscribes it by providing that there should be not only a prosecution but also a punishment in the first instance in order to operate as a bar to a second prosecution and punishment for the same offence.” (p. 325)

Article 20(2) contemplates proceedings of criminal nature and the prosecution in this context means an initiation of proceedings of criminal nature. The first part of article 20(1) prohibits a conviction while the second part deals with penalty that may be inflicted on conviction. The word ‘penalty’ has been used to denote the sentence or punishment. Like clause (2), clause (1) also contemplates proceedings of criminal nature.

A criminal proceeding may be defined as one, which if carried to its conclusion, may result in imposition of sentence such as death, imprisonment, fine or forfeiture of property. It also includes proceedings in which, in the larger interests of the State, orders to prevent apprehended breach of the peace, orders to bind down persons who are a danger to the maintenance of peace and orders aimed at preventing vagrancy are contemplated to be passed.

For instance, the imposition of penalty under the Income-tax Act is neither a prosecution nor a punishment for any offence and, therefore, the accused is not exposed to any double jeopardy. The proceedings, for the imposition of penalty, taken against an assessee under Income-tax Act are distinct from the criminal complaints filed against him. They can, therefore, continue simultaneously. The offences punishable under section 277 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961, and section 193 of the Indian Penal Code may be somewhat similar, but they are not identical.1 There is no legal bar on the prosecution of the accused for both these offences in view of section 26 of the General Clauses Act.

ITO cannot make use of statements recorded under FEMA - Income-tax proceedings are entirely different from and dissimilar to proceedings under FEMA. Therefore, ITO cannot make use of statements recorded by Enforcement Directorate (ED) for prosecuting deponents of those statements in a separate and independent proceeding under 1961 Act on the ground that deponents had retracted their statements given before ED [K. T. M. S. Mohammed v. UOI [1992] 65 Taxman 130 (SC)].

Judicial proceeding and Civil Court - For the purpose of investigation and enquiry, TRO is conferred with powers of a Civil Court and by virtue of their office and experience, TRO is an officer with trained judicial mind and, therefore, he can conduct enquiry as that of judicial proceedings [G. V. Films Ltd. v. S. Priyadarshan [2007] 163 Taxman 74 (Mad.)].

False evidence - Mere suppression of circumstances which would entitle assessee to an exemption under the 1961 Act will not amount to 'false evidence' within the meaning of section 193 of the IPC. Thus, assessee could not be convicted of an offence u/s 193 qua false statement made in verification clause of return of income [S. Harnam Singh Suri v. CBDT [1983] 15 Taxman 52 (Delhi)].

Cognizable offence - Section 136 makes a proceeding before the ITO a proceeding also u/s 228 of the Indian Penal Code and, thus, an interruption in his proceedings or an insult to him has become punishable under that section. It could not have been intended by the Legislature in enacting this provision that whereas an insult made to a public servant acting judicially, or interruption caused in his proceedings, would normally be cognizable only on the complaint of the public servant himself, the same offence if committed in respect of the proceedings before the ITO should be cognizable on the complaint of a private party. Thus, where the allegation was that a third party made a false statement on oath during the assessment proceedings of an assessee, the complaint against the offence would be cognizable only if it was filed by the ITO and not by the assessee [Lalji Haridas v. State of Maharashtra [1964] 52 ITR 423 (SC)].

Cross-examination - Though the proceedings before the income-tax authorities are not governed by the strict rules of evidence, before the income-tax authorities could rely upon a piece of evidence, they were bound to produce it before the assessee so that the assessee could controvert the statements contained in it by asking for an opportunity for cross-examination of the person with reference to the statements made by him [Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 4 Taxman 29 (SC)].

Technically, it 'may' be transferred. However, the discretion is to be exercised judicially by Board or authorised authority and should not be exercised arbitrarily. It is in no one's interest that a matter fully heard be transferred as it will involve the rigours of rehearing the case by JCIT (Appeals). However, if too much time has elapsed after completing the hearings and the matter is still pending for decision, it may be in assessee's interests that the matter be transferred to JCIT (Appeals) and decided expeditiously after a rehearing by JCIT (Appeals). The Supreme Court was conscious of possible prejudice to parties where Court reserves its judgment and takes a long time to pronounce the judgment without rehearing.

In R.C. Sharma v. It is not unlikely that some points which the litigant considers important may have escaped notice. But, what is more important is that litigants must have complete confidence in the results of litigation. This confidence tends to be shaken if there is an excessive delay between hearing of arguments and delivery of judgments."

(a)

Where a judgment is not pronounced within three months from the date of reserving judgment, any of the parties in the case is permitted to file an application in the High Court with prayer for early judgment. Such application, as and when filed, shall be listed before the Bench concerned within two days, excluding the intervening holidays.

(b)

If the judgment, for any reason, is not pronounced within a period of six months, any of the parties of the said list shall be entitled to move an application before the Chief Justice of the High Court with a prayer to withdraw the said case and to make it over to any other Bench for fresh arguments. It is open to the Chief Justice to grant the said prayer or to pass any other order as he deems fit in the circumstances.

The discretion to receive additional evidence is to be exercised only when any point is required to be cleared up in the interests of justice. This power given to the Tribunal has to be exercised cautiously and sparingly in order to advance the interests of justice. Rule 29 is not intended to allow an assessee who has been unsuccessful throughout to patch up the weak parts of his case or to fill up omissions [A. K. Babu Khan v. CWT[1976] 102 Taxman 757 (AP)].

5.14

Case Studies

1. The Company has received a Show Cause Notice during the year 2022-23 from Initiating Officer for holding a benami property and alleging that company is only a shell company and its properties are held by it as benamidar for the real person controlling the company who has channeled his ill gotten funds into the company as share capital through a network of benami shell companies. The alleged benami properties were acquired prior to 25-10-2016. The Company contends that auditor need not report on this as company has sent reply with all details and, in view of Supreme Court judgment in Ganapati Dealcom, the IO will drop proceedings. Proceedings have not been dropped at the time of audit reporting. Company also contends that ARI disclosures are not required in view of the Supreme Court decision. How will you as auditor deal with this?

Auditor is not to sit in judgment on the merits of the case. For auditor, all that matters is that the proceedings are initiated during the year and are pending as of the date of audit report. Therefore, he needs to report the fact of initiation and pendency of the same. Company may disclose its opinion on the merits of the case in notes to financial statements while giving required ARI disclosures.

2. If in Case Study 1, what if, prior to date of audit report, the proceedings are dropped by IO after considering the reply of the Company ?

In that case also, auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings were initiated and subsequently dropped. The wordings in clause 3(i)(e) are "proceedings have been initiated or are pending against the company". Therefore, in view of the word "or" separating the words "initiated" and "are pending", auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings have been initiated during year and dropped after the year-end but prior to date of audit reporting.

3. What if show cause notice dated 1st April 2023 from Initiating Officer is received on 5th April 2023 and audit report is being signed on 30th April 2023? Will auditor have to report it in audit report for FY 2022-23?

No. Auditor will not report this in Audit report for the year under audit i.e. FY 2022-23. Auditor will report it in his report for FY 2023-24.

Audit report for the year is on events during the year. Post-balance sheet date developments in respect of such events which have occurred during the year will be considered. It is one thing that Show Cause Notice is issued during the year and there are further developments after the year-end in the matter which will have to be considered.

It is entirely a different matter that Show Cause Notice is issued and received after the year-end which has nothing to do with conditions existing as at the Balance sheet date. Auditor will not consider such post-balance sheet events in report for the year under audit.

33.5

Compounding of offences

Provisions of compounding have been introduced in customs law.

Section 137(3) of Customs Act provides that any offence under the Act can be compounded by Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioner of Customs. Such compounding can be done either before or after the institution of prosecution. Central Government is authorised to make Rules to provide for amount to be paid for compounding.

In Vinod Kumar Agarwal v. UOI (2008) 223 ELT 19 (Bom HC DB), it was held that compounding under Customs Act cannot result in discharge of offences under other Acts like IPC.

Awareness about provision of compounding should be enhances. People should be encouraged to compound offense. Disposal should be within six months - MF(DR) circular No. 15/2022-Cus dated 23-8-2022.

What is compounding ? - Fine and imprisonment can be imposed only by competent criminal Court. However, instead of going to Court, the offender may agree to pay composition amount. Order for paying composition money can be made by quasi-judicial authorities. This is called 'compounding of offences'.

'Compounding' is essentially a compromise arrangement between administrator of the enactment and person committing an offence. Compounding crime consists of receipt of some consideration (termed as compounding fees) in return for an agreement not to prosecute one who has committed an offence - Reliance Industries, In re - (1997) 24 CLA 214 (CLB).

'Compounding' means that the accused and the complainant have come to terms and the dispute between the parties has been settled amicably or adjusted by agreement and the complainant agrees not to prosecute the accused. If the case is pending, the accused and the complainant then make a joint application to the Court that the parties have come to terms and the case may not be proceeded with.

Thus, in compounding, there is a compromise or agreement, while in case of imposition of fine under provisions of an Act, there is no agreement as such. Section 320 of Criminal Procedure Code permits compounding of various offences under Indian Penal Code.

Such compounding can be done either before or after institution of prosecution. After payment of such composition amount, prosecution will not be launched, or if it was launched, it will be withdrawn.

Full and bona fide disclosure required for compounding of offence - In UOI v. Anil Chanana (2008) 4 SCC 175 = 222 ELT 481 (SC), it was held that compounding of offences is based on the principle of disclosure. If there are demonstrable contradictions or inconsistencies or incompleteness, application for compounding cannot be entertained. Applicant cannot hoodwink the authority. Applicant has to be a one-time evader. He has to make a clean breast of his affairs. Otherwise, offence should not be compounded. Compounding should be allowed only in case of doubtful benefit to the Revenue and to prevent needlessly proliferating litigation and holding up of collection.

Compounding means acquittal - As per section 320 of CrPC, composition will have the effect of acquittal of accused. It is not mere discharge. Thus, if offence is compounded, the person is deemed to be acquitted, and hence does not become ineligible to be appointed as a director [confirmed in circular No. 5/23 dated 28-4-1993 of Department of Company Affairs].

No penalty or prosecution after compounding - In P P Varkey v. STO (1999) 114 STC 251 (Ker HC), it was held that once offence is compounded, penalty or prosecution proceedings cannot be taken for same offence. In S Viswanathan v. State of Kerala (1999) 113 STC 182 (Ker HC DB), it was held that once the matter is compounded, neither department nor assessee can challenge the compounding order. Department cannot reopen the matter on the reason that actual suppression was much higher.

No appeal against order of composition - A person having agreed to the composition of offence is not entitled to challenge the said proceedings by filing appeal. - S V Bagi v. State of Karnataka (1992) 87 STC 138 = ILR 1992 Kar 1123 (Karn HC FB) - followed in Sakharia Bandhu v. ADCCT (1999) 112 STC 449 (Karn HC DB).

Appeal if application for compounding rejected - If authority rejects application for compounding, appeal can be filed before Tribunal - CCE v. Girish B Mishra (2016) 339 ELT 67 (Guj HC DB).

Article 20(3) of the Constitution—that no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself—cannot be invoked on vague allegations that the questions asked may have a bearing on charges pending against the person in a criminal Court nor an investigation stopped on that account: Sushil Kumar Sanghi v. R.R. Kini (1966) 36 Comp. Cas. 201 (Punj.).

Section 235 not applicable to unregistered companies

25.6-5 Section 235 is not applicable to unregistered companies and so also section 237, Bangalore Timber Industries v. Madras Sapper Ex-Servicemen’s Rehabilitation Association (1990) 69 Comp. Cas. 641 (Kar.).

GIVING SECURITY FOR COSTS [SECTION 632] : Where a limited company is plaintiff or petitioner in any suit/legal proceeding, the jurisdictional Court has the power sufficient security being given by the company and stay further proceedings until the same is complied with, in the event that it has reason to believe that the company will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant if he is successful in his defence.

Compensation against false, frivolous or vexatious accusation and prosecution [Section 625] 1.40-16 In respect of a shareholder’s complaint instituted against the company or any of its officers, the provisions of section 250 of the Code of Criminal Procedure do not apply, and instead, the provisions contained in section 625 of the Act apply: if the Magistrate hearing the accusation discharges or acquits all or any of the accused and is of the opinion that the accusation was false, frivolous or vexatious, by the same order of discharge call upon the shareholder-complainant if present to show cause why he should not pay compensation to the accused or any of them, and if not present by the summons issued to him to appear and show cause; then, the Magistrate shall record the cause shown, and if satisfied for reasons to be recorded that the accusation was false and either frivolous or vexatious, direct the payment of such compensation determined by him to the accused by the complainant-not exceeding one thousand rupees in all-or in default to suffer simple imprisonment for a term not exceeding two months in accordance with sections 68 and 69 of the Indian Penal Code, without prejudice to any civil and criminal liability in respect of the complaint made by him but subject to the compensation thus paid being taken into account in the award of any compensation to such person in any subsequent civil suit relating to the same matter. In Ratansi Morarji (P.) Ltd. v. Kirti D. Morarji [2004] 55 SCL 310 (Bom.), it was held that where the plaintiff filed a false claim before the Court and obtained certain order adversely affecting the interests of the defendant, the defendant would be entitled to damages. The order directing the payment of compensation is appealable as if it were an order of conviction on a trial held by the Magistrate, and the compensation shall not be payable before expiry of the time to prefer the appeal, and if the appeal is admitted until its disposal, section 625(7) and (8).

Coverage of employees under the Act

1.40-17 At par with the directors, company employees are eligible for sweat equity shares at a discount or for a consideration other than cash for providing know-how or making available rights in the nature of intellectual property or value addition, under section 79A; and otherwise they are eligible for financial assistance by the company to acquire company’s shares as provided under section 77. The service-bonds or securities furnished by employees to the company are protected, securing their right to receipt for moneys under sections 417 and 419; and their provident funds are protected by requiring the same to be banked by the company in a scheduled bank (as defined in section 2(43)) or post office savings bank, section 418. The services of employees during investigation under sections 235, 237, 239 and 247 are protected against discharge or punishment by the company under section 635B by an obligation cast on the company to notify the Tribunal by previous intimation in writing for objections, and if none received within thirty days, only then can the company proceed to act as proposed by it against any employee, section 635B. Section 633 provides for relief and presumptive relief against liability for negligence, default, breach of duty, misfeasance or breach of trust when the employees had acted honestly and reasonably, subject to the condition that in a criminal proceeding the Court shall have no power to grant relief from any civil liability due to such negligence etc. The acts of employees done under the Act in good faith are protected under section 635A, and they are immune from being compelled by any Court, tribunal or authority to disclose whence they got the information furnished to the Central Government for any special audit under section 233A or investigation under section 235, 237 or 247, section 635AA, but they are liable to provide information and assistance within their control to the special auditor/inspector. Employees are liable to be prosecuted for defaults and offences against the Act, if they constitute officers who are in default in accordance with the provisions of section 5, particularly, the obligation as to disclosures on unethical market practices indulged in the company to the auditor under section 221(3). Employees, past and present, are liable to be compelled by the Court to give back possession of company’s property in their hands under section 630. Officers of a company if convicted as officers who are in default under section 209A will vacate their offices and debarred from employment in any company as determined by the Court up to five years.

in the case of Risal Singh v. State of Haryana (2014) 13 SCC 244, emphasised that while assigning the reason in writing it is imperative that such reason must be plausible and based on definite material. In the said case, the Court relied upon on para 130 on the judgment of Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel 1985 taxmann.com 1415 (SC)/(1985) 3 SCC 398. [Para 38]

■ In the case of Reena Rani v. State of Haryana (2012) 10 SCC 215 this Court has again applied the law laid down in the judgment of Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel 1985 taxmann.com 1415 (SC)/(1985) 3 SCC 398 and Jaswant Singh v. State of Punjab (1991) 1 SCC 362 and held that the order of dismissal did not disclose the reasons explaining why it was not reasonably practicable to hold a regular departmental enquiry and applicability of the proviso in such a case is not justified. [Para 39]

■

On overall analysis of the intent of Article 311(2), it is vivid that an employee holding a post in Union or State ought not to be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to the one by which he was appointed. It is further specified that a person shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank after an inquiry supplying the charges if any against him and giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges. The applicability of the said clause is restricted in a situation wherein his conduct led to his conviction of criminal charges or where the authority empowered who dismissed, removed or reduced in rank records reason in writing upon satisfaction that it is not 'reasonably practicable' to hold an enquiry against him. In addition, where such power has been exercised by the President or the Governor it may be in the interest of security of the State or if not expedient to hold such an enquiry, then exceptional power under clause (c) of second proviso to Article 311 ought to be exercised. [Para 40]

■

In case such a decision invoking the extraordinary power is taken by the competent authority in light of the judgment Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel 1985 taxmann.com 1415 (SC)/(1985) 3 SCC 398 within the parameter as discussed, the scope of judicial review is available to the Constitutional Courts wherein the reasons as assigned for satisfaction of the authority must be reasonable, valid, justified and in writing. In addition, the satisfaction as recorded must be the objective satisfaction on the basis of material brought on record which ordinarily the disciplinary authority may take as a prudent person. Otherwise, dispensing with the enquiry is not permissible in law. In the present case, Section 21 of the 1978 Act confers power of punishment and Section 22 prescribes the procedure for awarding such punishment. The procedure as contemplated has been elaborated under the 1980 Rules. In the present case, in the Court’s view, the power exercised by the authority is completely without application of mind, thus, the question of recording of satisfaction as affirmed by the appellate authority, the CAT and the High Court does not arise. Therefore, it can be held that the order dispensing with the regular procedure of inquiry is arbitrary and consequently the order of dismissal of the appellant is liable to be quashed and the orders of the CAT and the High Court affirming the said dismissal order stand set aside. [Para 41]

■

In light of the above discussion, the irresistible conclusion is to set aside the order passed by the CAT and the High Court and to quash the order of dismissal passed by the DCP and confirmed by the appellate authority. In consequence, the appellant shall forthwith be reinstated with continuity of service. He shall be entitled for all consequential benefits notionally. Since, the appellant is found involved in a criminal case, therefore, in the facts of the case, back wages from the date of dismissal till reinstatement are restricted to 50%. [Para 42]

■

The setting aside of the order passed under Article 311(2) proviso (b) of the Constitution and direction for reinstatement shall be without prejudice to the right of the respondent to take recourse as permissible by initiating a departmental enquiry in accordance with law. Accordingly, and with the aforesaid directions, the present appeal stands allowed to the extent indicated. Parties to bear their own costs. [Para 43]

Acquittal by a criminal court would not debar an employer from exercising power in accordance with the Rules and Regulations in force. The two proceedings, criminal and departmental, are entirely different and operate in different fields and have different objectives." [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section 276C/277 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Offence and prosecution - Wilful attempt to evade tax, etc. - Whether mere expectation of success in some proceeding in appeal or reference under Act cannot be a ground for holding that institution of criminal proceeding under section 276C and 277 is unauthorized - Held, yes

FACT: On the basis of a complaint filed by the ITO, a case was instituted against the petitioner and other partners of a firm on the allegations that they wilfully attempted to evade payment of tax, penalty or interest, chargeable or imposable under the Act, by suppressing and/or concealing their assessable income, thereby rendering them liable to be prosecuted under section 276C, and that the accused persons made false statements during verification by knowingly delivering statements and/or accounts which were false, thereby committing an offence under section 277. After appearance in Court the accused persons filed an application to defer hearing of the case till disposal of the appeal filed before the Commissioner (Appeals). The prayer was rejected on the ground that pendency of the appeal could not stand as a bar to the criminal court’s proceeding in the matter and to launching prosecution, and there was no necessary to stay the proceeding.

On writ :

HELD: The result of a proceeding under the Act does not, in all cases, become binding on the criminal court and the court has to judge the proceeding placed before it independently. Otherwise, there is a danger of a contention being advanced that, whenever an assessee or any other person liable under the Act has failed to convince the authorities in the proceedings under the Act that he has not violated any provision, the conviction of such person should invariably follow in the criminal court. No. doubt, the criminal court has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and, in an appropriate case, may direct the proceeding to be dropped in the light of an order passed under the Act. In a given case, the conviction recorded by a subordinate court can be set aside in the light of the judgment of the appellate authority where the order forming the basis of prosecution is completely nullified by the order of the appellate court. In a given case, even if prosecution is initiated, the court may decide not to proceed in the light of a finding favourable to the assessee recorded by an authority under the Act subsequent to the launching of the prosecution.

A mere expectation of success in some proceeding in appeal or reference under the Act cannot be a ground for holding that the institution of the criminal proceeding under sections 276C and 277 is unauthorized.

In the instant case, the plea that prosecution could not be launched and/or the proceeding could not be initiated under sections 276C and 277 as long as some proceeding under the Act in which there was a chance of success of the assessee was pending was without substance.

In the instant case, the complaint had been filed in 1991 and the Magistrate had not rendered any finding whether the result of the appeal would have any effect on a criminal proceeding or not. It was stated by the Revenue that the appeal could be disposed of by the Commissioner (Appeals) within a short time if the accused before the Commissioner (Appeals) co-operate. Considering the fact situation, the petitioner was directed to appear before the Commissioner (Appeals) and move for fixing an early date for the hearing of the appeal.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

sought a writ of mandamus to direct respondent to provide adequate and effective opportunity to petitioner to defend himself and to permit him to cross examine witnesses, who had deposed against him in aforesaid disciplinary case - Whether since petitioner was not provided statements of witnesses whose evidence had been recorded, petitioner could not have effectively cross examined those witnesses - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, petitioner was to be granted an opportunity to cross examine those witnesses to prevent breach of principles of natural justice - Held, yes FACT: 'P', a chartered accountants firm, was statutory auditor of 'Satyam' and petitioner was working with 'P'. On 7-1-2009, the then Chairman of Satyam, 'R' informed the board of directors of Satyam of the systematic fudging of accounts of the said company by him. This disclosure, which was widely publicized, was acted upon as information against the petitioner under section 21. The CID, Hyderabad registered a criminal case under section 120B, read with sections 406, 420, 467, 471 and 477A IPC against the Chairman and directors of Satyam and other accused persons, including the petitioner. The petitioner was arrested by the police. Thereafter, the case was transferred to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) for investigation, and R.C. was registered against the petitioner and eight others by the CBI, Hyderabad. The Director (Discipline) acted on the information which came to him. The Director (Discipline) arrived at a prima facie opinion, dated 17-9-2009 on the occurrence of alleged misconduct falling under the Second Schedule to the Act against the petitioner. Consequently, the Council of the ICAI constituted a Disciplinary Committee in terms of section 21B. The procedure to be adopted by the Disciplinary Committee is prescribed in rule 18 of the Chartered Accountants (Procedure of Investigations of Professional and Other Misconduct and Conduct of Cases) Rules, 2007. The Disciplinary Committee after considering the prima facie opinion dated 17-9-2009, decided to proceed further in the matter under Chapter V of the Rules. The respondent sent a letter to the petitioner, calling upon him to submit his written statement along with supporting documents, if any, and a list of witnesses, if any, that the petitioner might desire to examine under rule 18(4) of the Rules. The petitioner did not respond to the said communication, presumably because he was still behind bars, and was granted bail by the Supreme Court only on 4-2-2010. After the petitioner was released on bail, as aforesaid, he was served with a letter, directing him to appear before the Disciplinary Committee. The petitioner preferred a writ petition before the Court against the holding of the disciplinary enquiry, primarily on the ground that on the same subject-matter the petitioner could not be simultaneously proceeded with in criminal proceedings and in disciplinary proceedings. He claimed that the same would be violative of his fundamental rights under the Constitution of India. The Court vide order dated 16-4-2010 stayed the aforesaid disciplinary proceedings. During the pendency of the aforesaid writ petition, the Supreme Court directed that the trial in the criminal proceedings be conducted on a day-to-day basis. The petitioner's writ petition was eventually dismissed by the Single judge later on, the respondent issued a notice to the petitioner requiring him to appear before the Disciplinary Committee. In the meantime, the petitioner preferred a Letters Patent Appeal. The Division Bench issued notice on the said appeal to the respondent, and directed the petitioner to appear before the Disciplinary Committee, and to accept, or deny the charges. The petitioner appeared before the Disciplinary Committee at Hyderabad, and denied the charges read out by the Disciplinary Committee. Subsequently, the petitioners LPA was dismissed. However, the Division Bench directed that the respondent would proceed with the disciplinary enquiry keeping in view the convenience of the petitioner and affording him adequate opportunity to put forth his case. The petitioner was again issued notice by the respondent requiring him to appear before the Disciplinary Committee. The petitioner, vide letter dated 11-6-2011, sought an adjournment on the ground that the criminal trial was at a crucial stage and he was facing genuine difficulty in appearing before the Disciplinary Committee, as he required adequate time and opportunity to face the enquiry. The request for adjournment was accepted by the respondent. The petitioner sought repeated deferment of the proceedings finally on 31-7-2011 the Disciplinary Committee rejected petitioner's request for deferment and recorded the deposition of one witness, 'K' D.I.G., CBI who was produced to prove the charges against the petitioner. The petitioner's representative was thereafter given the opportunity to cross-examine the said witness. However, he refused to do so. The Supreme Court disposed of the petitioner's Special Leave Petition, directing the respondent-Institute to commence the disciplinary proceedings. The respondent issued notice requiring the petitioner to appear before the Disciplinary Committee. The petitioner sent his preliminary reply to the respondent. The petitioner also sought the documents which formed part of the SEBI investigation report, the main CBI chargesheet and the two supplementary charge sheets, relied upon by the Director (Discipline) for forming the prima facie opinion

HEADNOTE: Section 21, read with section 22, of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - Misconduct - Procedure in inquiries relating to misconduct of members of institute - Appellant, a chartered accountant and a member of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), was a partner of PW, a firm of Chartered Accountants registered with ICAI - PW was appointed as statutory auditors of SCSL - Statutory audits of SCSL for years 2001 to March, 2007 were conducted and reports were signed by appellant - Subsequently, ‘R’ Chairman of SCSL, in a communication sent to Board of Directors, disclosed that balance sheet of SCSL carried inflated (non-existent) cash and bank balances and liability was understated - On basis of statement made by ‘R’, which was also published in newspaper, ICAI initiated disciplinary proceedings against appellant - However, by that time appellant had already been arrested by local police for allegedly committing offences punishable under various sections of Indian Penal Code, 1860 - Appellant filed a writ petition before High Court contending that disciplinary proceedings initiated against him under Act should be deferred since alleged acts of commission or omission on basis of which disciplinary proceedings had been commenced also formed basis of various charges against him in criminal cases and, hence, any disclosure of his explanation or defences until final conclusion of criminal trial pending before Special Court would seriously impact his defence in criminal trial - Single Judge dismissed petition filed by appellant - On instant appeal, it was noted that charges levelled in disciplinary proceeding and chargesheet in criminal proceeding, list of witnesses, nature of enquiry, purpose of enquiry and arraigning appellant as accused person in criminal case were on a different base - Moreover, charges levelled against appellant in departmental proceeding/proceeding under Act did not involve grave and complex questions of law - Whether in view of aforesaid, Single Judge rightly concluded that appellant had failed to make out a case for stay of disciplinary proceedings pending conclusion of criminal trial - Held, yes

in disciplinary proceeding and chargesheet in criminal proceeding, list of witnesses, nature of enquiry, purpose of enquiry and arraigning appellant as accused person in criminal case were on a different base - Moreover, charges levelled against appellant in departmental proceeding/proceeding under Act did not involve grave and complex questions of law - Whether in view of aforesaid, Single Judge rightly concluded that appellant had failed to make out a case for stay of disciplinary proceedings pending conclusion of criminal trial - Held, yes FACT: The appellant, a chartered accountant and a member of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), was a partner of PW, a firm of Chartered Accountants registered with ICAI. In the year 2000, the firm was appointed as the statutory auditors of SCSL. The statutory audits of SCSL for the years 2001 to March, 2007 were conducted and the reports were signed by the appellant. Subsequently, ‘R’ the Chairman of SCSL, in a communication sent to the Board of Directors, disclosed that the balance sheet of SCSL carried inflated (non-existent) cash and bank balances and the liability was understated. The ICAI corresponded with PW, referring to the letters of ‘R’ the Chairman of SCSL, that the said firm had failed to carry out necessary checks which were required while undertaking the audit of the financial statements and certifying the quarterly results of the company. The ICAI alleged that the firm had violated the accounting principles while auditing and certifying the accounts/quarterly results of SCSL for the aforementioned years and quarters and did not give a true and fair view of the accounts and further did not exercise due diligence and were negligent in their professional duties as statutory auditors. The ICAI treated the newspaper report as information within the meaning of section 21(2) of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 [as amended by the Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2006. Thus, PW was called upon to disclose the name or names of the member or members who was/were answerable to the allegation/s and send a copy of the aforesaid information letter along with its enclosures to the said member/members. After certain correspondence, PW replied to the ICAI stating, inter alia, that the key members included the appellant herein. PW informed that the appellant had been arrested by the local police for committing offences punishable under sections 409, 420, 468, 471, 477A, 201 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. At this juncture, the Director (Discipline) of ICAI placed a prima facie opinion before the disciplinary committee and the committee was of the prima facie view that the said chartered accountants including the appellant were guilty of professional misconduct within the meaning of clauses (5), (6), (7), (8) and (9) of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Act. A prima facie opinion was also formed that the said chartered accountants were guilty of other misconduct within the meaning of section 22, read with section 21 of the Act. On the basis of the said prima facie opinion, a notice was sent to the chartered accountants enclosing a copy of the prima facie opinion and requiring each of them to send their written statement along with supporting documents. In domestic enquiry the test for proof of charge is preponderance of probability. It is not necessary to prove charges beyond reasonable doubt. It is not for the Labour or Industrial Courts to comment on quality or quantity of evidence. So long as there is some evidence on record to support findings of the Enquiry Officer, Labour and Industrial Courts cannot go into aspect of adequacy of evidence. [Para 26]

■

Thus, in a domestic enquiry the strict and sophisticated rules of Indian Evidence Act do not apply. Any material which is logically probative for a prudent man can be taken into consideration by the Enquiry Officer. So long as there is some evidence on record, however compendious it may be, the same can be relied upon for recording finding of guilt. It is only in a case involving total absence of evidence that a finding can be treated as perverse. [Para 28]

In the present case, it is difficult to hold that there is absolutely no evidence to prove the allegations in the two charges levelled against the respondent. The Labour and Industrial Courts have failed to appreciate well settled principles relating to test of preponderance of probability for proving charges in the domestic enquiry. [Para 29]

The question assumes importance for the reason that in such cases, the Settlement Commission has necessary jurisdiction under section 245H to grant immunity to the assessee from prosecution for any offence under the Act or under the Indian Penal Code, 1860 or under any other Central Act for the time being in force. In the light of the judgment of the Supreme Court in CIT v. B.N. Bhattachargee [1979] 118 ITR 461/ 1 Taxman 348 , the Settlement Commission is required to exercise its power of immunising against criminal prosecution by using its power only sparingly and in deserving cases. There is, therefore, no ground to believe that if the Settlement Commission has allowed an application to be proceeded with, it shall grant as a matter of course immunity from criminal prosecution to the applicant under section 245H. The power to grant such immunity is dependent upon the satisfaction of the Settlement Commission that the applicant has co-operated with the Settlement Commission in the proceeding before it and has made a full and true disclosure of his income and the manner in which such income has been derived. Thus, a mere expectation of success in some proceeding or appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of institution of criminal proceedings under sections 276C and 277. If a criminal prosecution has been validly instituted, it is in the interest of justice that the trial of the case should be concluded as early as possible. Thus, the Apex Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal (First ITO) [1984] 149 ITR 696/19 Taxman 1 after observing that "it may be that in an appropriate case, a criminal court may adjourn or postpone the hearing of a criminal case in exercise of its discretionary power under section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if the disposal of any proceeding under the Act which has a bearing on the proceedings before it is imminent so that it may take also into consideration the order to be passed therein," had also taken care to make a further observation that "Even here the discretion should be exercised judicially and in such a way as not to frustrate the object of the criminal proceedings." The Apex Court then went on to emphasise that "There is no rigid rule which makes it necessary for a criminal court to adjourn or postpone the hearing of a case before it indefinitely or for an unduly long period only because some proceeding which may have some bearing on it is pending elsewhere. The principle laid down by the Apex Court in P. Jayappan’s case (supra) in another context is also applicable in the matter of staying criminal proceedings pending before the criminal court, which has been validly instituted and where on the application of the assessee, the Settlement Commission has allowed an application to be proceeded with but has not yet passed any final orders including an order granting or refusing immunity from the criminal prosecution. A blanket order staying criminal proceedings only because the Settlement Commission has allowed an application before it to be proceeded with and the Commission has the necessary authority under the Act to grant immunity from criminal prosecution is also not necessary in the interest of justice. If any such proceeding is decided in favour of the applicant and immunity from criminal prosecution is granted, he can take advantage of any such decision even after his conviction before the appellate or the revisional Court or before the Supreme Court in an application under article 136 for special leave to appeal. The process of criminal law including the trial, appeal and revision is a protracted one and it is difficult to visualise a situation where the Settlement Commission in a particular case shall take such a long time for disposing of the application and in granting immunity from criminal prosecution that the accused shall have lost all opportunities to take benefit of such an order granting immunity even before the appellate or the revisional Court.

As has been argued by the learned Solicitor General and the learned Counsel appearing for MSRTC, subclause (ii) of Section 4(6)(b) enables forfeiture of gratuity, wholly or partially, if the delinquent employee is terminated for any act which constitutes an offence involving moral turpitude, if the offence is committed in the course of his employment. An 'Offence' as defined in the General Clauses Act, means 'any act or omission made punishable by any law for the time being' and does not call for a conviction. The standard of proof required in a criminal proceeding is quite different from that required in a disciplinary proceeding; the former being regulated by a higher standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt while the latter governed by preponderance of probabilities. The provision of forfeiture of gratuity under the Act does not speak of a conviction in a criminal proceeding, for an offence involving moral turpitude. On the contrary, the Act provides for such forfeiture in cases where the delinquent employee is terminated for a misconduct, which constitutes an offence involving moral turpitude. Hence, the only requirement is for the Disciplinary Authority or the Appointing Authority to decide as to whether the misconduct could, in normal circumstances, constitute an offence involving moral turpitude, with a further discretion conferred on the authority forfeiting gratuity, to decide whether the forfeiture should be of the whole or only a part of the gratuity payable, which would depend on the gravity of the misconduct. Necessarily, there should be a notice issued to the terminated employee, who should be allowed to represent both on the question of the nature of the misconduct, whether it constitutes an offence involving moral turpitude, and the extent to which such forfeiture can be made." On appeal: HELD: In the case at hand, as was evident, the charges levelled related to the departmental proceeding under the Act as amended from time to time. The said enactment had been enacted to make provisions for the regulation of the profession of Chartered Accountant and for that purpose to establish the Institute of Chartered Accountants. The purpose of enacting such legislation was to authorize the incorporation by a statute of an autonomous professional body. The body has been conferred the certain responsibilities. No member of the institute is entitled to practise unless he has obtained certificate of practice from the council. Certain disqualifications have been stipulated in section 8. The Legislature confers numerous functions on the council. The institute has the power to take disciplinary action against the registered Chartered Accountants. The Act also defines professional or other misconduct to include any act or omission provided in the Schedule to the Act. There is a provision for appeal. If the Act and the Schedule appended thereto are appreciated with studied scrutiny, it is quite evident that a legislative endeavour has been made to ensure high standards, confidence and integrity in the profession. Keeping in view, in fiscal matters, responsibility and sanctity attached to accounts, audit and role of a statutory auditor are the fundamental paradigms. The professional conduct stands on a different footing than a delinquent employee facing a disciplinary enquiry. Keeping the aforesaid in view, it is obligatory on the part of the court to see whether such a proceeding should be interdicted. The submission of the appellant basically conveyed that there was similarity of charges; that there were same witnesses; that the element of prejudice was involved; that if the simultaneous proceedings were continued the appellant accused in criminal trial would be compelled to disclose his defence; that the standard of proof was not the only test; that the impact of verdict in criminal proceeding on the disciplinary authority in case of acquittal would be of great magnitude; and that the direction given by the Supreme Court to conclude the trial by end of July 2011 became an additional reason on the part of the institute not to proceed with the enquiry. The submissions, in oppugnation, by the respondents were that the charges were absolutely different; that the question of fraud and cheating were not involved in the departmental enquiry; that the witnesses were few in number in the departmental proceeding; that there was a violation of accounting standards by the CA which could not be gone into in the criminal trial; that they had not functioned appositely as statutory auditors; that they had not shown due diligence and acted with gross negligence; that they had failed to obtain sufficient information and there had been material departure from the generally accepted procedure of accounting; that the direction for conclusion of trial did not help as there were number of witnesses; that the standard of proof was totally different; and that the conspiracy and other factors were not the matter in the disciplinary proceeding. Quite apart from the above, it was contended that the appellant could not take shelter under the umbrella that he had stopped practising inasmuch as the institute had no power to suspend his registration. Additionally, it was urged by the respondent that the charges levelled against appellant did not involve complex questions of law and fact and, hence, it was not desirable to invite an interdiction in exercise of the inherent jurisdiction of this Court. [Para 28]

On a perusal of the comparative chart of the charges levelled in the disciplinary proceeding and the chargesheet in the criminal proceeding, the list of witnesses, the nature of enquiry, the purpose of enquiry and arraigning the appellant as accused person in the criminal case were on a different base. The theory of prejudice that had been canvassed was not to be routinely inferred. It could not be held in the obtaining factual matrix, that participation of the appellant in the departmental enquiry would seriously prejudice the defence at the trial in the criminal case. That apart, it was not desirable to interdict in the proceeding initiated by the institute as that would be against the public interest since the Act has its rigorous technical norms and the Chartered Accountants registered with it are required to function with statutory responsibility. In addition, the charges levelled against the appellants in the departmental proceeding/the proceeding under the Act did not involve grave and complex questions of law. [Para 29]

At this juncture, a contention was canvassed that the appellant would not be able to participate in the departmental enquiry as the Supreme Court had directed the trial to proceed on day-to-day basis. The respondents fairly stated that enquiry would be fixed on such dates which would be suitable and convenient for the Chartered Accountant-appellant and he would not face any kind of difficulty on that score. [Para 30]

Part IV of the First Schedule the expression 'other misconduct' includes any conduct, which brings disrepute to the profession or the ICAI as a result of an action whether or not related to professional work. Thus, it is not necessary that the misconduct complained of should be a conduct in exercise of the profession of Chartered Accountancy. Any conduct, which tends to bring disrepute, would be a subject matter of proceedings under Chapter V. [Para 18] In view of the above, it is unable to accept the contention that the Board of Discipline does not have the jurisdiction to examine the alleged misconduct on the part of the petitioner. It is relevant to mention that the standards of proof as required in disciplinary proceedings and criminal proceedings are different. WHETHER A FRESH SHOW-CAUSE NOTICE FOR PUNISHMENT WAS REQUIRED AFTER THE DE NOVO PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE LABOUR COURT?

■

The Appellant's principal submission is that the show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008 was issued on the basis of the domestic enquiry. That enquiry was thereafter found to be not fair. The Industrial Court, by order dated 14.08.2015, remanded the matter to the Labour Court and permitted the Respondent-management to establish the misconduct before the Labour Court. According to the Appellant, once misconduct was proved in the de novo proceedings before the Labour Court, the Respondent could not have mechanically acted upon the earlier show-cause notice issued based on the earlier domestic enquiry which was found to be defective. [Para 38]

■

The submission requires consideration in the light of Regulation 88(j) of the MSEDCL Service Regulations. Regulation 88(j), titled "Show Cause Notice", reads as follows: "After the enquiry is completed, the Competent Authority shall serve a notice on the employee communicating to him its findings and asking him to show cause within a specified time as to why the contemplated punishment involving dismissal, removal or reversion or withholding of increment/s should not be inflicted on him. The employee may be supplied with a copy of the findings of the Competent Authority or of those of the Enquiry Officer, as the case may be, or he may be given an opportunity to take a copy of such findings." [Para 39]

■

The language of Regulation 88(j) is significant. It contemplates a notice to be issued after the enquiry is completed. The purpose of such notice is not an empty formality. The employee must be informed of the findings based on which the competent authority proposes to impose punishment and must be given an opportunity to show cause why the contemplated punishment should not be inflicted. [Para 40]

■

Court is conscious that a second opportunity against proposed punishment is not a mandate in every disciplinary proceeding. However, where the applicable service regulation expressly provides for a post-enquiry notice communicating the findings and calling upon the employee to show cause against the contemplated punishment, the authority must comply with that regulation. In the present case, therefore, the issue arises not as an abstract constitutional requirement, but from the express language of Regulation 88(j). [Para 42]

■

In Managing Director, ECIL v. B. Karunakar, (1993) 4 SCC 727, this Court emphasized the importance of giving the delinquent employee an opportunity to meet the findings which may influence the disciplinary authority. [Para 43]

■

The principle in Workmen of Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. of India (P) Ltd. v. Management, (1973) 1 SCC 813 enables the employer to sustain the charge of misconduct by leading evidence before the Labour Court where the domestic enquiry is defective. That principle, however, operates at the stage of proving misconduct. It does not dispense with the disciplinary authority's duty to consider the findings that ultimately survive and to decide the appropriate penalty under the applicable Service Regulations. The Labour Court decides whether misconduct is proved. The competent disciplinary authority decides what punishment should follow. [Para 46]

 pending before Tribunal - On same day assessee informed Tribunal of its acquittal from criminal court and requested it to give some time for producing a copy of said judgment before it - Tribunal, however, did not grant any time and delivered its judgment on 23-8-1979 confirming AAC's order - Whether when Tribunal had not relied upon judgment of Magistrate in criminal proceedings, was it necessary to adjourn matter or postpone delivery of judgment to enable assessee to produce judgment of criminal appellate court acquitting its partners - Held, no

FACT: For the assessment year 1970-71, the assessee-firm filed a return showing certain income. The ITO made few additions to the Income disbelieving certain entries in the account books maintained by the assessee. He also initiated proceedings under section 271(1)(c) and levied a penalty. On appeal, the AAC by its order dated 28-3-1978 dismissed the appeal. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Tribunal. In the meantime, the partners of the assessee were also prosecuted in a criminal court for the said concealment of income and for filing a false return. They were convicted by the trial court and sentenced to imprisonment for six months on 31-3-1979. On appeal, the Metropolitan Additional Sessions Judge by his judgment and order dated 20-8-1979 acquitted them. When the Sessions Judge's Order was pronounced, the appeal was still pending before the Tribunal for its order. The assessee filed an application before the Tribunal informing the said fact and requesting for some time to enable it to produce a copy of the said judgment before the Tribunal. The Tribunal, however, passed no orders nor did it grant any time for producing the judgment. It proceeded to deliver its judgment on 23-8-1979. The assessee filed a petition for review contending that the judgment of the Tribunal may be set aside and the matter be reheard taking into consideration the judgment of the Metropolitan Additional Sessions Judge. The Tribunal, however, dismissed the said petition.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case, the penalty was levied by the ITO on the facts and circumstances before him de hors any judgment or opinion of the Magistrate or any other Court. The orders of the criminal court were not even pronounced by the date of the judgment of the AAC. The Tribunal also confirmed the levy of penalty on the facts and circumstances of the case, unrelated to and without reference to the judgment of the Magistrate. After having come to that conclusion, it merely referred to the argument of the department based upon the judgment and order of the Magistrate, but it neither referred to the contents of the said order nor to the conclusion of the Magistrate but reiterated that it had confirmed the penalty on the facts and circumstances before it and for reasons already recorded by it. It was, thus, clear that the judgment of the Magistrate had played no part in the conclusion that was arrived at by the Tribunal. If so, the judgment of acquittal would equally be not relevant. Thus, when the Tribunal was not placing any reliance upon the judgment of the Magistrate in the criminal proceedings, it was not bound nor it was necessary for it to adjourn the matter or postpone the delivery of judgment to enable the assessee to produce the judgment of the criminal appellate court acquitting the partners.

M. Suryanarayana Murthy and A.V. Krishna Koundinya for the Applicant.

T. Anantha Babu for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 276C, read with sections 278B and 271(1)(c), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Offences and prosecutions - Wilful attempt to evade tax, etc. - Subsequent to imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) on assessee, 
 department initiated criminal proceedings against assessee under section 276C - Assessee filed discharge petition on ground that Tribunal had deleted penalty - Trial court rejected said petition on ground that against order of Tribunal, department had preferred an appeal before High Court and same was pending - On revision, Additional Sessions Judge, observing that fate of application for discharge was dependent upon orders to be passed by High Court in income-tax appeal, set aside order of trial court and remanded matter to trial court for a decision afresh, after appeal filed by department was decided by High Court - Whether since proceedings under section 271(1)(c) would have a clear and definite bearing on those under section 276C, order passed by Additional Sessions Judge was in consonance with law - Held, yes

FACT: Subsequent to imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) on the assessee, the department initiated criminal proceedings under section 276C, read with section 278B, against the assessee. The assessee filed discharge petition on ground that the Tribunal had deleted the penalty sought to be imposed on the assessee under section 271(1)(c). The trial court, however, rejected said application on ground that income-tax authorities had preferred an appeal before the High Court and, therefore, the penalty proceedings under the provisions of section 271(1)(c) had not attained finality. On revision, the Additional Sessions Judge observing that the fate of the application for discharge was dependent upon the order to be passed by the High Court in the Income-tax Appeal, set aside the order of the trial court and remanded the matter to the trial court for a decision afresh after the appeal filed by the department was decided by the High Court.

In revision petition, the department contended that the said order was not tenable in law inasmuch as penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) and the criminal proceedings under section 276C, read with section 278B, were independent and the pendency of the proceedings under section 271(1)(c) could not be taken as a ground to stay the proceedings under section 276C, read with section 278B.

HELD: In CIT v. Bhupen Champak Lal Dalal [2001] 248 ITR 830/ 116 Taxman 746 , the Supreme Court was mindful of the fact that the prosecution in criminal law and proceedings under the Act were undoubtedly independent proceedings and, therefore, there was no impediment in law for the criminal proceedings to proceed even during the pendency of the proceedings under the Act. However, the Supreme Court observed that wholesome rule will have to be adopted in matters of this nature where the Courts have taken the view that when the conclusions arrived at by the appellate authorities have a relevance and bearing upon the conclusions to be reached in the criminal case necessarily, one authority will have to await the outcome of the other authority. [Para 5]

The decision of the Supreme Court in K.C. Builders v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 135 Taxman 461, makes it more than clear that the proceedings under section 271(1)(c) would have a clear and definite bearing on those under section 276C. Insofar as the proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were concerned, the penalty against the assessee stood deleted. However, the department had preferred an appeal which was pending before the Court. Therefore, clearly, the assessee could not claim for quashing of the proceedings. The assessee submitted that although the initial application was filed by it for discharge, yet in the light of the decision of the Supreme Court, it was not at this stage claiming quashing of the proceedings and according to it, the order, keeping the criminal proceedings before the trial court in abeyance, need not be interfered with and the same should await the decision in the appeal before the Court. [Para 6]

b) are satisfied. In other words, before embarking on the question as to whether the further requirements of section 33(2)(b) are complied or not, the Authority has to consider the question whether the domestic enquiry is fair and proper. Thus, it logically flows that to consider the compliance of section 33(2)(b), the Authority under section 33(2)(b) should also satisfy itself that the domestic enquiry is fair and proper. [Para 16]

■ In G. Mckenzie and Co. Ltd. v. Its WorkmenAIR 1959 SC 389, in a proceeding under section 33(2)(b), the approval for dismissal was rejected on the premise that the disciplinary enquiry was not proper. The Management initiated fresh disciplinary enquiry and again imposed a penalty of dismissal. In this context, the Apex Court has held that the proceeding under section 33(2)(b) has a limited scope and a second disciplinary proceeding is not hit by the principle of Res judicata. [Para 18]

■

On a reading of the said judgement, it is evident that the Apex Court has held that the authority under section 33(2)(b) has no jurisdiction to adjudicate the dispute. One has to notice the context in which such an observation is made. It is made in the context of the contention that the finding on the proof of charges recorded in a proceeding under section 33. The said observations are not made on the findings as to the fairness of the disciplinary enquiry. Thus, said judgment in G. McKenzie (supra) cannot be construed as having held that the Authority acting under section 33, has no jurisdiction to adjudicate on the question whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper. [Para 20]

■

The scope of section 33(2)(b), is also considered in Punjab National Bank Ltd. v. All India Punjab National Bank Employees Federation. AIR 1960 SC 160 [Para 21]

■

What emerges from the said judgement is that the Authority, while deciding the application under section 33(2)(b), has no jurisdiction to adjudicate on the merits of the finding in the disciplinary proceeding. However, the Authority, before granting or refusing approval, has to record a finding as to whether: (a) the employer has acted malafide, (b) has resorted to any unfair labour practice, (c) violated any basic principles of natural justice, and whether the enquiry is fair and proper. (d) the enquiry conforms with the binding Standing Orders (e) Wages are paid as required under the proviso to section 33(2)(b). [Para 22]

■

In view of the law declared in Punjab National Bank Ltd. supra, on considering the above aspects, the authority may pass appropriate orders on the application. Thus, the order on the fairness of the domestic enquiry in a proceeding under section 33, is not an empty formality. It involves an adjudication on the aspects referred to above. And the Authority is vested with the jurisdiction to decide those aspects. Thus, it is opined that the question “whether domestic enquiry was fair and proper?” if raised in an application under section 33(2)(b), and if the finding on such an application is recorded after full fledged enquiry, such finding is not just a prima facie finding on the said question as to the fairness and validity of the domestic enquiry and it is a finding on adjudication which attains finality if not questioned, and cannot be re-agitated in subsequent proceedings between the same parties. [Para 23]

■

In the Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation v. Bharat Singh Jala,(2023) III LLJ 519 SC relied on by the management, on an application under section 33(2)(b), the employer sought approval for the penalty of dismissal, the Tribunal held that enquiry was bad and the permitted both parties to lead evidence. Thereafter, the application under section 33(2)(b) was allowed, and approval was granted to the order of termination. The workman raised the industrial dispute challenging the order of termination. The Labour Court accepted the challenge, and the order of termination was set aside. The Labour Court’s award was upheld by the High Court, in Writ Petition as well as Writ Appeal. The Apex Court held that once an elaborate enquiry was held under section 33(2)(b), further challenge to the order is not permissible. [Para 24]

■

This Court is of the view that it was a case where the Authority under section 33, held that the domestic enquiry was bad and a fresh enquiry was held before the Tribunal. Based on fresh enquiry before the Tribunal, the issues relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry and the merit of the charges were adjudicated. However, in the instant case, the enquiry was held to be valid, and later the order on termination was approved. There is no adjudication on the merits of the charges when the issue relating to the fairness of the enquiry was considered. Thus, the said judgment does not apply to the fact situation. [Para 25]

■

(1973) 1 SCC 813 enables the employer to sustain the charge of misconduct by leading evidence before the Labour Court where the domestic enquiry is defective. That principle, however, operates at the stage of proving misconduct. It does not dispense with the disciplinary authority's duty to consider the findings that ultimately survive and to decide the appropriate penalty under the applicable Service Regulations. The Labour Court decides whether misconduct is proved. The competent disciplinary authority decides what punishment should follow. [Para 46]

■ The Appellant's submission has to be examined from this limited perspective. After the domestic enquiry was found defective, the Respondent-management was permitted to adduce evidence before the Labour Court. The Appellant was a party to those proceedings. The Labour Court considered the evidence and held that the misconduct stood proved. That finding was carried in revision before the Industrial Court and attained finality. The Appellant cannot, therefore, reopen the finding of misconduct merely on the ground that no fresh notice was issued after the Labour Court recorded its finding. The issue is whether the disciplinary authority, while imposing dismissal on 12.07.2017, could rely substantially on the earlier show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008, though misconduct was ultimately proved in a different manner, namely by adducing evidence adduced before the Labour Court after remand. [Para 47]

■

The show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008 was undoubtedly issued after the domestic enquiry. But once the domestic enquiry was found defective, the legally sustainable basis for holding misconduct proved was no longer the domestic enquiry report, but the finding recorded by the Labour Court after evidence was led before it. [Para 48]

■

Court is conscious that the Labour Court and the Industrial Court are adjudicatory bodies, that the Appellant had participated in the proceedings before those fora, and that the show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008 was not invalidated. Therefore, the absence of a fresh notice after the Labour Court's finding cannot be treated as causing prejudice in relation to the adjudication of guilt or misconduct. [Para 49]

■

However, the question of punishment stands on a different footing. The disciplinary authority was required to consider the findings which ultimately survived, namely the findings recorded in the de novo adjudication before the Labour Court, and thereafter apply its mind to the appropriate punishment. This consideration necessarily included the gravity of the misconduct, the nature of the charges proved, the Appellant's long service, past record, absence or presence of financial loss or dishonesty, and whether a lesser penalty would meet the ends of justice. [Para 50]

■

The dismissal order dated 12.07.2017 proceeds substantially on the footing that a show-cause notice had already been issued after the departmental enquiry and that no explanation had been received from the Appellant. Such an approach does not sufficiently reflect independent consideration by the competent authority of the findings recorded after remand by the Labour Court, or of the factors relevant to the quantum of punishment. The Appellant's failure to reply to the earlier show-cause notice could not have been treated as conclusive when the enquiry on which that notice was founded had itself been found defective and the misconduct was subsequently thereafter established through a separate adjudicatory process and not before the departmental forum. [Para 51]

■

The Labour Court, in Complaint (ULP) No. 34 of 2008, held that misconduct stood proved and that the show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008 was legal and proper. That finding was affirmed in revision. But the question before Court is not merely whether the earlier show-cause notice was valid when issued. The question is whether the disciplinary authority could impose dismissal by relying substantially on the earlier notice, without independently considering the findings which ultimately survived after remand and without giving the Appellant an opportunity to place her explanation on the quantum of punishment in the light of those later findings. [Para 52]

■

Court also clarifies the role of the Labour Court in the post-remand proceedings. Once the domestic enquiry was found defective and the Respondent-management was permitted to prove the misconduct before the Labour Court, the Labour Court was required to decide whether the charges stood proved on the evidence adduced before it. Any observation by the Labour Court describing the misconduct as grave or serious could not substitute the independent satisfaction of the competent authority on the question of penalty. Similarly, the finding that the earlier show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008 was legal and proper could not relieve the competent authority of its obligation to consider the findings which ultimately survived after remand and to apply its own mind on the quantum of punishment. [Para 53]

■

Regulation 88(j) contemplates that, after the enquiry is completed, the competent authority shall communicate its findings and call upon the employee to show cause against the contemplated punishment. In the peculiar facts of the present case, the enquiry which ultimately sustained the charges was the de novo adjudication before the Labour Court after the earlier enquiry was found defective. Therefore, the decision-making process on punishment could not be treated as complete merely because the earlier show-cause notice was held valid. [Para 54]
