It was also the contention of the assessee that the alleged offence under section 35B was not a continuing offence. [Paras 43, 44] The Supreme Court, in the case of P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal First ITO [1984] 149 ITR 696/19 Taxman 1, has clearly laid down that a mere expectation of success in some proceeding in appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of the institution of the criminal proceedings under the Income-tax Act, 1961. In an appropriate case, the Criminal Court may adjourn or postpone the hearing of a criminal case in exercise of its discretionary power under section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if the disposal of any proceeding under the Act, which has a bearing on the proceedings before it,is imminent so that it may also take into consideration the order to be passed therein. But in the instant case, even according to the assessee, the tax case had been filed with a huge delay and the delay itself was yet to be condoned and, thereafter, the tax case was to be disposed of and it was not certain as to when the tax case would be finally disposed of. Therefore, when the disposal of the proceedings under the Act namely the tax case pending before the Court was not imminent, there was no scope for either adjourning or postponing the hearing of the criminal case. In the very same decision, the Apex Court itself has observed that there is no rigid rule which makes it necessary for a Criminal Court to adjourn or postpone the hearing of a case before it indefinitely or for an unduly long period only because some proceeding which may have some bearing on it, is pending elsewhere. This, however, has no relevance to the question of maintainability of the prosecution. The prosecution in those circumstances cannot be quashed on the ground that it is a pre-mature one. Further, it was contended by the public prosecutor that all the witnesses to be examined in the instant case were aged and already three witnesses had retired from service and one witness was above 75 years and another witness was due to retire within few days. Therefore, it was not a fit case where the criminal proceedings could be stayed awaiting the outcome of the tax case filed by the assessee. Further, since admittedly the criminal case was of the year 1997, it was not just or proper to adjourn or postpone the hearing of the case pending before the Criminal Court indefinitely or for an unduly long period. Therefore, the third contention of the petitioner was also liable to be rejected. [Para 47]

Further, the Supreme Court in the case of Maya Rani Punj v. CIT [1986] 157 ITR 330/ 24 Taxman 1 after referring its own decision rendered in the case of State of Bihar v. Deokaran Nenshi [1972] 2 SCC 890 has held that the non-compliance of an obligation of making a return is an infraction as long as the default continues. Therefore, the contention of the assessee, that the alleged offence under section 35B was not a continuing offence, could not be countenanced. [Para 48]

Further contentions of the assessee were that a notice under section 16(4) alone had been given and no notice under section 17 had been issued and, therefore, the non-filing of the return even after the issuance of a notice under section 16(4) could not be construed to be wilful; and that before the Magistrate, a contention had been raised that the notice issued under section 16(4) was not a proper notice and it was also not properly served on the assessee and the Magistrate while considering the contention had observed that the question whether the notice issued by the Assessing Officer asking the assessee to file the report was issued under correct provision of law and whether that notice was properly served on the person could be proved only during the trial by letting the oral and documentary evidence by the prosecution. According to the assessee, the Magistrate had erred in making such observation and the said contention ought to have been considered by the Magistrate on merits. [Para 50]

The observations made by the Magistrate were perfectly in order and it could not be said that he had committed any error of law. When admittedly the notice issued under section 16(4) was not produced before the Court and the proof of service of the same was also not produced before the Court, it was not proper on the part of the assessee to expect the Magistrate to consider the said issue at that stage. The said contention was beyond the scope of section 245(2). [Para 52]

HEADNOTE: Section 2A, read with section 33, of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and Rule 64 of the Tamil Nadu Industrial Disputes Rules, 1958 - Dismissal, etc., of an individual workman to be deemed to be an industrial dispute - Petitioner-Management had initiated disciplinary action against respondent-workman following a complaint that he used abusive language and physically attacked a co-employee - Respondent was suspended pending enquiry - A charge memo with four charges of assault, intimidation, and use of abusive language was issued - His explanation was found unsatisfactory; an external Enquiry Officer conducted a domestic enquiry, examined witnesses, issued findings, which were forwarded for show cause; thereafter, Management terminated his services - Respondent consistently denied charges and alleged that domestic enquiry was not fair and proper - Management filed an application under Section 33(2)(b) seeking approval of termination and paid approximately Rs. 0.52 lakhs towards final settlement along with one month’s wages - Deputy Commissioner of Labour (Conciliation II) approved termination - Challenging termination, respondent invoked Section 2A before Deputy Commissioner of Labour - As no order was passed within 45 days, dispute was filed before Additional Labour Court - Respondent filed a memo seeking a preliminary decision on fairness of domestic enquiry - Labour Court treated approving authority as a quasi-judicial authority not superior to Labour Court, noted that parties had let in evidence and were cross-examined before approving authority, treated approving authority’s finding on correctness of domestic enquiry as beyond jurisdiction and a nullity, and directed Management to adduce evidence afresh on preliminary issue of fairness of domestic enquiry - Whether Conciliation Officer erred in discussing evidence and drawing his own conclusion regarding charges on basis of evidence - Held, yes - Whether Labour Court could not decide issue regarding correctness of domestic enquiry as though sitting in an appeal against approval by Conciliation Officer - Held, yes - Whether if Labour Court prima facie found that prejudice was caused to employee for reason of domestic enquiry not being carried out in accordance with law, it could grant permission to Management to let in evidence to establish that domestic enquiry was conducted properly - Held, yes - Whether therefore, impugned order passed by Labour Court was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 20, 21, 22 and 23]LABOUR LAWS: Where Management terminated a workman after a domestic enquiry for serious misconduct and Conciliation Officer approved termination, but Labour Court treated officer’s findings as beyond jurisdiction, Labour Court could not decide correctness of enquiry as though sitting in appeal over such approval, but could allow Management to lead evidence if prima facie prejudice was shown, making Labour Court’s order liable to be set aside

It is clear from the law declared by the Supreme Court in the case of Uttam Chand v. ITO [1982] 133 ITR 909, that when the penalty proceedings are set aside or cancelled by the competent authority, on the same allegations the prosecution cannot be continued. But, in the instant case, the proceedings had not reached finality since the Department had already preferred an appeal before the Tribunal against the order of the Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) who cancelled the penalty proceedings.

In such circumstances, the prosecution could not be quashed. However, it had to await the result of the Tribunal. In case the Department succeeds before the Tribunal the prosecution may continue from the stage it stood and if the Department ultimately fails in its appeal before the Tribunal, the prosecution cannot be allowed to go on. What exactly would be the result could not be anticipated as on today. In that view of the matter, the proceedings before the Criminal Court could be stayed till the disposal of the appeals filed by the Department before the Tribunal.

The instant petitioner was accordingly disposed of.

HEADNOTE: Section 276C, read with sections 277 and 278 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Offences and prosecutions - Wilful attempt to evade tax - Assessment year 1981-82 - Whether, in case of an assessee who has filed a petition in High Court against order of Tribunal refusing to refer case and such petition has been admitted for hearing, prosecution proceedings separately initiated can be quashed - Held, no - Whether a mere expectation of success in some proceeding in appeal or reference under Act cannot come in way of institution of criminal proceedings under sections 276C and 277 - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1981-82, petitioner-firm, with three other petitioners as partners, submitted return of income disclosing a loss of Rs. 22,198. They also showed the payment of interest to a firm 'MK' to the tune of Rs. 34,721 and further disclosed that they had received loan from 'BKL' to the tune of Rs. 21,000. The ITO did not accept this contention. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted petitioner's appeal. The Tribunal, however, accepted appeal by department and found that loss shown as above and the loan from 'BKL' was not correct. The petitioner's reference application was dismissed by the Tribunal. Thereafter, they filed a petition in the High Court which had been admitted for hearing. During the pendency of these proceedings the ITO filed a criminal case against the petitioner under sections 276C, 277 and 278. The Court recorded the evidence and framed charges. The petitioner's revision against the framing of charges had been dismissed by Addl. Sessions Judge.

On petition under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 for quashing the proceedings, it was contended by the petitioner that the continuance of two separate proceedings would be unjust and that the petitioner would be put to double jeopardy. On the other hand, the respondent contended that merely because petitioner was contesting the assessment order or appellate order, it could not be said that prosecution was wholly baseless.

HELD: Civil Court decision or a decision of the civil proceedings is relevant in a criminal prosecution, but criminal courts are required to reach an independent finding and conclusion. There is no provision in law which provides that the prosecution for the offences cannot be launched until the assessment proceedings initiated against the assessee are completed. Further, a mere expectation of success is some proceedings in appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of the institution of the criminal proceedings under sections 276C and section 277. In the criminal case all the ingredients of the offence in question have to be established in order to secure the conviction of the accused. The criminal court, no doubt, has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and in an appropriate case it may drop the proceedings in the light of an order passed under the Act. It does not, however, mean that the result of a proceeding under the Act would be binding on the Criminal Court. In view of the above opinion expressed by the Apex Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO [1984] 149 ITR 696, it could not be said, in the instant case, that merely because a proceeding under the Act was pending, the prosecution under sections 276 and 277 could not be started or that the proceedings in any way deserved to be quashed. Since the two proceedings are different and the standard of proof in both the proceedings are also different, it would not be proper to quash the criminal prosecution, merely because proceedings under the Act in appeal or reference were pending.

Accordingly, the petition was dismissed.

In the proceeding note dated 5-6-1992, the authority, after taking note of the fact that the appellant had been discharged by a criminal court, noted that administrative action can still be initiated against the appellant since the effect of a discharge is that the appellant was neither 'acquitted nor convicted'. Based on this understanding, the authority proceeded to initiate disciplinary action against the appellant. [Para 17]

■ This understanding, at first glance, is fallacious. Discharge is a pre-trial termination of proceedings for lack of evidence. As and when ordered, discharge signifies and reinforces the position that there is no material against the accused for him to stand trial. Whereas, acquittal is a posttrial outcome declaring the accused either innocent due to lack of credible material or on account of grant of the benefit of doubt. Insufficient evidence to even frame charges for standing trial would lead to a discharge while evidence presented not proving guilt leads to acquittal. In that sense, an accused discharged of a criminal offence stands on a better footing than an accused who is finally acquitted after a full-fledged trial. It is not the law that an accused, unless he is acquitted, must still carry the label on his forehead that he is accused of a criminal offence. Once an accused has been discharged, he is entitled to avail of all benefits that are otherwise available to an acquitted person and cannot be placed in a less advantageous position. The Court is left surprised at the understanding of the officer who prepared the proceeding note. [Para 18]

■

In support of the Court's view of discharge standing on a 'better footing' than acquittal, one may profitably refer to the decision of this Court in Yuvraj Laxmilal Kanther v. State of Maharashtra 2025 SCC OnLine SC 520 holding that Acquittal is at the end of the trial process, may be for a technicality or on benefit of doubt or the prosecution could not prove the charge against the accused; but when an accused is discharged, it means that there are no materials to justify launch of a criminal trial against the accused. Once he is discharged, he is no longer an accused.[Para 19]

■

At this juncture, it is apposite to refer to the decision of the three-Judge Bench of this Court in Harjeet Singh Sandhu (2001) 5 SCC 593 again. [Para 20]

■

The said decision supports the case of the armed forces, inasmuch as it recognizes their authority to take disciplinary action even in circumstances where the option of convening a court martial has become time-barred. In this regard, paragraphs 43 and 44 of the said decision are relevant holding that Major Radha Krishan case [(1996) 3 SCC 507 : 1996 SCC (L&S) 761] lays down propositions too broad to be acceptable to the extent it holds that once the period of limitation for trial by court martial is over, the authorities cannot take action under Rule 14(2). Court also do not agree with the proposition that for the purpose of Rule 14(2), impracticability is a concept different from impossibility (or impermissibility, for that matter). The view of the Court in that case should be treated as confined to the facts and circumstances of that case alone. The submission of the Additional Solicitor-General that the case of Dharam Pal Kukrety [(1985) 2 SCC 412 : 1985 SCC (Cri) 222] being a three-Judge Bench decision of this Court, should have been placed before the two-Judge Bench which heard and decided Major Radha Krishan case (supra) is agreeable. Reverting back to the two cases under appeal, it is opined that the High Court was not right in allowing the two writ petitions filed by Harjeet Singh Sandhu and Harminder Kumar, respectively, by placing reliance on the decision of this Court in Major Radha Krishan case (supra) and holding that the exercise of power under section 19 read with Rule 14 by the Chief of the Army Staff was vitiated solely on account of the bar of limitation created by section 122.[Para 21]

■

The aforesaid paragraphs were duly considered and relied upon by the Division Bench while passing the impugned order, on the basis of which it was held that the disciplinary action against the appellant were not time-barred. The Court quite agrees with this part of the impugned order. [Para 22]

■

However, significantly, another crucial aspect of the very same decision - one that squarely operates against the armed forces - appears to have escaped the attention of the Division Bench. [Para 23]

In the instant case, the penalty was levied by the ITO on the facts and circumstances before him de hors any judgment or opinion of the Magistrate or any other Court. The orders of the criminal court were not even pronounced by the date of the judgment of the AAC. The Tribunal also confirmed the levy of penalty on the facts and circumstances of the case, unrelated to and without reference to the judgment of the Magistrate. After having come to that conclusion, it merely referred to the argument of the department based upon the judgment and order of the Magistrate, but it neither referred to the contents of the said order nor to the conclusion of the Magistrate but reiterated that it had confirmed the penalty on the facts and circumstances before it and for reasons already recorded by it. On appeal to the Supreme Court: HELD: During suspension, relationship of master and servant continues between the employer and the employee. However, the employee is forbidden to perform his official duties. Thus, suspension order does not put an end to the service. Suspension means the action of debarring for the time being from a function or privilege or temporary deprivation of working in the office. In certain cases, suspension may cause stigma even after exoneration in the departmental proceedings or acquittal by the Criminal Court, but it cannot be treated as a punishment even by any stretch of imagination in strict legal sense. [Para 7]

The power of suspension should not be exercised in an arbitrary manner and without any reasonable ground or as vindictive misuse of power. Suspension should be made only in a case where there is a strong prima facie case against the delinquent employee and the allegations involving moral turpitude, grave misconduct or indiscipline or refusal to carry out the orders of superior authority are there, or there is a strong prima facie case against him, if proved, would ordinarily result in reduction in rank, removal or dismissal from service. The authority should also take into account all the available material as to whether in a given case, it is advisable to allow the delinquent to continue to perform his duties in the office or his retention in office is likely to hamper or frustrate the inquiry. [Para 9]

In view of the above, the law on the issue can be summarised to the effect that suspension order can be passed by the competent authority considering the gravity of the alleged misconduct i.e., serious act of omission or commission and the nature of evidence available. It cannot be actuated by mala fide, arbitrariness, or for ulterior purpose. Effect on public interest due to the employee's continuation in office is also a relevant and determining factor. The facts of each case have to be taken into consideration as no formula of universal application can be laid down in this regard. However, suspension order should be passed only where there is a strong prima facie case against the delinquent, and if the charges stand proved, would ordinarily warrant imposition of major punishment i.e., removal or dismissal from service, or reduction in rank etc. [Para 10]

Long period of suspension does not make the order of suspension invalid. However, in State of H.P. v. B.C. Thakur [1994] SCC (L & S) 835, the Supreme Court held that where for any reason it is not possible to proceed with the domestic enquiry the delinquent may not be kept under suspension. [Para 12]

There cannot be any doubt that the Rules 1965 are a self contained code and the order of suspension can be examined in the light of the statutory provisions to determine as to whether the suspension order was justified. Undoubtedly, the delinquent cannot be considered to be any better off after the charge sheet has been filed against him in the court on conclusion of the investigation than his position during the investigation of the case itself. [Para 13]

Suspension is a device to keep the delinquent out of the mischief range. The purpose is to complete the proceedings unhindered. Suspension is an interim measure in aid of disciplinary proceedings so that the delinquent may not gain custody or control of papers or take any advantage of his position. More so, at this stage, it is not desirable that the Court may find out as which version is true when there are claims and counter claims on factual issues. The Court cannot act as if it an appellate forum de hors the powers of judicial review. [Para 14]

There is nothing on record which reflects that regular enquiry was not conducted by the authority concerned and admittedly, no such objection was taken even before the appellate authority. Further admitted fact remains that during enquiry proceedings the employee had never claimed either before the Enquiry Officer or in his reply or before the disciplinary authority or even in the departmental appeal that he was on leave for a certain period out of the total period mentioned in the charge levelled against him and only submission made by the appellant-petitioner was that he could not join duty due to his illness. A writ Court has the jurisdiction in such proceedings to only ensure that the person aggrieved has had a fair trial and that principle of natural justice was followed while deciding the case and as to whether the punishment given is proportionate to the offence committed. ■ In Central Industrial Security Force v. Abrar Ali, [2017] 12 taxmann.com 894 (SC)/(2017) 4 SCC 507, the Supreme Court held that, "In State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur v. Nemi Chand Nalwaiya reported in (2011) 4 SCC 584, this Court held as follows: It is now well settled that the courts will not act as an appellate court and reassess the evidence led in the domestic inquiry, nor interfere on the ground that another view is possible on the material on record. If the inquiry has been fairly and properly held and the findings are based on evidence, the question of adequacy of the evidence or the reliable nature of the evidence will not be grounds for interfering with the findings in departmental enquiries. Therefore, courts will not interfere with findings of fact recorded in departmental enquiries, except where such findings are based on no evidence or where they are clearly perverse. The test to find out perversity is to see whether a tribunal acting reasonably could have arrived at such conclusion or finding, on the material on record. The courts will however interfere with the findings in disciplinary matters, if principles of natural justice or statutory regulations have been violated or if the order is found to be arbitrary, capricious, mala fide or based on extraneous considerations. (Vide B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India [(1995) 6 SCC 749: 1996 SCC (L&S) 80: (1996) 32 ATC 44], Union of India v. G. Ganayutham [(1997) 7 SCC 463: 1997 SCC (L&S) 1806], Bank of India v. Degala Suryanarayana [(1999) 5 SCC 762: 1999 SCC (L&S) 1036] and High Court of Judicature at Bombay v. Shashikant S. Patil. In Union of India & Ors. v. P. Gunasekaran reported in (2015) 2 SCC 610, this Court held as follows: Despite the well-settled position, it is painfully disturbing to note that the High Court has acted as an appellate authority in the disciplinary proceedings, re-appreciating even the evidence before the inquiry officer. The finding on Charge I was accepted by the disciplinary authority and was also endorsed by the Central Administrative Tribunal. In disciplinary proceedings, the High Court is not and cannot act as a second court of first appeal. The High Court, in exercise of its powers under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India, shall not venture into reappreciation of the evidence. The High Court can only see whether: (a) the inquiry is held by a competent authority. (b) the inquiry is held according to the procedure prescribed in that behalf. (c) there is violation of the principles of natural justice in conducting the proceedings. (d) the authorities have disabled themselves from reaching a fair conclusion by some considerations extraneous to the evidence and merits of the case. (e) the authorities have allowed themselves to be influenced by irrelevant or extraneous considerations. (f) the conclusion, on the very face of it, is so wholly arbitrary and capricious that no reasonable person could ever have arrived at such conclusion. (g) the disciplinary authority had erroneously failed to admit the admissible and material evidence. (h) the disciplinary authority had erroneously admitted inadmissible evidence which influenced the finding. (i) the finding of fact is based on no evidence. Under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India, the High Court shall not: (i) re-appreciate the evidence. (ii) interfere with the conclusions in the inquiry, in case the same has been conducted in accordance with law. (iii) go into the adequacy of the evidence. (iv) go into the reliability of the evidence. (v) interfere, if there be some legal evidence on which findings can be based. (vi) correct the error of fact however grave it may appear to be. (vii) go into the proportionality of punishment unless it shocks its conscience." [Para 21]

Section 21A contains provisions for constitution of a Board of Discipline. Sub-section (3) of section 21A provides that where the Board of Discipline is of the opinion that a member is guilty of professional or other misconduct as specified in the First Schedule, it shall afford to the member an opportunity of being heard and may, thereafter, take any one of the actions as specified therein. Section 21B contains provisions relating to the Disciplinary Committee. [Para 15]

The First Schedule is divided into four parts. Part I of the First Schedule specifies certain acts or omissions, which renders a Chartered Accountant in practice guilty of professional misconduct. Part II of the First Schedule relates to professional misconduct in relation to members of an Institute in service. Part III of the First Schedule relates to professional misconduct. Part III lists out certain instances which would deem to be professional misconduct on the part of a member of the ICAI, irrespective of whether the said member is in practice or not. Part IV of the First Schedule lists out other misconduct. [Para 17]

Part IV of the First Schedule the expression 'other misconduct' includes any conduct, which brings disrepute to the profession or the ICAI as a result of an action whether or not related to professional work. Thus, it is not necessary that the misconduct complained of should be a conduct in exercise of the profession of Chartered Accountancy. Any conduct, which tends to bring disrepute, would be a subject matter of proceedings under Chapter V. [Para 18]

In view of the above, it is unable to accept the contention that the Board of Discipline does not have the jurisdiction to examine the alleged misconduct on the part of the petitioner. Clause (2) of Part-IV of the First Schedule is wide, and would include within its scope, any conduct that would tend to bring disrepute to the profession or the Institute. If a Chartered Accountant is found to have been guilty in outraging the modesty of a woman and/or other offences involving moral turpitude, it would not be inapposite for the Board of Discipline to also conclude that the conduct did, in fact, lower the dignity of the profession. In this view, is not able to accept that the proceedings before the Board of Discipline are without jurisdiction. [Para 22]

It is relevant to mention that the standards of proof as required in disciplinary proceedings and criminal proceedings are different. Whereas, the standard of proof as required in the criminal proceedings is beyond reasonable doubt, the standard of proof as required in Disciplinary proceedings is preponderance of probability. Whilst, it is correct that the Board of Discipline has no jurisdiction to sentence the petitioner, it would be erroneous to contend that the Board of Discipline does not have the jurisdiction, to examine the allegations made against the petitioner, in the context of determining whether the petitioner is guilty of other misconduct as defined under Part-IV of the Schedule-I. There may be cases where it may be apposite to await the decision in a trial, and the Board of Discipline has the power to defer the consideration of the complaint in such cases. However, that is a matter of exercising discretion and cannot be considered as denuding the Board of its jurisdiction. [Para 23]

Thus, instant court is refraining from expressing any opinion on the merits of the complaint made by R2, as the question whether the petitioner is guilty of other misconduct is yet to be decided by the Board of Discipline. There is no reason for instant Court to believe that the Board of Discipline will not give the matter the consideration it deserves. Further, if the petitioner is aggrieved by any decision rendered by the Board of Discipline, he has the remedy of an appeal before the Appellate Authority under section 22G. [Para 24]

than anything else, paragraph No.19 of the judgment of the Apex Court in Lakshmidevi Sugar Mills v. PT. Ram Sarup AIR 1957 SC 82(4 Judges bench) dealt with section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950 which in substance is pari materia with section 33 when it comes to nature of enquiry is not brought to the notice of the Division Bench of this Court. [Para 30]

■ The aforementioned paragraph would lead to the inevitable conclusion that while exercising jurisdiction under section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal Act), 1950 which is similar to section 33 when it comes to the nature of enquiry, the authority has to consider whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper and then, has to proceed to decide as to whether approval sought is to be granted or not by considering other requirements. This being the position, the jurisdiction of the authority under section 33, is adjudicatory on the question whether the domestic enquiry is fair and proper. Though the judgment in Lakshmidevi Sugar Mills supra is quoted in RPG Cables supra, it appears paragraphs extracted above are not brought to the notice of the Division Bench of this Court. [Para 31]

■

The said judgement would lead to the conclusion that while dealing with an application under section 33(2)(b) of Act, 1947 if the authority gives a finding and holds that the enquiry was not fair and proper and thereafter permits the parties to lead evidence afresh on the charges levelled, then in such situation the defect in enquiry gets cured. In such an event, in a subsequent proceeding under section 10, there cannot be any further enquiry relating to the fairness of the disciplinary enquiry. [Para 32]

■

Though judgments in G. McKenzie and Punjab National Bank Ltd. supra at the first glance indicate that the jurisdiction under section 33(2)(b) is limited to consider prima facie aspects and not adjudicatory, on consideration of the factual background in which those judgments are rendered one cannot but conclude that jurisdiction exercised while refusing or granting approval under section 33(2)(b), is adjudicatory on few aspects namely, "Whether the domestic enquiry is fair and proper, which in its fold may include few aspects like, compliance of principles of natural justice, compliance of requirements of the Standing Orders governing domestic enquiry or compliance of any other binding contract of employment, payment of wages as provided under section 33(2)(b)?" [Para 33]

■

After considering the above aspects, if the Authority takes a final call approving the punishment imposed, then the order granting approval for the punishment is neither an adjudication on the merits of the finding in the domestic enquiry nor on the proportionality of the punishment. It is in this context, it has been held that the scope of enquiry under section 33(2)(b) is limited to lifting the ban on the punishment. [Para 34]

■

The interpretation that the scope of enquiry under section 33(2)(b) is limited cannot be stretched to contend that the finding as to whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper is not on adjudication. For the reasons recorded above, it is held that the finding on the issue relating to fairness of domestic enquiry is adjudicatory. And said question cannot be revisited in an industrial dispute challenging the penalty. [Para 35]

■

In the case on hand, the Court has secured the records pertaining to the proceeding under section 33(2)(b) and after going through the said records, it is noticed that the parties have led evidence on the issue relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry. Later, the finding is recorded holding that the enquiry was fair and proper, and approval is granted for dismissal of the employee. [Para 36]

■

Conclusions: (a) The enquiry under section 33(2)(b), as to whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper, is adjudicatory. (b) The enquiry under section 33(2)(b) as to whether domestic enquiry was fair and proper (rendered after recording of evidence before the authority) is binding on the parties to the proceeding as the authority has the jurisdiction to adjudicate on the fairness of the domestic enquiry and said finding cannot be re-agitated in a subsequent industrial dispute assailing the order of penalty as it operates as Res judicata between the same parties in a subsequent proceeding. (c) The Authority under section 33(2)(b) cannot adjudicate on the merits of the finding in the domestic enquiry or on the penalty, as it has no jurisdiction to adjudicate on the merits of the findings in a domestic enquiry. Those questions have to be adjudicated in a subsequent industrial dispute, if raised. [Para 37]

HEADNOTE: Section 276C/277 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Offences and prosecution - Wilful attempt to evade tax, etc. - Criminal proceedings were initiated against assessee-firm under sections 276C and 277 for allegedly making false entries in its account books and for false verification of its stock so as to avoid income-tax - While Commissioner (Appeals) deleted major portion of suppressed income, appeal thereagainst was still pending before Tribunal - Meanwhile civil writ petition filed by assessee was admitted - Whether mere expectation of success in civil writ petition could come in way of institution of criminal proceedings under sections 276C and 277 - Held, no - Whether since criminal court has to judge case independently on evidence placed before it and trial court is, therefore, not supposed to await decision of civil writ petition, proceedings in criminal complaint could not be stayed - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was criminally charged for having allegedly made false entries in account books and improperly verified stocks so as to evade income-tax. The first appellate authority did not accept revenue's allegation regarding improper verification of stock whereupon revenue filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The assessee contended before the trial court that since discrepancies in the stock of assessee on basis of which prosecution was launched against it had been set aside the criminal proceedings were no longer maintainable. The trial court, accepting revenue's contention that matter was sub judice in the Tribunal, held that even if order passed by appellate authority be taken at face value, it did not in any way absolve assessee of its liability under section 276C. The assessee's revision petition against this order was dismissed.

On petition seeking quashing of criminal proceedings assessee prayed that since matter was sub judice and since its civil writ petition had already been admitted, criminal proceedings be stayed till decision of the writ petition.

HELD: Following the decision of the Supreme Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO [1984] 149 ITR 696, it was to be held that mere expectation of success in a civil writ petition could not come in the way of institution of criminal proceedings under sections 276C and 277. The criminal court has to judge the case independently on the evidence placed before it and the trial court was not supposed to await the decision of the civil writ petition. The petition was, therefore, dismissed.

Legislative intent that criminal proceedings should be different and independent from adjudication proceedings is highlighted in Section 127 which clearly shows that the two proceedings do not affect each other; hence order of acquittal by criminal court does not invalidate an order of penalty by the Department. "Even though the petitioner might have been acquitted in these criminal proceedings, so far as adjudication and penalty proceedings are concerned, they stand entirely on a different footing. The legislature has contemplated that for alleged contravention of the provisions, the concerned delinquent can be proceed depart mentally by way of adjudication and penalty proceedings and can also be criminally prosecuted. These are two independent proceedings and one would not impinge on the other......On/acts, the criminal court, in the light of the burden of proof which lay on the prosecution in such cases, found that the prosecution had failed to prove its case against the petitioner and acquitted him. That can certainly not be pressed in service for scuttling the departmental proceedings or for treating them as barred under any provision of law. As shown by us earlier, section 127 of the Act clearly indicates a contrary legislative intention."

2. Delay in initiation of proceedings was not unreasonable enough to render proceedings subsequent to issue of show cause notice unauthorised as evidenced by the facts of the case which show that the notice was issued within reasonable time.

"Whether delay in a given case is reasonable or not depends upon the facts of each case. On the facts of the present case, nothing could be shown to as by Mr. Vyas to indicate that issuance of the show cause notice within one year of the appellate order had in any way prejudiced the petitioner or that the said delay was so grossly unreasonable as to render the subsequent proceedings unauthorised. ......Thereafter, the department had come to this court and ultimately leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was rejected by a Division Bench of this Court on 10.1.1977 as seen from the order at annexure 'G'. Within two months and for days thereafter, show cause notice was issued by the first respondent. On the peculiar facts of this case, therefore, it cannot be said that the show cause notice was issued by the first respondent beyond reasonable time."

HEADNOTE: Section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 - Criminal proceedings - Powers of Court to postpone or adjourn - Assessee was prosecuted under sections 876 and 277 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) washed away all the omissions and commissions pointed out by the income-tax authorities - When appeal was subjudice before the Tribunal, criminal proceedings were initiated against assessee - Whether under section 309 criminal proceedings should be stayed, till Tribunal had given its decision after examination of order of Commissioner (Appeals) - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was prosecuted under sections 276 and 277 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for evasion of tax and filing of false statement. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) washed away all the omissions and commissions pointed out by the income-tax authorities. An appeal was preferred before the Tribunal. In the meantime, the criminal proceedings were initiated against the assessee.

On application under section 482:

HELD: Normally in economic offences, the provisions of section 482 should not be invoked and when prosecutions are launched, they should be allowed to take their own way because the assessee has every right to defend, here and there. However, in view of the decided cases by the Supreme Court, in some rare cases, the present Court cannot remain a silent spectator if it finds that there is going to be avoidable harassment, humiliation, torture to a citizen without there being any foundation, base or bedrock.

In the instant case, it was common ground that unless the Tribunal took a view different from the one which had been taken by the Commissioner, omissions and commissions pointed out by the prosecution on the basis of which evasion was alleged or false statement was attributed to the assessee, would, normally subject to the other circumstances order or evidence, became non-existent. At the moment, the judgment of the Commissioner was in existence as prima facie valid protective umbrella to the assessee. That being so, it would certainly be abuse of process of the Court and might even appear to be unusual and improbable if, for the same, the assessee was being prosecuted. It would, therefore, be in the interest of justice that by invoking the exercise of power under section 309 further proceedings were not taken till the judgment of the Commissioner which was subjudice before the Tribunal, was examined and the decision was given by the Tribunal.

Accordingly, the proceedings were stayed under section 309.

LABOUR LAWS: Where Management terminated a workman after a domestic enquiry for serious misconduct and Conciliation Officer approved termination, but Labour Court treated officer’s findings as beyond jurisdiction, Labour Court could not decide correctness of enquiry as though sitting in appeal over such approval, but could allow Management to lead evidence if prima facie prejudice was shown, making Labour Court’s order liable to be set aside

held before the Tribunal. Based on fresh enquiry before the Tribunal, the issues relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry and the merit of the charges were adjudicated. However, in the instant case, the enquiry was held to be valid, and later the order on termination was approved. There is no adjudication on the merits of the charges when the issue relating to the fairness of the enquiry was considered. Thus, the said judgment does not apply to the fact situation. [Para 25]

■ The union has relied on the judgments of the Division Bench of this Court in The Management of Amalgamated Electric Company Ltd. v. Workmen1975 LAB I C 879 and RPG Cables Limited v. G.M. Kulkarni [WA NO.600 of 2012 (L-RES), dated 26.11.2012] to contend that under section 33(2)(b), there is no jurisdiction to adjudicate the dispute. [Para 26]

■

In The Management of Amalgamated Electric Company and RPG Cables supra, the Division Bench of this Court has referred to the judgment in Punjab National Bank Ltd. supra, and this Court has already discussed the said judgment. This Court is of the view that the judgment in Punjab National Bank Ltd. supra does not lay down a law, that a finding under section 33(2)(b), holding the domestic enquiry as fair and proper, (that too after recording evidence in section 33(2)(b) proceeding), can be re-agitated in an Industrial dispute. [Para 27]

■

Moreover, it is not forthcoming from the facts in The Management of Amalgamated Electric Company supra as to whether any evidence was recorded by the parties on an application under section 33(2)(b). [Para 28]

■

More than anything else, paragraph No.19 of the judgment of the Apex Court in Lakshmidevi Sugar Mills v. PT. Ram Sarup AIR 1957 SC 82(4 Judges bench) dealt with section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950 which in substance is pari materia with section 33 when it comes to nature of enquiry is not brought to the notice of the Division Bench of this Court. [Para 30]

■

The aforementioned paragraph would lead to the inevitable conclusion that while exercising jurisdiction under section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal Act), 1950 which is similar to section 33 when it comes to the nature of enquiry, the authority has to consider whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper and then, has to proceed to decide as to whether approval sought is to be granted or not by considering other requirements. This being the position, the jurisdiction of the authority under section 33, is adjudicatory on the question whether the domestic enquiry is fair and proper. Though the judgment in Lakshmidevi Sugar Mills supra is quoted in RPG Cables supra, it appears paragraphs extracted above are not brought to the notice of the Division Bench of this Court. [Para 31]

■

The said judgement would lead to the conclusion that while dealing with an application under section 33(2)(b) of Act, 1947 if the authority gives a finding and holds that the enquiry was not fair and proper and thereafter permits the parties to lead evidence afresh on the charges levelled, then in such situation the defect in enquiry gets cured. In such an event, in a subsequent proceeding under section 10, there cannot be any further enquiry relating to the fairness of the disciplinary enquiry. [Para 32]

■

Though judgments in G. McKenzie and Punjab National Bank Ltd. supra at the first glance indicate that the jurisdiction under section 33(2)(b) is limited to consider prima facie aspects and not adjudicatory, on consideration of the factual background in which those judgments are rendered one cannot but conclude that jurisdiction exercised while refusing or granting approval under section 33(2)(b), is adjudicatory on few aspects namely, "Whether the domestic enquiry is fair and proper, which in its fold may include few aspects like, compliance of principles of natural justice, compliance of requirements of the Standing Orders governing domestic enquiry or compliance of any other binding contract of employment, payment of wages as provided under section 33(2)(b)?" [Para 33]

■

After considering the above aspects, if the Authority takes a final call approving the punishment imposed, then the order granting approval for the punishment is neither an adjudication on the merits of the finding in the domestic enquiry nor on the proportionality of the punishment. It is in this context, it has been held that the scope of enquiry under section 33(2)(b) is limited to lifting the ban on the punishment. [Para 34]

■

The interpretation that the scope of enquiry under section 33(2)(b) is limited cannot be stretched to contend that the finding as to whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper is not on adjudication. For the reasons recorded above, it is held that the finding on the issue relating to fairness of domestic enquiry is adjudicatory. And said question cannot be revisited in an industrial dispute challenging the penalty. [Para 35]

HEADNOTE: Section 276C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Offences and prosecution - Wilful attempt to evade tax, etc. - Respondents applied for stay of criminal proceedings in cases filed for offences punishable under the Income-tax Act on ground that appeals against assessments were pending before appellate authorities and Tribunal - Magistrate allowed work of recording evidence to proceed but stayed passing of order about framing of charges, discharge or acquittal of accused during pendency of appeals before income-tax authorities - High Court passed interim order staying proceedings in criminal cases - Whether since ultimate result of proceedings before appellate authorities would have a definite bearing on cases alleged against respondents, High Court was justified in passing interim order and its order called for no interference - Held, yes

FACT: Several cases were filed against the respondents in the Magistrate Court for offences punishable under the Act. As appeals were pending before the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal, the respondents filed applications for the stay of criminal proceedings. The Magistrate, after examining the position in law as to whether the findings of appellate authorities were relevant for the purpose of criminal proceedings and to avoid conflicting decisions of Criminal Court and appellate authorities, allowed the work of recording evidence to proceed but stayed the passing of order about framing of charges, discharge or acquittal of accused during pendency of appeals before income-tax authorities. Revision petitions were dismissed by the sessions court. The High Court granted an interim order staying the proceedings in the criminal cases.

On special leave petition :

HELD: The prosecution in criminal law and proceedings arising under the Act are undoubtedly independent proceedings and, therefore, there is no impediment in law for the criminal proceedings to proceed even during the pendency of the proceedings under the Act. However, a wholesome rule will have to be adopted in matters of this nature where courts have taken the view that when the conclusions arrived at by the appellate authorities have a relevance and bearing upon the conclusions to be reached in the case, necessarily one authority will have to await the outcome of the other authority.

In the present case, there was no claim of quashing of the proceedings. When ultimately the result to come out of the proceedings before the appellate authorities would have a definite bearing on the cases alleged against the respondents, the High Court was justified in granting the interim order it did and such an interim order did not call for interference.

The petitions were, therefore, dismissed.

EX/ST/VAT : Adjudication and criminal prosecution being separate proceedings, adjudication cannot be deferred on ground that criminal proceedings are pending and witnesses to be cross-examined in adjudication may be witnesses in prosecution proceedings also

a lesser penalty - Held, yes - Whether since dismissal order was wholly disproportionate, same was to be set aside, while leaving finding of misconduct undisturbed - Held, yes - Whether competent authority was to be directed to consider any punishment other than ultimate penalty of dismissal from service, after considering appellant’s long service, past record, age, nature of misconduct, absence or presence of financial loss, and other relevant circumstances - Held, yes [Paras 111.2 and 111.7] FACT: ■

The appellant, a clerical employee of the respondent–company, was appointed in 1985 and later promoted. Earlier service disputes included a transfer to Warora that was set aside. On 04.09.2006, she was suspended pending enquiry on allegations of indiscipline, insubordination, disobedience, tampering with official documents, negligence and misuse of company property. The suspension order recorded entitlement to subsistence allowance as per rules and required weekly reporting at Warora. A charge-sheet was issued on 19.09.2006. The domestic enquiry commenced in March 2008; on 25.03.2008, her request for time was declined, the enquiry proceeded ex parte, five witnesses were examined, and the Enquiry Officer submitted a report on 25.04.2008. A show-cause notice proposing dismissal was also issued on 25.04.2008.

■

The appellant challenged the show-cause notice by Complaint (ULP) No. 34 of 2008. On 29.11.2014, the Labour Court held that the enquiry was not fair and the finding was perverse. In Revision (ULP) No. 4 of 2015, the Industrial Court on 14.08.2015 set aside the Labour Court’s order and remanded the matter, permitting the respondent–management to establish misconduct by leading evidence before the Labour Court, as the domestic enquiry was found defective.

■

After remand, the respondent–management led evidence before the Labour Court. The appellant’s request to respond to the charge-sheet at that stage was declined. By judgment dated 27.06.2017, the Labour Court held the misconduct proved on the evidence led post-remand and also held the earlier show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008 legal and proper, dismissing Complaint (ULP) No. 34 of 2008.

■

On 12.07.2017, the respondent issued the dismissal order removing the appellant from service and directing that the suspension period be treated as punishment. The order recorded that no explanation was submitted to the show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008. No fresh show-cause notice on punishment was issued after the post-remand findings. The appellant’s Revision (ULP) No. 37 of 2017 against the Labour Court’s judgment dated 27.06.2017 was dismissed by the Industrial Court on 08.06.2018, and was not carried further.

■

Separately, the appellant challenged the dismissal order by Complaint (ULP) No. 28 of 2017, inter alia, on the grounds that the Executive Engineer lacked competence since she was appointed by the Superintending Engineer, that a fresh notice under Regulation 88(j) was required after the de novo proof of misconduct before the Labour Court, that subsistence allowance was not paid during the entire suspension, that treating the suspension period as punishment was illegal, and that the dismissal was disproportionate. By judgment dated 08.08.2019, the Labour Court dismissed Complaint (ULP) No. 28 of 2017, holding that misconduct could not be reopened; the Executive Engineer was competent to impose dismissal; no fresh show-cause notice was required; the treatment of the suspension period as punishment was valid; and the penalty was not shockingly disproportionate. In Revision (ULP) No. 14 of 2019, the Industrial Court on 18.01.2023 dismissed the revision and affirmed the Labour Court’s judgment.

■

The appellant’s writ petition (No. 1200 of 2023) before the High Court was dismissed on 05.04.2024, upholding the concurrent findings on competency of the disciplinary authority, form of the dismissal order, show-cause notice, treatment of the suspension period, and proportionality; her review application was also dismissed on 11.11.2024.

On appeal to the Supreme Court.

HELD: ■

WHETHER THE DISMISSAL ORDER DATED 12.07.2017 WAS PASSED BY THE COMPETENT AUTHORITY ?

■

The Appellant has laid considerable emphasis on the fact that she was appointed by the Superintending Engineer but dismissed by the Executive Engineer. According to her, the dismissal order is invalid because it was passed by an authority lower than the appointing authority. [Para 30]

■

The courts below examined the applicable MSEDCL Employees Service Regulations and found that the Appellant was a Pay Grade-III employee. They further held that, under the relevant regulations and schedules governing disciplinary action, the Executive Engineer was competent to impose punishment on an employee belonging to that category. The High Court also considered the Appellant's reliance on the schedule relating to transfers and held that the said schedule did not govern dismissal from service. [Para 31]

Magistrate had yet not taken cognizance of the offences alleged to have been committed by the accused named therein but merely had referred the complaint to the police for investigation and to file a challan/charge sheet if there was evidence. From the above, it was clear that there was no criminal proceeding pending so as to tantamount to a parallel proceeding as contended by the respondents. The application for stay was liable to be dismissed on that ground alone. Therefore, the arguments advanced by the respondents/applicants that they would be prejudiced by the continuance of the instant proceedings were without any basis and were not tenable. Relying on the judgment of the Supreme Court in Karamchand Ganga Pershad v. Union of India [1970] 3 SCC 694, it can be said that the proceedings before the CLB can continue even when criminal case is pending which may have been filed by either parties against each other. For the assessment year 1970-71, the assessee-firm filed a return showing certain income. On reference :

Court do not entitle such a court to direct that the order of conviction should stand suspended The conviction can only be set aside.

The contention that the expression 'order' covers even the order of conviction cannot be accepted because the expression used by the Legislature is 'execution of the sentence or order'. The section makes it clear that the appellate court can suspend the execution of the sentence or the execution of the order and in respect of the order of conviction, there is no question of execution and consequently suspension. The Appellate Court exercising powers under sub-section (1) of section 389 is not concerned with the consequences which may flow from the order of conviction in regard to the provisions of some other statute. The Appellate Court which entertains appeal against the order of conviction is entitled to suspend the execution of the sentence or the orders which flow as a consequence of the judgment either of conviction or acquittal and such a Criminal Appellate Court is not concerned with the consequences in respect of some other statutes which are visited upon the person who is convicted by a Criminal Court. The submission that the order of conviction will have automatic impact with reference to some other statutes is devoid of any merit because the Legislature has taken sufficient precaution in respect of those other statutes to protect a person who has preferred an appeal against the order of conviction. As mentioned earlier, the recording of order of conviction against a director, will not automatically disqualify the director of a company from holding the post, in a case where appeal is preferred within the stipulated period of limitation or where the Central Government exempts such person or the company from disqualification. Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act provides that the disqualification shall not take effect until three months have elapsed from the date of conviction or, if an appeal or revision application against the order of conviction is preferred, then until that appeal or application is disposed of by the court. Section 11 of the Representation of the People Act confers power upon the Election Commission to remove any disqualification. It is, therefore, obvious that whenever the Legislature thought it fit, statutory provisions were made to lessen the rigour of the consequences of recording of conviction. The Legislature, in its wisdom, did not make any such provision under section 267 when conviction is recorded against the person who is a managing director. Therefore, it is not permissible for the appellate court which entertains the appeal against the order of conviction to suspend the order of conviction and the only power available under section 389(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is to suspend the execution of the sentence of the order, which expression does not include conviction. The mere fact that the order of conviction leads to some consequences in respect of provisions of other statutes is not sufficient for assuming powers which the Appellate Court does not possess under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The powers of the criminal court flow from the Code and it is not open for the criminal court to assume powers only because the convicted person is likely to suffer certain disqualification under the provisions of other statutes.

It was not possible to accept the respondents' argument that even assuming that provisions of sub-section (1) of section 389 do not confer power on the appellate court to direct suspension of the order of conviction, still such a power can be gathered from the provisions of section 482. Section 482 deals with the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under the Code or to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The respondent urged that the order of conviction could be suspended to secure the ends of justice. The submission was fallacious and could not be acceded to. The inherent powers cannot be exercised to find some means to pass orders which are not permissible under the Code. It could not be appreciated how it could be even suggested that conviction could be suspended to secure the ends of justice. In any event, it was not for the Criminal Appellate Court hearing an appeal to decide what the ends of justice were in respect of enforcement of provisions of some other statutes. The powers of the Appellate Court flow from the provisions of the Code and the contention that the Appellate Court hearing the criminal appeal should pass orders to avoid consequences flowing from the provisions of statutes like the Companies Act or the Representation of the People Act could not be accepted Such other statutes have taken care of the consequences which flow from the order of conviction recorded by the criminal court. The provisions of section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not at all attracted to claim that the order of conviction can be suspended by an order of the Court.

As regards the order of the Delhi High Court staying operation of the order of conviction of respondent No. 1, the order of the Delhi High Court could not be read as suspending the order of conviction and, even assuming it to be so, the Delhi High Court had no power to suspend the order of conviction. In any event, while determining whether respondent No. 1 was disqualified to hold the post of managing director under section 267 it was entirely immaterial what the Delhi High Court had contemplated while passing such order. The consequences flowing from the provisions of section 267 did not depend upon the passing of the order by the Delhi High Court. The right of respondent No. 1 to hold the post of managing director come to an end the moment the order of conviction was recorded.

■ The concept of fairness may require the Adjudicating Authority to furnish the copies of the documents upon which reliance has been placed by him to issue show cause notice requiring a notice to explain why an inquiry under section 16 of the Act, should not be initiated. To this extent, the principles of natural justice and concept of fairness are required to be read into rule 4(1) of the rules. The noticee is always entitled to satisfy the Adjudicating Authority that those very documents upon which reliance has been placed, do not make out even a prima facie case requiring any further inquiry. Therefore, all such documents relied on by the Authority are required to be furnished to the notice enabling him to show a proper cause as to why an inquiry should not be held against him. [Para 42]

Therefore, it was held in the case of Natwar Singh (supra), that the documents and the evidence relied upon by the Adjudicatory Authority, must be made available to the accused, to ensure reasonable opportunity of being heard and also to ensure the fairness of the procedure. The duty of adequate disclosure is only an additional procedural safeguard in order to ensure the attainment of the fairness. A distinction was drawn between the stage of enquiry under rule 4(1) and the final adjudication and it was observed that at the stage of show cause notice, it is sufficient that only documents that are relied upon are disclosed. [Para 43]

The logic behind such disclosure is the likelihood of being influenced by the documents referred in the enquiry whether relied or not. It was observed in the case of Khudiram Das v. State of West Bengal, (1960) 1 SCR 820 in the context of preventive detection, that it can hardly be disputed that if there was before the District Magistrate material against the detenu, which is of a highly damaging character and has nexus and relevancy with the object of detention, and proximity with the time when the subjective satisfaction forming part of the detention order was arrived at, it would be legitimate for the Court to infer that such material must have influenced the District Magistrate in arriving at the subjective satisfaction and the Court would refuse to accept the bald statement of the District Magistrate that he did not take any material into account and excluded it from consideration. The human mind does not function in compartments. [Para 44]

■

When it receives impressions from different sources, it is the totality of the impressions, which goes into the making of the decision. It is not possible to analyse and dissect the impressions and predicate which impressions went into the making of the decision. Nor is it any easy exercise to erase the impression created by particular circumstances so as to exclude the influence of such impression in the decision-making process. [Para 45]

■

Therefore, where there is material before the District Magistrate, which is of the character as would have reasonable probability to influence the decision of a reasonable man, the Court would be reluctant to accept the ipse dixit of the District Magistrate that he was not so influenced and a fortiori, if such material is not disclosed to the detenu, the order of detention would be vitiated. This principle was again reaffirmed by the Constitution Bench of the Apex Court in the case of ECIL v. B. Karunakar, (1993) 4 SCC 727. The principles of natural justice require that the employee should have a fair opportunity to meet, explain and controvert it before he is condemned. It is negation of the tenets of justice and a denial of fair opportunity to the employee, to consider the findings recorded by a third party like an enquiry officer, without giving an opportunity to reply. Although the disciplinary authority is required to arrive at its own findings on the basis of the evidence, but it is equally true that the disciplinary authority takes into consideration the findings recorded by the enquiry officer along with the evidence on record. INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES ACT: Where employer dismissed petitioner solely due to an offence registration without conducting domestic enquiry and failed to reserve right to adduce evidence on misconduct in its written statement, Industrial Court erred in remanding matter for employer to prove misconduct and its order was to be set aside.

HEADNOTE: Section  33,  read with section  20,  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Conditions of service to remain unchanged under certain circumstances during pendency of proceedings - Whether proceedings before Tribunal are deemed to continue until date on which award becomes enforceable under Section 17A - Held, yes - Whether where award recording settlement, disposal or other closure has been made, legal pendency under Section 20(3) does not vanish because parties may feel that dispute has ended - Held, yes - Whether once it is held that proceedings were pending in eye of law on relevant date, compliance with Section 33(2)(b) became obligatory if employer intended to dismiss workman for misconduct not connected with dispute - Held, yes - Whether where termination of workman was effected during pendency of References and was in contravention of Section 33(2)(b), workman was to be reinstated in service to his original post, or to an equivalent post carrying same pay scale, status and service benefits, with continuity of service for all purposes including seniority, increments and retiral benefits, subject to applicable rules - Held, yes - Whether workman was to be entitled to full back wages from date of termination till commencement of grocery shop in 2016, fifty percent back wages for period from 2016 till closure of grocery shop during Covid period and full back wages thereafter till date of reinstatement - Held, yes [Paras 27, 28, 30, 39 and 40]

FACT: ■

A charge-sheet dated 12 October 2012 was issued to the workman alleging misconduct under various Standing Orders. A domestic enquiry was conducted, and on 31 July 2014 the Enquiry Officer held the workman guilty; the report was forwarded on 6 October 2014. The workman submitted an apology on 16 October 2014, and the recognised Union also requested a sympathetic view. An industrial dispute was pending between the company and the recognised Union, and during its subsistence an MoU dated 14 August 2014 was executed stating that 13 of 18 suspended workmen would be taken back subject to conditions at the management’s discretion, while enquiries against the remaining five, including the workman, would continue. After considering the apology and the Union’s request, management decided to dismiss the workman, and he was terminated on 17 October 2014.

■

It was pleaded that he remained unemployed for about two years, then started a grocery business, and that the business suffered losses and was closed on 28 November 2021, after which he remained without gainful employment.

■

The workman filed a complaint under Section 33A challenging the dismissal as arbitrary and illegal and sought reinstatement with back wages, also alleging discriminatory treatment vis-à-vis 13 similarly situated workmen who were given minor punishment. By order dated 27 September 2019 on preliminary issues, the Tribunal held the domestic enquiry fair and proper and the findings not perverse.

■

By final Award dated 18 January 2024, the Tribunal declined reinstatement with back wages and awarded compensation of Rs. 7 lakhs, while recording that the termination occurred during pendency of References and thus amounted to breach of Section 33(2)(b).

■

On writ petitions before the High Court.

HELD: ■

Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is enacted as a provision of protection, made by Legislature with intention to preserve industrial peace during time when conciliation proceedings or adjudication proceedings are pending before competent authority. The object behind such provision is that when dispute between employer and workmen has reached legal forum, atmosphere between parties remains strained. At such stage, if employer is permitted to alter service conditions against workers, then pending proceedings may get influenced by pressure. Therefore, law intervenes and places temporary restraint upon employer's powers. In that sense, Section 33 is a statutory device for maintaining fairness. It keeps pending proceedings free from coercion. [Para 23]

■

Sub-section (1) of Section 33 deals with matters which are connected with pending industrial dispute. In such matters, Act requires prior permission in writing from authority before whom proceeding is pending. This shows that where subject matter of proposed action touches the dispute under consideration, employer cannot act and then justify later. Sub-section (2), however, addresses another category, namely matters not connected with pending dispute. There Act gives wider liberty to employer to proceed according to standing orders or contractual terms. Yet even there, if employer proposes discharge or dismissal of workman concerned in dispute, proviso imposes two mandatory pre-conditions. One month wages must be paid, and application for approval must be made before competent authority. Hence, even where misconduct is outside dispute, disciplinary power is not uncontrolled. [Para 24]

In the present case, if Tribunal allows the appeal on a permanent basis, the department cannot issue a show-cause notice for revocation of licence in view of the fact that no show-cause notice has been issued for revocation of licence and the regulations require that if there is a complaint of a misconduct licence should not be renewed. Assessees' claim is that the complaints of misconduct are not proven one. If they are proved against the assessees, the assessees' claim itself would render the assessee liable for non-renewal of licence. Under these circumstances, appeal was allowed with a condition that this decision would be purely temporary in nature subject to completion of the proceedings as a result of show-cause notice issued to the assessees. As regards charge sheet filed against the employee also, as and when the charge sheet gets completed and charges are framed by the court, based on the nature of charges framed and considering the issue of vicarious responsibility and the liability of the assessees as per the principles of vicarious responsibility, department will be free to reopen the issue relating to renewal of licence.

To sum up, Tribunal only set aside the order of non-renewal and not the proceedings for non-renewal. Department will have liberty to start proceedings at an appropriate time in line with observations above if and when matter reached to a certain stage in the court of law, or after the show-cause notice issued under customs Act reaches finality, the show-cause notice can be preceded further.

Section 14(2) states that a person aggrieved by an order pertaining to any service matter may make an application to the Tribunal. The application, therefore, lies against an "order". A show cause notice issued to the petitioner cannot, by any stretch of imagination, be treated as an "order". The order would follow the show cause notice, after the noticee tenders his response thereto, and the response is considered by the competent authority. [Para 25]

■ Thus, Section 14(2) clearly does not render a show cause notice issued to an officer amenable to challenge before the Tribunal. This position is also fortified when one refers to Section 3(o) to which Mr. Bhandari himself drew attention. Clause (iii) of Section 3(o) includes, within the meaning of "service matters", "summary disposal and trial where the punishment of dismissal is awarded". Thus, prior to the awarding of any punishment to the officer concerned, it cannot even be said that his grievance constitutes a "service matter". [Para 27]

■

Thus, the provisions of the AFT Act, too, do not support Mr. Bhandari's contention that the show cause notice was answerable to the Tribunal or that any appeal, against the recommendations of the ICC, would lie before the Tribunal so as to enable the petitioner to bypass the requirement of responding to the show cause notice. [Para 28]

■

Thus, the Supreme Court has clearly laid down the protocol to be followed in a case where there is an allegation of sexual harassment by an officer at the workplace. Briefly stated, the matter has to be referred to an ICC. However, the recommendations of the ICC do not put a full stop to the proceedings. If the ICC exonerates the officer, the matter may rest there. However, if the findings of the ICC are against the officer, of which the ICC finds the officer complicit, it constitutes actionable misconduct under the service rules, and disciplinary action has to follow. [Para 30]

■

The Supreme Court has, in its decision in Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India (2013) 1 SCC 311, modified the directions in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) 6 SCC 241 by clarifying that the findings of the ICC would constitute an inquiry report as envisaged in the service rules applicable to the officer and that, therefore, once the ICC rendered its findings, the ball would, so to speak, be in the Court of the disciplinary authority. It would be for the officer concerned to respond to the findings of the ICC, before the disciplinary authority, which would then take a conscious decision as to whether to exonerate the officer or, if the officer is found guilty, to punish him appropriately. [Para 31]
