■

However, significantly, another crucial aspect of the very same decision - one that squarely operates against the armed forces - appears to have escaped the attention of the Division Bench. [Para 23]

■ In Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra), while examining sections 19 and 125 of the Army Act and Rule 14 of the Army Rules, which are pari materia sections 19 and 124 of the AF Act and Rule 6 of the 1969 Rules, respectively, this Court observed that where the commanding officer, exercising discretion vested in him to choose between a trial by a criminal court and a court-martial, opts for trial before a criminal court, an acquittal of the accused by such court brings finality to the matter. In such circumstances, the initiation or continuation of disciplinary action would not be sustainable. [Para 24]

■

Though the law laid down in Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra) is on consideration of the provisions of the Army Act and the Army Rules, there is no reason why it would not squarely apply to a case covered by pari materia provisions of the AF Act and the AF Rules. [Para 25]

■

True though, as per Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra), initiation of administrative proceedings is barred when an accused is 'acquitted'; however, the Court finds no reason for the ratio of the decision to not apply in a case where the accused is 'discharged' (which stands on a better footing than acquittal, as discussed supra). Once the appellant has been discharged by the criminal court, that should mark the end of the matter. [Para 26]

■

Thus, the Air Force upon electing to have the alleged offence tried by the criminal court, it is clear (in view of the discussion above) that they then cannot fall back on either a court martial or any disciplinary action. Once the road is chosen, the traveller must walk it to the end. [Para 27]

■

Initiation of administrative proceedings for disciplinary action against the appellant is unhesitatingly held to be bad in law and non-est. [Para 28]

■

This reason alone is sufficient to allow the present appeal. However, the decision is not proposed to rest on this sole reason; the discussion is taken forward as to why, independent of the aforesaid discussion, the disciplinary action is also otherwise considered to be flawed. It is solely for the reason that the decision in Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra) is subsequent to the appellant's dismissal from service and the Court wishes to test whether, even in view of the law prevailing prior thereto, disciplinary action which had been taken was justified on facts and in the circumstances. [Para 29]

Reasons given in proceeding note dated 5-6-1992

■

The reasoning given in the proceeding note dated 5-6-1992 has been noted above. From the same, there is absolutely no discussion on the merits of the case. [Para 30]

■

What is found is that there was sufficient 'morally convincing evidence' against the appellant. Such an expression, vague and indeterminate in nature, falls far short of the standard required for recording findings in disciplinary proceedings. It neither discloses the material relied upon nor indicates the process of reasoning by which the authority arrived at its conclusion. [Para 31]

■

Further, as noted above at paragraph 2(l), the appellant, in his reply to the show cause notice, had raised various contentions which required due consideration by the competent authority. However, it is a matter of surprise that there is a complete absence of any discussion on such contentions, particularly concerning the lack of evidence and the illegality of the proceedings before the Court of Inquiry. Although some discussion was undertaken regarding the permissibility of initiating disciplinary proceedings after the appellant's discharge by a criminal court, even that aspect, in the Court's view, remains doubtful. While adverting to the appellant's reply, the authority merely noted their dissatisfaction in respect thereof, at paragraph 15 of the proceeding note dated 5-6-1992. [Para 32]

■

■

The narrow question of law that arises for consideration is the correct statutory interpretation of Rule 69(1)(c) of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972. The appellant contends that the expression "departmental or judicial proceedings" in Rule 69(1)(c) must be construed to mean that gratuity becomes payable upon the conclusion of either set of proceedings. [Para 11]

■

Such a submission totally misapprehends the nature of the Rule. As the learned Single Judge had rightly noted at the first instance, Rule 69(1)(c) operates as an 'embargo' or a statutory bar, not as an enabling provision. The use of the ordinary disjunctive "or" expands the scope of this bar, indicating that gratuity shall not be paid so long as either departmental or judicial proceedings are pending. [Para 12]

■

Applying the aforesaid reasoning, it is the construction advanced by the appellant that would in fact yield an anomalous result. Rule 69(1)(c) of the 1972 Rules has a wide import and operates in respect of any proceeding that may be pending against an employee at the time of retirement; indeed, the breadth of the provision reflects its protective character. If the appellant's interpretation were accepted, an employee could contend that once any one set of proceedings against him/her stands concluded, the embargo stands lifted and gratuity must be released. This would altogether defeat the purpose of the provision, which is to safeguard the financial interests of the State. [Para 13]

■

Even in the instant case, where both the proceedings stem from identical allegations, their nature, scope, and standard of proof remain fundamentally different. By way of illustration, consider if the converse were true i.e., the criminal case against the appellant had concluded in an acquittal due to failure to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It would nevertheless be possible that the appellant was eventually found liable in the pending departmental proceedings on a preponderance of probabilities. An acquittal in that case could not be determinative. If such an approach is impermissible in one direction, it cannot be countenanced in the other either. Moreover, this distinction assumes increased significance in the instant case, as the Inquiry Officer had expressly noted that the matter was sub judice and any definitive conclusion would rest on the outcome of the criminal trial. [Para 14]

■

The appellant relies on the above Rule to urge that the respondent Corporation would not be left remediless, as any amounts disbursed could be recovered in the event of a subsequent conviction. This submission has already been clearly negatived by the Division Bench. Simply put, the provision is downstream in its operation and cannot be invoked to justify the release of gratuity during the interregnum when proceedings are admittedly pending, on the premise that recovery could be effected at a later stage. [Para 16]

■

All of the appellant's remaining contentions pertain to questions of fact. The Court is not unmindful of his advanced age and the circumstance that he was exonerated in departmental proceedings. He has also brought to notice that the students accused in the CPMT paper leak, who had been charged under Sections 109, 420 and 120B of the IPC read with Section S-7 of the Himachal Pradesh Prevention of Malpractices at University, Board or other Specified Examinations Act, 1984, were acquitted thereof vide judgment dated 28.01.2016 in Criminal Case No. 68-2/2008. These aspects may, no doubt, lend some support to the appellant's case in the criminal trial, but cannot alter the statutory position governing the release of gratuity under Rule 69(1)(c) of the 1972 Rules. [Para 17]

■

Therefore, the Court finds no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment. The Appeal is, accordingly, dismissed. The direction issued by the High Court is reiterated and the Trial Court concerned is impressed upon to expedite the trial arising out of FIR No. 140/2006. [Para 18]

In the proceeding note dated 5-6-1992, the authority, after taking note of the fact that the appellant had been discharged by a criminal court, noted that administrative action can still be initiated against the appellant since the effect of a discharge is that the appellant was neither 'acquitted nor convicted'. Based on this understanding, the authority proceeded to initiate disciplinary action against the appellant. [Para 17]

■

This understanding, at first glance, is fallacious. Discharge is a pre-trial termination of proceedings for lack of evidence. As and when ordered, discharge signifies and reinforces the position that there is no material against the accused for him to stand trial. Whereas, acquittal is a posttrial outcome declaring the accused either innocent due to lack of credible material or on account of grant of the benefit of doubt. Insufficient evidence to even frame charges for standing trial would lead to a discharge while evidence presented not proving guilt leads to acquittal. In that sense, an accused discharged of a criminal offence stands on a better footing than an accused who is finally acquitted after a full-fledged trial. It is not the law that an accused, unless he is acquitted, must still carry the label on his forehead that he is accused of a criminal offence. Once an accused has been discharged, he is entitled to avail of all benefits that are otherwise available to an acquitted person and cannot be placed in a less advantageous position. The Court is left surprised at the understanding of the officer who prepared the proceeding note. [Para 18]

■

In support of the Court's view of discharge standing on a 'better footing' than acquittal, one may profitably refer to the decision of this Court in Yuvraj Laxmilal Kanther v. State of Maharashtra 2025 SCC OnLine SC 520 holding that Acquittal is at the end of the trial process, may be for a technicality or on benefit of doubt or the prosecution could not prove the charge against the accused; but when an accused is discharged, it means that there are no materials to justify launch of a criminal trial against the accused. Once he is discharged, he is no longer an accused.[Para 19]

■

At this juncture, it is apposite to refer to the decision of the three-Judge Bench of this Court in Harjeet Singh Sandhu (2001) 5 SCC 593 again. [Para 20]

■

The said decision supports the case of the armed forces, inasmuch as it recognizes their authority to take disciplinary action even in circumstances where the option of convening a court martial has become time-barred. In this regard, paragraphs 43 and 44 of the said decision are relevant holding that Major Radha Krishan case [(1996) 3 SCC 507 : 1996 SCC (L&S) 761] lays down propositions too broad to be acceptable to the extent it holds that once the period of limitation for trial by court martial is over, the authorities cannot take action under Rule 14(2). Court also do not agree with the proposition that for the purpose of Rule 14(2), impracticability is a concept different from impossibility (or impermissibility, for that matter). The view of the Court in that case should be treated as confined to the facts and circumstances of that case alone. The submission of the Additional Solicitor-General that the case of Dharam Pal Kukrety [(1985) 2 SCC 412 : 1985 SCC (Cri) 222] being a three-Judge Bench decision of this Court, should have been placed before the two-Judge Bench which heard and decided Major Radha Krishan case (supra) is agreeable. Reverting back to the two cases under appeal, it is opined that the High Court was not right in allowing the two writ petitions filed by Harjeet Singh Sandhu and Harminder Kumar, respectively, by placing reliance on the decision of this Court in Major Radha Krishan case (supra) and holding that the exercise of power under section 19 read with Rule 14 by the Chief of the Army Staff was vitiated solely on account of the bar of limitation created by section 122.[Para 21]

■

The aforesaid paragraphs were duly considered and relied upon by the Division Bench while passing the impugned order, on the basis of which it was held that the disciplinary action against the appellant were not time-barred. The Court quite agrees with this part of the impugned order. [Para 22]

revisional Court or before the Supreme Court in an application under article 136 for special leave to appeal. The process of criminal law including the trial, appeal and revision is a protracted one and it is difficult to visualise a situation where the Settlement Commission in a particular case shall take such a long time for disposing of the application and in granting immunity from criminal prosecution that the accused shall have lost all opportunities to take benefit of such an order granting immunity even before the appellate or the revisional Court. It is not possible to take the view that the Settlement Commission while exercising its exclusive jurisdiction under section 245F(2) may exercise the power of an income-tax authority and stay the prosecution and, hence, in the interest of justice and to obviate anamolous situation being created it is just and proper to stay the criminal prosecution. The Settlement Commission has no such jurisdiction. This is so for the reason that once a criminal proceeding has been validly instituted for committing any offence under Chapter XXII, no income-tax authority under the Act has been vested with the jurisdiction to stay the proceedings before the criminal court. Section 279(2) provides that any offence under this Chapter may either before or after the institution of the proceeding be compounded by the Commissioner or a Director General. Once the offence is compounded, the proceeding before the Criminal Court comes to an end and the question of stay of criminal proceeding does not arise. Criminal proceedings are proceedings independent of assessment proceedings. The question of either grant of sanction for prosecution or compounding the offence under section 279(1) and (2) is not before the Settlement Commission and, hence, keeping in view the provision of section245F(4), in the absence of any express direction of the Settlement Commission to the contrary, the income-tax authority can exercise its power under section 279(1) and (2) even after the Settlement Commission has allowed the application to be proceeded with and section 245F(2) cames into play. Be that as it may, the fact remained that since no income-tax authority under the Act has the authority to stay the criminal proceeding, the Settlement Commission has no such jurisdiction, either exclusive or concurrent.

The stay of criminal proceeding in all cases in which the Settlement Commission has allowed the application to be proceeded with also does not appear necessary for saving the provisions of section 245H from being rendered rendundant. If the criminal proceeding is allowed to continue and the accused is held not guilty and acquitted, the matter comes to an end. If the accused is convicted and immunity from criminal prosecution is subsequently granted by the Settlement Commissioner after recording necessary satisfaction under section 245H or the Commission simply passes favourable orders without granting immunity from such criminal prosecution, it should be open to the accused to challenge his conviction on such grounds either in appeal or revision or special leave to appeal under article 136 of the Constitution of India. Also, a favourable finding recorded by the Settlement Commission even in a case in which grant of immunity from criminal prosecution is refused is required to be considered by the criminal court when brought to its knowledge provided such a finding has a bearing on the merits of the case before the Court. For that matter even in cases where the criminal prosecution has been launched before the date of filing of the application before the Settlement Commission and the Commission has no jurisdiction to grant immunity from criminal prosecution, favourable orders can be passed by the Commission in favour of the assessee and such favourable orders need be given due regard by the criminal court.

Thus, just as pendency of an application before the Settlement Commission at any stage, i.e., even after the application has not been rejected and has been allowed to be proceeded with, is no ground for quashing criminal prosecution, its pendency is also not a good ground for staying the criminal proceeding. However, if the decision in a proceeding before any income-tax authority or the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal or the Settlement Commission having a bearing on the fate of the criminal prosecution is imminent, the criminal court can in an appropriate case stay the proceeding under section 309 of Code. However, such exercise of discretion on the part of the criminal court in an appropriate case would depend on the facts of each case and it is not possible to lay down any proposition that if the Settlement Commission has allowed an application to be proceeded with, an order refusing to stay the criminal proceeding by the trial court under section 309 of the Code on that ground will amount to an abuse of the process of the Court to make it a fit case for interference by the High Court in the exercise of its inherent powers under section 482 of the Code.

Hence, the petitioners had failed to make out any case either for quashing of the criminal prosecution or for stay of the criminal proceedings. Therefore, the petitions, having no merit, were dismissed.

The aforesaid paragraphs were duly considered and relied upon by the Division Bench while passing the impugned order, on the basis of which it was held that the disciplinary action against the appellant were not time-barred. The Court quite agrees with this part of the impugned order. [Para 22]

■ However, significantly, another crucial aspect of the very same decision - one that squarely operates against the armed forces - appears to have escaped the attention of the Division Bench. [Para 23]

■

In Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra), while examining sections 19 and 125 of the Army Act and Rule 14 of the Army Rules, which are pari materia sections 19 and 124 of the AF Act and Rule 6 of the 1969 Rules, respectively, this Court observed that where the commanding officer, exercising discretion vested in him to choose between a trial by a criminal court and a court-martial, opts for trial before a criminal court, an acquittal of the accused by such court brings finality to the matter. In such circumstances, the initiation or continuation of disciplinary action would not be sustainable. [Para 24]

■

Though the law laid down in Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra) is on consideration of the provisions of the Army Act and the Army Rules, there is no reason why it would not squarely apply to a case covered by pari materia provisions of the AF Act and the AF Rules. [Para 25]

■

True though, as per Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra), initiation of administrative proceedings is barred when an accused is 'acquitted'; however, the Court finds no reason for the ratio of the decision to not apply in a case where the accused is 'discharged' (which stands on a better footing than acquittal, as discussed supra). Once the appellant has been discharged by the criminal court, that should mark the end of the matter. [Para 26]

■

Thus, the Air Force upon electing to have the alleged offence tried by the criminal court, it is clear (in view of the discussion above) that they then cannot fall back on either a court martial or any disciplinary action. Once the road is chosen, the traveller must walk it to the end. [Para 27]

Initiation of administrative proceedings for disciplinary action against the appellant is unhesitatingly held to be bad in law and non-est. [Para 28]

■

This reason alone is sufficient to allow the present appeal. However, the decision is not proposed to rest on this sole reason; the discussion is taken forward as to why, independent of the aforesaid discussion, the disciplinary action is also otherwise considered to be flawed. It is solely for the reason that the decision in Harjeet Singh Sandhu (supra) is subsequent to the appellant's dismissal from service and the Court wishes to test whether, even in view of the law prevailing prior thereto, disciplinary action which had been taken was justified on facts and in the circumstances. The respondent-workman was a Conductor of the State-owned Road Transport Corporation. He had a long record of prior misconduct, including deferment of annual increments on twenty-three occasions, seven censures, and two earlier removals for unauthorized absenteeism followed by reinstatement with penalty. During inspection of the STAR ticketing system for the period from late October to early November 2011, serious financial and ticketing irregularities by the workman were detected. A preliminary inquiry was conducted; statements, including that of the workman, were recorded; and a report was submitted. A charge sheet alleging nine charges was issued and he was suspended pending inquiry. After supply of documents, his explanation was found unsatisfactory. A domestic inquiry was held and the Inquiry Officer found him guilty of the charges, including selling tickets not assigned to his tray, recycling tickets, and not remitting proceeds, with total misappropriation of about Rs. 0.09 lakhs. A show-cause notice for removal was issued, and after considering his explanation, the Disciplinary Authority ordered removal from service. His departmental appeal, review, and a mercy petition were rejected.

The workman raised an industrial dispute. The Labour Court held the domestic inquiry valid, recorded that the workman had committed serious misconduct and was guilty of the charges, yet directed his reinstatement as a fresh Conductor at the entry level without any past service benefits.

Respondent No. 1 herein was convicted by the trial court by its order dated 22-12-1986 and was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for 2½ years for an offence punishable under section 420, read with sections 114 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. On appeal, the Delhi High Court granted bail to him and also stayed the operation of the order of conviction, pending the disposal of the appeal. Subsequently, on 25-6-1990 he was appointed managing director of a company in a meeting of the board of directors of that company held on the same date.

Subsequently, on 14-11-1990, the appellant herein (who was a son of respondent No. 1 and also joint managing director of the company) filed a company petition before the company Judge, challenging the appoint-ment of respondent No. 1 as managing director on 25-6-1990 on the ground that having been convicted of an offence involving moral turpi- tude, he was disqualified to be appointed as managing director under section 267. However, the petition was subsequently withdrawn with the Court's permission as a result of a family settlement. Still later, another person filed a petition before the Company Law Board on 12-7-1991 challenging the appointment of respondent No. 1 as managing director of the company which, too, was disposed of by consent terms to which the appellant herein was a party and which provided that respondent No. 1 had been validly appointed and continued to be the managing director of the company and had not been disqualified to act as such. However, as a result of a subsequent family dispute, the appellant, who was the joint managing director of the company, terminated the appointment of respondent No. 1 on the ground that he could not continue as managing director as he had been convicted by the Criminal Court. The appellant, purporting to act as the managing director, issued a notice on 13-7-1992 and convened a meeting of the board of directors and allegedly passed several resolutions including the one declaring that respondent No. 1 had ceased to be the managing director in view of the provisions of section 267. This led to the filing of a suit by respondent No. 1 in the High Court, praying for a declaration that the board meeting purported to have been held on 13-7-1992 and all decisions purported to have been taken therein were null and void, illegal and of no effect, and asking for a permanent injunction restraining the appellant from in any manner acting upon or implementing the decisions taken in the meeting. Pending disposal of the suit, respondent No. 1 sought for interim order restraining the appellant from giving effect to the board decisions and restraining the appellant from obstructing respondent No. 1 from functioning as chairman and managing director of the company. The suit as well as the interim reliefs were resisted by the appellant, mainly on the ground that respondent No. 1 could not be appointed nor continued as managing director in view of the provisions of section 267 as he had earlier been convicted by a criminal court. The single Judge, however, granted the interim reliefs prayed for.

On appeal against the order of the single Judge, while the appellant contended that respondent No. 1 was not eligible to hold the office of the managing director in view of his conviction by criminal court as section 267 was mandatory, respondent No. 1 contended that since the order of conviction stood suspended by the Delhi High Court in his appeal against the conviction by the criminal court the disqualification stood removed and, therefore, he could continue to hold the post of managing director. A consequential question that arose for decision was whether the Appellate Court entertaining appeal against order of conviction had power to suspend conviction.

The Honourable high Court stated that the Hon'ble Supreme Court while issuing directions in Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India reported in AIR 2013 SC 93, stated that the report of the ICC shall be deemed to be an enquiry report as the ICC would be deemed to be the inquiring authority for the purpose of disciplinary action. Necessary amendments have been made in the Tamil Nadu State Service Conduct and Disciplinary Rules, Industrial Employment Standing Order Rules, consequent to the direction given by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the order dated 26th April 2004 in Medha Kotwal Lele's v. Union of India and others in Writ Petition (CRIMINAL) NOS. 173-177 OF 1999. Hence the inquiry made by the ICC in the instant case should be deemed to be an inquiry made for the purpose of disciplinary action as done by the Enquiring authority.

(viii)

The Honourable high Court further stated that while considering the ICC as an inquiry authority it was needless to state that a reasonable opportunity should be given to both the parties. But the complication came when the standards of the reasonableness and fairness was set by the ICC. As far as the second respondent is concerned, the respondent, claimed that non- furnishing of CCTV footage had deprived him to get a fair opportunity and the Labour Court had also endorsed his views. In any enquiry made against the delinquent by the inquiry authority, a fair amount of reasonableness should be there in the interest of justice. But the object of reasonableness was to ensure that the respondent should not become a scape goat at the hands of someone due to some malice. However, there cannot be any straight-jacket or a rigid formula to suggest the standards of reasonableness to be adopted during the departmental inquiry. So far as the charges of sexual harassment was concerned, the privacy, secrecy and safety of the victims also need to be given priority and hence the fairness formula to be adopted during such inquiry could be flexible and suiting to the nature of the complaint, type of the institution and even the conduct of the parties also.

(ix)

The Honourable High Court further recorded that in this regard it was appropriate to refer the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court held in Union of India v. P.K Roy reported in (ILLJ 633 SC) wherein it is stated that the doctrine of natural justice cannot be imprisoned with the straight-jacket or a rigid formula and its application depends upon several factors.

(x)

The Hon'ble Supreme Court had taken cue from the earlier judgment rendered in Hira Nath Mishra v. Principal, Rajendra Medical College, Ranchi, AIR 1973 SC 1260 to endorse the above view. In Hiranath's case the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held in paragraph No.11 that the rules of natural justice cannot remain the same applying to all conditions and for a better clarity, it is extracted hereunder: "

Paragraph 11. Rules of natural justice cannot remain the same applying to all conditions.

(xi)

The Honourable High Court further stated that the Honourable Court know of statutes in India like the Goonda Acts which permit evidence being collected behind the back of the goonda and the goonda being merely asked to represent against the main charges arising out of the evidence collected. Care was taken to see that the witnesses who gave statements would not be identified. In such cases there was no question of the witnesses being called and the goonda being given an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses. The reason was obvious. No witness would come forward to give evidence in the presence of the goonda. However unsavoury the procedure may appear to a. judicial mind, these were facts of life which were to be faced. The girls who were molested that night would not have come forward to give evidence in any regular enquiry and if a strict enquiry like the one conducted in a court of law were to be imposed in such matters, the girls would have had to go under the constant fear of molestation by the male students who were capable of such indecencies. Under the circumstances the course followed by the principal was a wise one. The Committee whose integrity could not be impeached, collected and sifted the evidence given by the girls. Thereafter the students definitely named by the girls were informed about the complaint against them and the charge. They were given an opportunity to state their case. The Honourable High Court did not think that the facts and circumstances of this case require anything more to be done.

During her employment with ICICI Bank applicant had signed in acceptance various policies of ICICI Bank which included Code of Conduct, Framework for dealing with conflict of interest, Deeds for Covenants and Clawback agreement. Applicant was also required to make various disclosures in compliance of the Companies Act, 1956, the Companies Act, 2013, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the SEBI (Listing Obligation and Disclosure) Regulations, 2015, RBI Master Circular on Loans and Advances and RBI Guidelines on Compensation of Whole Time Directors/CEOs.

There were news articles which contained allegations of nepotism against applicant with regard to grant of loans to companies affiliated with Videocon Group 'Venugopal Dhoot' as a quid pro quo for investments by 'Venugopal Dhoot' or his affiliates in NuPower Renewables, a company promoted by the husband of applicant.

ICICI Bank appointed a reputed law firm to conduct independent enquiry into the allegations appearing in these news articles.

Applicant and her husband in the aforementioned enquiry had provided information and documents indicating that there were no investments made by 'Venugopal Dhoot' and his affiliates in NRPL. Based on the information submitted by applicant and her husband, the law firm submitted its report with ICICI Bank stating that there was no merit in the allegations.

Later on, ICICI Bank received whistleblower letters primarily alleging abuse of position by applicant and the business dealings between Videocon Group and husband of applicant.

The Board of Directors of ICICI Bank decided to conduct an enquiry into the allegations against applicant in accordance with the Terms of Reference. Relevant filings were also made by ICICI Bank with the stock exchanges.

Justice B.N. Srikrishna (Retired Judge of the Supreme Court) was appointed by Audit Committee of ICICI Bank to conduct an independent enquiry into the allegations against applicant.

At a Board meeting of ICICI applicant communicated her decision to go on leave until the said enquiry was completed. The Board in good faith accepted her decision and made necessary disclosures to the stock exchange.

While the enquiry was still pending applicant addressed a letter requesting the Board of Directors of ICICI Bank to grant her early retirement.

Necessity of mens rea - The Explanation does not in any way restrict or cut down the ambit of expression 'wilfully' occurring in section 276C(1). Mere possession or control of any books of account and other documents containing a false entry or statement is not punishable. It is only where a person in possession or control of such books of account or other document has knowledge of the false entry or statement he renders himself punishable. Any other interpretation would sometimes lead to disastrous results [Asstt. CIT v. Yerra Nagabhushanam[1997] 93 Taxman 550 (AP)].

What would be punishable u/s 276C would be dishonest intention or a mala fide intention and there should be mens rea for committing a particular crime before an assessee can be prosecuted. All bona fide mistakes made by an assessee while filling in the income-tax return forms would not necessarily amount to an intention to commit a crime and if section 276C were to be used for penalising every delinquent assessee on that score, it would wreck havoc what is to be found by the Court is as to whether the assessee wanted to defraud the Revenue [B. T. X. Chemicals (P.) Ltd. v. Suraj Bhan[1989] 177 ITR 425 (Guj.)].

Delay in launching prosecution - It will not be right to quash prosecution proceedings on ground of delay, if otherwise an offence has been committed, unless some special feature or prejudice is shown [Narain Dev Dhablania v. ITO[2004] 134 Taxman 70 (P&H)].

Presumption u/s 132(4A) - By applying presumption u/s 132(4A), ingredients of offences u/ss. 276C and 277 could not be said to have been established [Prem Dass v. ITO[1999] 103 Taxman 65 (SC)].

Setting aside of assessment order - Where an order of assessment is set aside, offence of tax evasion u/s 276C can still be tried [Gheru Lal Bal Chand v. ITO [2004] 137 Taxman 397 (P&H)].

Pendency of proceedings and grant of stay - The pendency of reassessment proceedings cannot act as a bar to the institution of criminal prosecution for offences punishable u/s 276C, nor does the institution of criminal proceedings in the circumstances amount to an abuse of the process of the Court [P. Jayappan v. S. K. Perumal, First ITO [1984] 19 Taxman 1 (SC)]. The criminal court in an appropriate case, however, may stay the proceedings in view of such pendency where the court takes a view that the conclusion arrived at by the appellate authority under the 1961 Act would have relevance upon the decision to be reached by the criminal court [Medivet v. CIT[2007] 291 ITR 209 (Pat.)].

If matter relating to assessment order is pending in appeal, prosecution proceedings u/ss. 276C and 276CC should not be launched [Naresh Prasad v. UOI[2005] 143 Taxman 291 (Pat.)].

Proceedings against petitioner were not liable to be quashed during pendency of appeal before Tribunal; however, prosecution proceedings should remain stayed till a decision was rendered by Tribunal [Prabhava Organics (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2008] 171 Taxman 360 (AP)].

The appellant was convicted for offences under sections 120B and 420, read with section 114 of the Indian Penal Code. On criminal appeal, the Delhi High Court stayed the operation of the order of sentence, subsequent to this the appellant was appointed as the managing director of the company. Respondent No. 1, claimed to be the managing director and convened a parallel meeting of the Board of directors on 13-7-1992 and allegedly passed resolution declaring that the appellant had ceased to be the managing director and director of the company in view of the provisions of section 267 on the ground that he had been convicted by a criminal court. This led to the filing of a suit by the appellant praying for a declaration that the board meeting purported to have been held on 13- 7-1992 was null and void and for a permanent injunction restraining the 1st and 2nd respondents from implementing the decision taken in the board meeting. The Single Judge granted interim stay in terms of prayer. On appeal, before the Division Bench, the main question was whether the appellant could be appointed as director and managing director of the company after his conviction. The Division Bench held that the provisions of section 267 were mandatory in nature and it was not permissible to appoint the appellant as managing director after he was convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude. While holding so the Division Bench further held that the power of the Appellate Court in criminal appeal does not entitle such a Court to direct that the order of conviction should stand suspended and as such the Delhi High Court had no power to suspend the order of conviction.

Enquiry - Nature determines whether discharge punitive

In order to determine whether the discharge is punitive in nature, it is necessary to ascertain firstly the nature of the enquiry, i.e., whether the termination is preceded by full scale formal enquiry into allegations involving misconduct on the part of the employee, which culminated in the finding of guilt, and secondly, the ‘purpose of enquiry’, i.e., whether the purpose of enquiry is to find out any misconduct on his part or it is aimed at finding out as to the employee being unlikely to prove efficient. Thus, the principle that in order to determine whether the misconduct is motive or foundation of order of termination, the test to be applied is to ask the question as to what was the ‘object of enquiry’. If an enquiry or an assessment is done with the object of finding out any misconduct on the part of the employee and for that reason his services are terminated, then it would be punitive in nature. On the other hand, if such an enquiry or an assessment is aimed at determining the suitability of an employee for a particular job, such termination would be termination simplicitor and not punitive in nature [State of Punjab v. Balbir Singh (2004) 23 ILD 23 (SC)]

19.9

SHOULD PROSECUTION PROCEEDING AWAIT TILL THE DECISION BY THE APPELLATE TRIBUNAL?

Under Income-tax Act, prosecution generally awaits the outcome of penalty proceeding. If penalty is deleted in appeal by the Tribunal in certain types of cases, the prosecution proceeding would abate. This principle as enunciated by the Apex Court in the cases of P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal [1984] 19 Taxman 1 (SC) and in K. C. Builder v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 135 Taxman 461 (SC) may apply in case of prosecution under PBPT Act, 1988. This is for the precise reason that section 53 opens with the expression "whoever enters into a benami transaction" shall be guilty of an offence under the said section. Whether a person has entered into a benami transaction or not can only attain finality upon delivery of order by the Appellate Tribunal. Hence, any hasty initiation of criminal proceeding merely because the Adjudicating Authority has treated the property as benami and passed order of confiscation may not be in consonance with the above decisions of the Apex Court. Moreover, as per the First Proviso to section 27 of the PBPT Act, 1988, the confiscation of the property by Adjudicating Authority is subject to outcome of appeal before Appellate Tribunal. This is a specific requirement under benami law. It is seen that in many cases, launching of prosecution has become a statistical exercise by the department resulting in hardship to a citizen and a wasteful exercise by the Department.

Impact of Notifications and Circulars vis-a-vis Judicial Decisions 7. Notifications are issued by competent authorities in exercise of their powers conferred under the relevant statute. Notifications supplement the primary and subordinate legislation, i.e., the Act and Rules, by filling up certain gaps in the law, which are required to be notified from time to time, as and when necessary. Notifications, thus, originate from and get merged with the main law. Circulars, on the other hand, are issued by competent bodies, in exercise of their general administrative powers, to elucidate, clarify or amplify any provision, or to remove any anomaly in its practical implementation. The Circular, however, does not supplement the law, it must complement it.

It has been held that it would be proper on the part of the authorities to ensure that neither the statutory provision nor the notification which forms part of the statute are paid scanty regard. [ITC Ltd. v. Commr. of Cus. (Port), Kolkata 2007 (6) STR 405 (Trib. - Kol.)]. As regards circulars in CCE v. H.M. Polycontainers Ltd. [2007] 9 STT 96 (Mum. - CESTAT), it has been observed that Board’s Circulars are not binding on Commissioner (Appeals). However, in judicial discipline, the Commissioner (Appeals) is bound by the decision of the higher Tribunal.

Essence of Appellate Power

8. Appeal implies in its natural and ordinary meaning the removal of cause from any inferior Court or Tribunal to a superior one for the purpose of testing the soundness or correctness of the decision and proceedings of the inferior Court or Tribunal. The superior forum shall have jurisdiction to reverse, confirm, annul or modify the order of the forum appealed against and in the event of remand the lower forum shall have to re-hear the matter and comply with such directions as may accompany the order of removal. The appellate jurisdiction inherently carries with it a power to issue corrective directions binding on the forum below and failure on the part of the latter to carry out such directions or show disrespect to or to question the propriety of such direction would be destructive of the hierarchial system in the administration of justice. Seekers of justice would lose faith in both and would only knock the doors of the High Courts under article 226 of the Constitution of India for correcting orders. [TVL Ragam Polymers v. CTO 2007 (6) STR 292 (Mad.)].

8.1 Impact of Stay in an Appeal - It is well-settled that during the appeal period or when the stay has been given to the appellants till further orders, the revenue authorities shall not make any recovery towards the demands made in the impugned orders. [Berger Paints India Ltd. v. CCE [Final Order No. 51 of 2006, dated 8-2-2006.]

When the Tribunal had already extended the stay granted to the appellants till further orders, the act of the concerned Assistant Commissioner to adjust the amount of duty without taking Tribunal’s order or any higher court’s order, was held completely irregular. If he had any grievances with the Tribunal’s order, he could have filed an appeal before any higher forum and since it had not been taken, he could have taken the Tribunal’s order before adjusting the amount which had also not been done. This was nothing but disregard shown to the Tribunal by the concerned Assistant Commissioner.

Conclusion

9. The importance of the doctrine of judicial discipline with regard to a statute has been reiterated and stressed upon time and again by various judicial fora. Ironically, the doctrine has been overlooked by the same (or similar) fora at several other occasions.

Service tax is a bubbly law, yet evolving and unsettled. It, thus, demands practice of judicial discipline with more sincerity. For aligned functioning and unanimity on interpretation of statute, it is immensely important that all members of the judiciary fraternity exercise their functions in strict observance of the principle of judicial discipline. Before rendering their own interpretation of the provisions of service tax law, which has today assumed ever growing significance both for the industry and the revenue, the courts must duly consider and follow the decisions given by higher authorities.

Rashmi Metaliks Limited v. Enforcement Directorate [2022] SCC OnLine Cal 2316]

A Single Bench of the Hon'ble High Court of Calcutta came to the rescue of the Accused and stayed the two orders of freezing of the accounts of the accused dated July 13, 2022.

The ED had claimed that the company made a wrongful declaration to avail benefits of the Indian Railways' dual freight policy of 2009. The Accused's challenge to the Show cause notice issued by the Railways & Civil Suit filed by the Union of India against the accused was stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 2015.

With freezing orders passed by ED in 2022, i.e. after seven (7) years from the date on which all pending proceedings were stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, and also the summons under the Act were issued prior to the stay order, it was held that the ED could not have initiated any action against the petitioners during the subsistence of the order of stay of the pending proceedings against the accused by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 2015.

Taking consideartion of the exception carved out in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra) for a person named in the criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence being absolved by a Court of competent jurisdiction, interestingly, the Court has drawn an analogy to the present facts where the proceedings have only been stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court & no discharge or no acquittal have been made while restraining the ED from proceeding ahead with its action against the accused.

B. Shanmugam v. Karthik Dasari [2022] SCC OnLine Mad 4417]

The genesis in the cited case rested with the ED registering ECIR on the basis of three (3) FIRs. Out of the three (3) FIRs, one (1) was quashed & the remaining two (2) were stayed till further orders.

Before the Division Bench of the Hon'ble High Court of Madras the primary question was about the implication of quashing & staying of FIRs on the proceedings initiated by the ED under the PMLA.

In line with the directions passed in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra), the ED fairly conceded that in so far as the quashed FIR is concerned, the department cannot proceed ahead under the Act. However, it was strenuously contended by them that the accused cannot take benefit of the stayed proceedings and plea before the court that proceedings under PMLA for the remaining two (2) FIRs too be quashed.

On the other hand, the petitioners refuted the said contention of the department, and relied upon the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Calcutta in Rashmi Metaliks Ltd. (Supra).

The Division Bench in its judgment discarded the contentions of the Department and answered in negative to the question whether the ECIR, which is also pursuant to the FIRs which have been stayed by the High Court, can be proceeded with or not.

Placing reliance on precedents on 'jurisdictional fact to be taken into account by a Court before assuming jurisdiction over a particular matter', the court opined that the existence of jurisdictional fact is a condition precedent for the exercise of power by a Court of limited jurisdiction. Therefore, in present matter, when there is no cause of action, since the proceeding in one (1) of the cases was quashed, and the proceedings in two (2) other cases have been stayed by the Court, there was no jurisdictional fact or cause of action for the respondent/department to initiate any proceedings during the period of order of stay operating against the two FIRs.

Finally, in its conclusion, the Hon'ble High Court opined that in view of the quashing of the proceedings in one (1) of the FIR and staying of the proceedings in the remaining two (2) FIRs, the scheduled offence was eclipsed, suspended or stop operating during the period of stay. Therefore, the Department has to await the finality of the said proceedings. In case, if the other two (2) remaining FIRs also get quashed pursuant to the orders in the applications filed by the respective accused to quash the proceedings, in which event, the Department cannot step in or initiate any proceedings under the PMLA, as held in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra).

Reliance on the Supreme Court decision

3. The Circular draws reference to the decision of the Apex Court in the case of Collector of Customs, Bombay v. Krishna Sales (P) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The Apex Court observed that "As is well known, mere filing of an Appeal does not operate as a stay or suspension of the Order appealed against". It should be noted that this decision of the Apex Court was somewhat in a different context and was issued when the service tax was not even in force. In fact, the decision was passed by the Apex Court in favour of the assessee.

The appeal before the Apex Court was preferred by the Collector of Customs against the judgment of the Delhi Tribunal. The assessee, Krishna Sales (P) Ltd., imported machinery and classified as a 'Bevel Gear Generator'. The Customs authorities raised an objection and classified the machinery as 'Bevel Gear Planer', thereby confiscating the machinery.

The assessee was given an option to pay a redemption fine of Rs. 70,000/- and penalty of Rs. 10,000/- and clear the goods. Assessee filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The appeal was allowed by the Tribunal which agreed with the classification claimed by the assessee. The counsel for the assessee requested that the customs authorities may be directed to issue a detention certificate for the entire period during which the goods were detained till the date of issuance of the detention certificate.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee by virtue of which the respondent was entitled to clear the machinery without payment of any duty. But the respondent required a detention certificate to clear the machinery. Evidently, in view of this problem, the Apex Court made the following interim order:

"Having heard Ld. Counsel for the Collector of Customs, Bombay and M/s. Krishna Sales (P) Ltd., we direct that the application made by the latter for a detention certificate should not be rejected on the ground that the Appeal is pending in this Court against the Order of the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi."

However,when the assessee applied for issuance of a detention certificate, no such certificate was issued. The assessee submitted that the action of the authorities is relatable to and influenced by the public notice issued by the Collector of Customs, Bombay on July 25, 1985. So far as the detention certificate for a period exceeding six months is concerned, it can be issued only with the approval of and under the signature of the Collector. Para 4 of the public notice deals with issue of detention certificates to the parties succeeding in appeals and read as follows:

"Detention Certificate, as a rule, will be issued by the concerned competent Customs Authority to the Appellants succeeding in Appeals on receipt of the copies of such Orders which the latter making formal application for issue of Detention Certificates. However, in cases where the Customs House decides to go in second Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, the issue of Detention Certificate will be considered only after such second appeal is finally disposed of in favour of the parties."

The Apex Court held as follows:

"6. According to the above mentioned para 4, the goods will not be released even where the party succeeds in cases where the Customs Authorities decide to go in Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court. They will consider the issuance of such certificate only after the decision of the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, as the case may be. The Counsel for the assessee characterised the direction as arbitrary and contrary to law. We see the force in his submission. If the authorities are of the opinion that the goods ought not to be released pending the Appeal, the straight forward course for them is to obtain an Order of Stay or other appropriate direction from the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, as the case may be. Without obtaining such an Order they cannot refuse to implement the Order under Appeal. As is well-known, mere filing of an Appeal does not operate as a Stay or suspension of the Order appealed against. Moreover, such detention is likely to create several complications relating to the demurrage charges besides the possible deterioration of the machinery and goods. We hope and trust that the Collector of Custom Bombay shall appropriately revise the said public notice in the light of the observations made herein. If he does not do so, there is a likelihood of the Customs Authorities being themselves made liable for demurrage charges in appropriate cases.

COMMENTS

SECTION NOTES

31.1 Protection against arbitrary dismissal [Section 31(1)]

An employer cannot terminate the services of an employee employed for six months or more unless:

Termination is for reasonable cause.

The employee is given at least one month's notice or wages in lieu of notice.

31.1-1 Exception [Provided]

Notice is not required if:

Termination is based on misconduct.

Misconduct is proven through an inquiry held by the employer.

The inquiry findings are supported by satisfactory evidence.

31.2 Appeal by the Employee [Section 31(2)]

31.2-1 Grounds for Appeal [Section 31(2)(a)]

The employee may appeal against dismissal, discharge, or retrenchment on the following grounds:

Absence of reasonable cause for termination.

Allegation of misconduct is unproven.

Punishment of discharge or dismissal is excessively severe.

31.2-2 Procedure for Appeal [Section 31(2)(b)]

Appeals must be made to the prescribed authority within the prescribed timeframe.

Notice of the appeal is given to both employer and employee.

The appellate authority may:

Dismiss the appeal.

Order reinstatement with or without back wages.

Award compensation instead of reinstatement.

Grant other relief deemed appropriate in the circumstances.

31.3 Powers of the Appellate Authority [Section 31(2A)]

The appellate authority is vested with powers equivalent to:

Those of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including:

Enforcing attendance of witnesses and examining them under oath.

Compelling production of documents and material evidence.

31.4 Finality of Appellate Decision [Section 31(3)]

The appellate authority's decision is final and binding on both employer and employee.

The order must be implemented within the time specified by the appellate authority.

The Court emphasized the Act's welfare objective, requiring a liberal construction of its provisions to protect vulnerable workers. AO performs a ministerial function - The AO, when he files the appeal under the direction of the Commissioner, performs merely a ministerial function. The officer selected must have some concern with the assessee against whom the appeal is filed by the Commissioner [CIT v. Anil Kumar Roy Chowdhury [1967] 66 ITR 367 (SC)].

Objection of Commissioner on order passed by CIT(A) - The objection of the Commissioner may cover not only the merits of the order passed by the CIT(A) but also what that officer had omitted to do in his order. The objection of the Commissioner for the purposes of maintainability of his appeal should, of course, be an order passed by the CIT(A). But the objection is not necessarily confined to what the order has stated but may extend to what the order has omitted to say. TEMPORARY PROTECTION OF EMPLOYEES *TEMPORARY PROTECTION OF EMPLOYEES*

254.1 Background note254.1 Background note

During the pendency of proceedings in relation to the company pursuant to sections 235, 237 & 247 or in relation to any person concerned with the conduct and management of the company’s affairs under Chapter IVA of Part VI of the Act, that is, under sections 388B to 388E relating to the removal of managerial personnel from office by Central Government on the recommendation of the Tribunal - the company and its associates lose their authority to discharge or to punish by dismissal, removal reduction in rank or otherwise punish their employees under the law of master-and-servant temporarily. 254.2 Procedure to punish254.2 Procedure to punish

During that period if the company or any of its associates intends to inflict any such punishment on any of its employees, the Tribunal should be approached first by presenting the proposal and a ‘no objection’ order to the action proposed should be obtained. However, if the Tribunal does not make and issue a ‘no objection order’ for 30 days of presenting the proposal to it, the proposed action may be proceeded with. On the other hand, if aggrieved by the objection order issued by the Tribunal, it may be appealed against in the Appellate Tribunal.

PROCEEDING MUST RELATE TO A DIRECT BUT NOT A RELATED PROCEEDING

The section refers to pendency of a direct and independent proceeding but not a related proceeding. In Smt. Rina Sen v. CIT [1999] 235 ITR 219 (Pat.), it was held that issuance of notice under section 143(2) for one assessment year would not enable the Assessing Officer to call for the details of an earlier year from a valuation officer by issuing commission under section 131(1)(d).

◆ In some cases, it is provided that the action should have been taken before the date of declaration. In other cases it is not so provided. Now the bar is against declaration of tax arrear, outstanding as on 31-3-1998 it seems the inability has to be examined on the date of declaration. “Accordingly, even if the order of Settlement Commission is received after 31-3-1998; but before the date of declaration a declaration cannot be made. ◆ Another issue is that the prohibition operates against Tax arrear where no appeal is pending. Should the appeal be against the assessment order or should it be against the additions which give rise to Tax arrear ? The objective of this provision is that where there are no disputes; but, mere Tax arrear, an assessee cannot take advantage of the Scheme. If it is contrued that the appeal should be against assessment, even Tax arrear in respect of undisputed addition would qualify for declaration. The other view is that in respect of each and every item of tax in arrears, one has to find whether an appeal is pending or not. The other view seems to be a far-fetched view and also contrary to the view that in respect of a partial Tax arrear a declaration cannot be made. No doubt, the first view can result into an unintended benefit to those assessees who have large tax arrear; but, only a small portion in dispute. However, that cannot be a ground for taking a view that in respect of each and every addition giving rise to tax arrear, appeal should have been filed.

1.6-1a Effect of conviction for concealment - Section 95(i)(a) of the Finance Act, apart from the above restrictions, also provides that a person who has been convicted for concealment on or before filing of declaration, the provisions of the Scheme would not apply, in respect of Tax arrear under any Direct tax enactment. It may be noted that where a prosecution is instituted, the bar is against Tax arrear in respect of the assessment year concerned. However, where the person has been convicted, it appears that, he would not be in a position to make any declaration under the Scheme. The manner in which the provision is drafted creates such ambiguity; but, the intention appears to be otherwise. The other view, is that the bar is against only in respect of Tax arrear for which he has been convicted, which cannot be ruled out and seems to be a more appropriate view. This view is based on reading the provision as follows :

“The provisions of this Scheme shall not apply—

(i) in respect of Tax arrear under any Direct tax enactment,—

(a) . . .; or in respect of a person who is convicted for concealment. . . .”.

Thus, for non-application of the Scheme, the primary requisite is that there should be a Tax arrear and further the person concerned ought to have been convicted. Had the intention been otherwise, possibly, such a provision would have been made in section 95(iii), which totally prohibits a person from making any declaration.

Accordingly, the second view is preferable.

1.6-2 Tax arrear in respect of Indirect Tax Enactment in respect of which a declaration cannot be made - Tax arrear in respect of Indirect Tax Enactment in respect of which a declaration cannot be made are as follows :

(i) Tax arrear in respect of which a prosecution for any offence punishable under any Indirect Tax Enactment has been instituted, on or before the date of filing of declaration; and

(ii) Where no show cause notice or notice of demand under any Indirect Tax Enactment has been issued.

(iii) In a case where an appeal or reference or writ petitions is not admitted and/or pending before the date of filing declaration before any appellate authority or court or Commissioner.

1.6-3 Certain circumstances under which a Declaration under the Scheme cannot be made - Based on the above understanding of the Scheme, it appears that apart from the situations specified under the Scheme itself, in the following cases also a person will not be able to make declaration:

◆ Where the whole of Tax arrear has been paid after 31- 03-1998; but, before the date of declaration under the Scheme (see para 1.4-6).

◆ Where the assessment has been set aside by an Appellate authority and effect thereto has been given as a result of which there are no Tax Arrear.

◆ An appeal filed before the first authority is decided in favour of a person and further appeal by the Tax Department is pending before the Tribunal, inasmuch as there would not be any outstanding Tax arrear.

◆ A person has raised many issues in appeal or revision, etc., in respect of some of which the person is certain that they would be decided in his favour and intends to settle only the other issues. He wants to settle Tax arrear only in respect of the other issues. Apparently, this is not permissible and, therefore, the person would not be able to make any declaration under the Scheme.

◆ In case of corporate assessees, who are liable to minimum alternate tax, the amount paid under the Scheme would not be available for credit. Accordingly, they may not come forward for settlement.

ANY PROCEEDINGS RELATING TO AN APPEAL - SUB-SECTION (1) OF SECTION 254

1147. Principal CIT v. ITAT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 269/[2016] 236 Taxman 39/382 ITR 321/[2015] 281 CTR 521 (Punj. & Har.)

A due consideration of the statutory provisions reveals that section 254(1) confers the power to decide an appeal and 'pass such orders thereon as it thinks fit' and when read along with the proviso includes the power to pass interim orders, 'in any proceeding relating to an appeal', thereby indicating that the stay order so passed must relate to proceedings in the appeal pending before the Tribunal. The question that, however, requires an answer is whether these words and expressions would include the power to stay proceedings or orders, which are not appealable or appealed against during pendency of an appeal but are likely to be affected by the outcome of the appeal.

A key to the understanding of the power to grant stay lies in the expressions 'pass such orders thereon as it thinks fit' and 'any proceedings relating to an appeal', used in section 254(1) and the proviso appended thereto. The aforesaid expressions confine the power of a Tribunal, to pass an interim order in relation to matters pending before the Tribunal and at best to matters that are so intrinsically linked to the lis pending before the Tribunal, as to be inseparable. The exercise of power must be confined to matters that are directly and substantially in issue or matters that flow directly and substantially from the order impugned before the Tribunal but cannot be extended to matters in which the Tribunal has no jurisdiction even, though, these matters may be incidentally affected by the outcome of the appeal.

This apart, once it is accepted that proceedings for prosecution are independent of assessment and penalty, and the Tribunal is neither the appellate nor the revisional authority in a case where prosecution is launched, the mere fact that the decision in the appeal may have an impact on the prosecution, cannot be used to read into the expressions 'pass such orders thereon as it thinks fit' or 'any proceedings relating to an appeal', a power in the Tribunal to direct that prosecution or a show-cause notice shall be kept in abeyance.

The appeal may have a bearing on the consideration of the show cause notice and the reply filed thereto, but one cannot read into section 254(1) or the proviso thereto, power in a Tribunal to stay consideration of the show cause notice or the power to direct that the show-cause notice be kept in abeyance.

10. Finding u/s 33(2)(b) of Industrial Disputes Act on fairness of domestic enquiry is binding and operates as res judicata in later dispute: HC

Fouress Engineering karmika Sangha v. Management of Fouress Engg. (I) (P.) Ltd. [2025] 176 taxmann.com 339 (HC - Karnataka)

In the instant case, three members of the petitioner-Union were dismissed from service. The Management invoked section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, seeking approval for a penalty of dismissal. In the said proceeding, workmen took a stand that the domestic enquiry was not fair and proper.

Evidence was led on the issue relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry. The Labour Court, on appreciation of evidence led before it by both sides, held that the domestic enquiry was fair and proper. Consequently, accorded approval for dismissal.

The Union later raised a dispute challenging the penalty of dismissal. Union contended that the domestic enquiry was not fair and proper. The Management urged that in a proceeding under section 33(2)(b), it had already been held that the domestic enquiry was fair and proper, and the said finding operates as res judicata and cannot be agitated again, in a proceeding challenging the penalty of dismissal of service.

The Labour Court accepted the Management's plea and declined to reconsider the said issue, holding that it operates as res judicata.

The High Court noted that the question as to whether domestic enquiry was fair and proper, if raised in an application under section 33(2)(b), and if finding on such an application is recorded after full-fledged enquiry, such finding is not just a prima facie finding on said question as to fairness and validity of domestic enquiry and it is a finding on adjudication which attains finality if not questioned, and cannot be re-agitated in subsequent proceedings between same parties.

Further, the High Court noted that a finding on an issue relating to the fairness of a domestic enquiry is adjudicatory and the said question cannot be revisited in an industrial dispute challenging a penalty.

The High Court held that the enquiry under section 33(2)(b) of the Act, as to whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper (rendered after recording of evidence before the authority), is binding on parties to the proceedings. Since the authority has jurisdiction to adjudicate on the fairness of the domestic enquiry, such a finding cannot be re-agitated in a subsequent industrial dispute challenging the order of penalty, as it operates as res judicata between the same parties in subsequent proceedings.

Further, the authority under section 33(2)(b) cannot adjudicate on the merits of the findings in the domestic enquiry or on the penalty, as it lacks jurisdiction to do so. These issues can be adjudicated only in a subsequent industrial dispute, if raised.

Res judicata - Issue estoppel and criminal proceedings

2.35 Issue estoppel is a branch of the law of res judicata applied to criminal proceedings. The binding nature of a finding arrived at between the parties in previous litigation, in a subsequent litigation between the same parties as applied to criminal proceedings is called “issue estoppel”. The effect of a verdict of acquittal pronounced by a competent Court on a lawful charge and after a lawful trial is not completely slated by saying that the person acquitted cannot be tried again for the same offence. To that it must be added that the verdict is binding as conclusive in all subsequent proceedings between the parties to the adjudication. The maxim res judicata pro vertiate accipitur is no less applicable to criminal than to civil proceedings.1 The principle of issue estoppel outside the scope of section 300 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to India.2 It applies not only in favour of the accused but also against him. But in all criminal proceedings, the principle of res judicata or issue estoppel may come in conflict with another principle, namely, that the prosecution must prove that the accused is guilty and unless this is done the accused is presumed to be innocent. The principle of issue estoppel cannot override the principle of presumption of innocence of the accused. Similarly, the following special features of the criminal proceedings would further modify the application of issue estoppel.

◆ First, in a criminal case, there is no duty on the accused to adduce evidence in defence while in a civil case adverse inference may be drawn from the refusal of a party to adduce evidence in his possession or power.

◆ Secondly, the burden of proof to prove the guilt of the accused is more on the prosecution in a criminal case as compared to the burden of proof on the plaintiff to prove his case against the defendant in a civil case.

◆ Thirdly, certain evidence such as confession in certain circumstances cannot be proved in a criminal case against the accused though there is no such restriction between the parties to a civil proceeding.

◆ Lastly, a finding of fact arrived at in a civil proceeding may not be binding in a criminal proceeding against the accused.

Generally speaking, the principle of issue estoppel is invoked to bar adducing of evidence to proved facts which have been already adjudicated upon in a previous proceeding between the parties. It is easier to obtain a finding of fact for a plaintiff against a defendant in a civil proceeding than for the prosecution to do so against the accused in a criminal proceeding. Therefore, the finding of fact given in a previous civil proceeding may not act as res judicata in a subsequent criminal proceeding. For the same reasons, a finding of fact in a criminal proceeding against an accused person should act as res judicata in a subsequent civil proceeding between the same parties. In Hollington v. F. Hewthorn & Co. Ltd.1, the Court of Appeal in England, however, did not accord the effect of res judicata to a summary conviction of the accused for a traffic offence in a subsequent civil proceeding in which the accused was sued for damages by the person who was injured by the negligence of the accused in driving a car. Similarly, in Anil Behari Ghosh v. Smt. Latika Bala Dassi2, the conviction by a Criminal Court of a person for the murder of his father was not regarded as conclusive in a subsequent proceeding for revocation of the grant of probate under section 263 of the Succession Act. These decisions apparently did not attach importance to the fact that the rules of procedure and evidence are more favourable to the accused in criminal proceeding and, therefore, there should be no objection to a finding against the accused in a criminal proceeding acting as res judicata in a subsequent civil proceeding.

The Supreme Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO3 observed:

“...In the criminal case all the ingredients of the offence in question have to be established in order to secure the conviction of the accused. The Criminal Court no doubt has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and in an appropriate case it may drop the proceedings in the light of an order passed under the Act. It does not, however, mean that the result of a proceeding under the Act would be binding on the Criminal Court. The Criminal Court has to judge the case independently on the evidence placed before it. Otherwise, there is a danger of a contention being advanced that whenever an assessee or any other person liable under the Act had failed to convince the authorities in the proceedings under the Act that he has not deliberately made any false statement or that he has not fabricated any material evidence, the conviction of such person should invariably follow in the criminal court. . .” (pp. 700, 701)

Annapurna Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. & Ors v. SORIL Infra Resources Limited (CP No. (IB)-22(PB)/2017] - Principal Bench, New Delhi

Date of Order: 24st March 2017

Facts of the Case:

Annapurna Infrastructure Private Ltd i.e. Operational Creditor have filed an application u/s 9 of the Code before the NCLT to initiate CIRP of SORIL Infra Resources Limited i.e. Corporate Debtor. Pursuant to an arbitration award dated 09.09.2016 passed by an arbitrator certain claims of the Operational Creditors have arisen against the Corporate Debtor. Corporate Debtor has filed further appeal u/s 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 ('Arbitration Act') for set-aside of the said arbitration award. However appeal u/s 34 of the Arbitration Act for setting aside the award has been dismissed by the arbitral tribunal vide its order dated 19.12.2016.

Subsequent to dismissal of appeal u/s 34 of the Arbitration Act, Operational Creditor has served a demand notice dated 16.01.2017 to Corporate Debtor u/s 8 of the Code for recovery of the claim as envisaged under arbitration award. In response to demand notice Corporate Debtor replied that a further appeal u/s 37 of the Arbitration Act have been filed before the Hon'ble High Court which is pending for adjudication and till the disposal of appeal Corporate Debtor is not liable for payment of any claim.

Objections and arguments of the parties:

Operation Creditor argued that appeal u/s 37 of the Arbitration Act cannot be regarded as continuation of arbitration proceeding because the arbitrator is the final judge of the facts and the High Court while hearing objections u/s 37 is not expected to scrutinize the award as an appellate forum1.

However, Corporate Debtor argued that arbitration proceeding do not come to an end on the announcement of arbitration award and the aggrieved party have a right for further appeal2 u/s 34 and 37 of the Arbitration Act.

NCLT Ruling:

(a)

Definition of Dispute is not exhaustive but illustrative:

NCLT held that conjoint reading of section 5(6) and section 8 makes it clear that corporate debtor has two option available under section 8(2) of the Code i.e. either disclosing existence of a dispute or pay the unpaid debt to the operational creditor. Further, definition of the word 'dispute' as provided u/s 5(6) of the Code, is not exhaustive but is, in fact illustrative. In other words a corporate debtor is not left with the only option of showing the existence of dispute by way of a pending suit, arbitration or to show the breach of representation or warranty. Corporate Debtor would be well within his right to show that goods and services were not supplied at all or the supply was far from satisfactory in case of demand raised by an operational creditor.

Further, NCLT observed that, it cannot be said that arbitration proceedings have come to an end merely on the dismissal of application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act as the proceedings are yet to attain finality as appeal under section 37 of the Arbitration Act is pending.

"The other judgment that no proceedings were pending on the date of issuance of demand notice in terms of section 8(1) of the Code is equally falicious. Admittedly appeal under section 37 of the Arbitration Act could be preferred within 30 days against an order passed under section 34 of the Arbitration Act. Merely because no appeal was pending on 16.1.2017 when the respondent have time to prefer the appeal would not entitle the applicant to invoke section 9 of the Code. If that view is taken then extreme technicality would result in nullifying the remedy of appeal within 30 days provided by section 37 of the Arbitration Act. No reasonable person would take such a view. Thus the argument is wholly devoid of merit and therefore we have no hesitation to reject the same"

(b)

Prohibition on forum shopping:

NCLT further held that, it is fundamental principles of judicial administration to allow only one remedy at one point of time and the same principal is evident from section 10 of the Civil Procedure Code. Therefore, where an issue is already pending adjudication in a Court having jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the same, a subsequently instituted suit on the same issue between the same parties, cannot be allowed to proceed.

Accordingly, based on the above finding NCLT dismissed application of operational creditor for initiation of CIRP with cost of INR 1,00,000/-
