The Assessing Officer initiated penalty proceedings against the assessee alleging that he had suppressed certain income in the return and thereby tried to evade the tax payable by him. On appeal, the Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the penalty. During the pendency of its appeal before the Tribunal, the department filed complaint under sections 276C and 277.

On criminal petition the assessee’s case was that since the Dy. Commissioner (Appeals) had already set aside the penalty proceedings, prosecution could not be continued. On the other hand, the department contended that the matter had not reached finality since the appeals were pending before the Tribunal and, therefore, prosecution could not be quashed.

In the instant case, the penalty was levied by the ITO on the facts and circumstances before him de hors any judgment or opinion of the Magistrate or any other Court. The orders of the criminal court were not even pronounced by the date of the judgment of the AAC. The Tribunal also confirmed the levy of penalty on the facts and circumstances of the case, unrelated to and without reference to the judgment of the Magistrate. After having come to that conclusion, it merely referred to the argument of the department based upon the judgment and order of the Magistrate, but it neither referred to the contents of the said order nor to the conclusion of the Magistrate but reiterated that it had confirmed the penalty on the facts and circumstances before it and for reasons already recorded by it. It was, thus, clear that the judgment of the Magistrate had played no part in the conclusion that was arrived at by the Tribunal. If so, the judgment of acquittal would equally be not relevant. Thus, when the Tribunal was not placing any reliance upon the judgment of the Magistrate in the criminal proceedings, it was not bound nor it was necessary for it to adjourn the matter or postpone the delivery of judgment to enable the assessee to produce the judgment of the criminal appellate court acquitting the partners.

COMMENTS

SECTION NOTES

31.1 Protection against arbitrary dismissal [Section 31(1)]

An employer cannot terminate the services of an employee employed for six months or more unless:

Termination is for reasonable cause.

The employee is given at least one month's notice or wages in lieu of notice.

31.1-1 Exception [Provided]

Notice is not required if:

Termination is based on misconduct.

Misconduct is proven through an inquiry held by the employer.

The inquiry findings are supported by satisfactory evidence.

31.2 Appeal by the Employee [Section 31(2)]

31.2-1 Grounds for Appeal [Section 31(2)(a)]

The employee may appeal against dismissal, discharge, or retrenchment on the following grounds:

Absence of reasonable cause for termination.

Allegation of misconduct is unproven.

Punishment of discharge or dismissal is excessively severe.

31.2-2 Procedure for Appeal [Section 31(2)(b)]

Appeals must be made to the prescribed authority within the prescribed timeframe.

Notice of the appeal is given to both employer and employee.

The appellate authority may:

Dismiss the appeal.

Order reinstatement with or without back wages.

Award compensation instead of reinstatement.

Grant other relief deemed appropriate in the circumstances.

31.3 Powers of the Appellate Authority [Section 31(2A)]

The appellate authority is vested with powers equivalent to:

Those of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including:

Enforcing attendance of witnesses and examining them under oath.

Compelling production of documents and material evidence.

31.4 Finality of Appellate Decision [Section 31(3)]

The appellate authority's decision is final and binding on both employer and employee.

The order must be implemented within the time specified by the appellate authority.

CASE LAWS

Appeal against termination without notice – The Supreme Court held that an appeal under section 31(2) of the Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966, is maintainable if an employee claims to have been arbitrarily terminated without reasonable cause, regardless of whether the termination was formalized in writing or executed through actions such as denying work access. The Court emphasized the Act's welfare objective, requiring a liberal construction of its provisions to protect vulnerable workers. It overturned the High Court's decision, which erroneously excluded such cases from the scope of section 31(2), and reinstated the prescribed authority's directive for arrears and compensation to the terminated worker. – Sudhoo v. Haji Lal Mohd. Biri Works AIR 1990 SC 1971.

There is no provision in law which provides that a prosecution for the offences in question cannot be launched until reassessment proceedings initiated against the assessee are completed. Section 279 provides that a person shall not be proceeded against for an offence punishable under section 276C Or section 277 except at the instance of the Commissioner. It further provides that a person shall not be proceeded against for an offence punishable under those provisions in relation to the assessment for an assessment year in respect of which penalty imposed or imposable on him under clause (iii) of sub-section (1) of section 271 has been reduced or waived by an order under section 273A. The Commissioner has the power either before or after the institution of proceedings to compound any such offence. In this case, it was not claimed that the Commissioner had not initiated the proceedings for instituting the complaints. No other legal bar for the institution of the proceedings was urged except stating that in the event of the petitioner being exonerated in the reassessment proceedings, the prosecutions may have to be dropped.

A mere expectation of success in some proceeding in appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of the institution of the criminal proceedings under section 276C and section 277. In the criminal case all the ingredients of the offence in question have to be established in order to secure the conviction of the accused. The criminal court no doubt has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and in an appropriate case it may drop the proceedings in the light of an order passed under the Act. It does not, however, mean that the result of a proceeding under the Act would be binding on the criminal court. The criminal court has to judge the case independently on the evidence placed before it. Otherwise there is a danger of a contention being advanced that whenever the assessee or any other person liable under the Act has failed to convince the authorities in the proceedings under the Act that he has not deliberately made any false statement or that he has not fabricated any material evidence, the conviction of such person should invariably follow in the criminal court.

It is only where the Commissioner reduces or waives the penalty imposed or imposable under section 271(1)(iii) in exercise of his discretion under section 273A, section 279(1A) comes into operation and acts as a statutory bar for proceeding with the prosecution under section 276C or section 277. It does not, however, provide that merely because there is a possibility of the Commissioner passing an order under section 273A, the prosecution shall not be instituted.

It may be that in an appropriate case the criminal court may adjourn or postpone the hearing of a criminal case in exercise of its discretionary power under section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if the disposal of any proceeding under the Act which has a bearing on the proceedings before it is imminent so that it may take also into consideration the order to be passed therein. Even here the discretion should be exercised judicially and in such a way as not to frustrate the object of the criminal proceedings. There is no rigid rule which makes it necessary for a criminal court to adjourn or postpone the hearing of a case before it indefinitely or for an unduly long period only because some proceeding which may have some bearing on it is pending elsewhere. But this, however, has no relevance to the question of maintainability of the prosecution.

Accordingly, notwithstanding the reassessment proceedings started against the petitioner, prosecutions for offences punishable under sections 276C and 277 and under sections 193 and 196 of the Indian Penal Code instituted by the department were maintainable.

Court do not entitle such a court to direct that the order of conviction should stand suspended The conviction can only be set aside.

The contention that the expression 'order' covers even the order of conviction cannot be accepted because the expression used by the Legislature is 'execution of the sentence or order'. The section makes it clear that the appellate court can suspend the execution of the sentence or the execution of the order and in respect of the order of conviction, there is no question of execution and consequently suspension. The Appellate Court exercising powers under sub-section (1) of section 389 is not concerned with the consequences which may flow from the order of conviction in regard to the provisions of some other statute. The Appellate Court which entertains appeal against the order of conviction is entitled to suspend the execution of the sentence or the orders which flow as a consequence of the judgment either of conviction or acquittal and such a Criminal Appellate Court is not concerned with the consequences in respect of some other statutes which are visited upon the person who is convicted by a Criminal Court. The submission that the order of conviction will have automatic impact with reference to some other statutes is devoid of any merit because the Legislature has taken sufficient precaution in respect of those other statutes to protect a person who has preferred an appeal against the order of conviction. As mentioned earlier, the recording of order of conviction against a director, will not automatically disqualify the director of a company from holding the post, in a case where appeal is preferred within the stipulated period of limitation or where the Central Government exempts such person or the company from disqualification. Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act provides that the disqualification shall not take effect until three months have elapsed from the date of conviction or, if an appeal or revision application against the order of conviction is preferred, then until that appeal or application is disposed of by the court. Section 11 of the Representation of the People Act confers power upon the Election Commission to remove any disqualification. It is, therefore, obvious that whenever the Legislature thought it fit, statutory provisions were made to lessen the rigour of the consequences of recording of conviction. The Legislature, in its wisdom, did not make any such provision under section 267 when conviction is recorded against the person who is a managing director. Therefore, it is not permissible for the appellate court which entertains the appeal against the order of conviction to suspend the order of conviction and the only power available under section 389(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is to suspend the execution of the sentence of the order, which expression does not include conviction. The mere fact that the order of conviction leads to some consequences in respect of provisions of other statutes is not sufficient for assuming powers which the Appellate Court does not possess under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The powers of the criminal court flow from the Code and it is not open for the criminal court to assume powers only because the convicted person is likely to suffer certain disqualification under the provisions of other statutes.

It was not possible to accept the respondents' argument that even assuming that provisions of sub-section (1) of section 389 do not confer power on the appellate court to direct suspension of the order of conviction, still such a power can be gathered from the provisions of section 482. Section 482 deals with the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under the Code or to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The respondent urged that the order of conviction could be suspended to secure the ends of justice. The submission was fallacious and could not be acceded to. The inherent powers cannot be exercised to find some means to pass orders which are not permissible under the Code. It could not be appreciated how it could be even suggested that conviction could be suspended to secure the ends of justice. In any event, it was not for the Criminal Appellate Court hearing an appeal to decide what the ends of justice were in respect of enforcement of provisions of some other statutes. The powers of the Appellate Court flow from the provisions of the Code and the contention that the Appellate Court hearing the criminal appeal should pass orders to avoid consequences flowing from the provisions of statutes like the Companies Act or the Representation of the People Act could not be accepted Such other statutes have taken care of the consequences which flow from the order of conviction recorded by the criminal court. The provisions of section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not at all attracted to claim that the order of conviction can be suspended by an order of the Court.

As regards the order of the Delhi High Court staying operation of the order of conviction of respondent No. 1, the order of the Delhi High Court could not be read as suspending the order of conviction and, even assuming it to be so, the Delhi High Court had no power to suspend the order of conviction. In any event, while determining whether respondent No. 1 was disqualified to hold the post of managing director under section 267 it was entirely immaterial what the Delhi High Court had contemplated while passing such order. The consequences flowing from the provisions of section 267 did not depend upon the passing of the order by the Delhi High Court. The right of respondent No. 1 to hold the post of managing director come to an end the moment the order of conviction was recorded.

As such, the OM dated 16-7-2015, in respect of employees of the Government of India treats inquiry into complaints of sexual harassment as a two-stage process where there is a preliminary / fact-finding inquiry at first and then a disciplinary proceedings based on the findings of the preliminary / fact-finding inquiry. [Para 66]

■ Much emphasis has been laid by the appellant on the fact that disciplinary action cannot be taken against him on the basis of the recommendations of an inquiry authority who is not from the same department. However, any punishment which is to be imposed upon the errant employee after completion of the disciplinary proceedings is to be imposed by the 'employer' or disciplinary authority of the 'respondent', based upon the findings which come through in the second-stage disciplinary proceedings. The fact that ultimately disciplinary action against the 'respondent' has to be taken by his employer and his department cannot be an impediment for the ICC constituted at the workplace of the aggrieved woman to take up the fact-finding inquiry under section 11 of the POSH Act when read with the OM dated 16-7-2015. In this context, particular reference must be made to section 13(3)(i) of the POSH Act which lays down that the ICC, upon reaching the conclusion that the allegations against the 'respondent' are proved, shall recommend to the employer to take disciplinary action for sexual harassment as a misconduct in accordance with the provisions of the service rules of the 'respondent'. [Para 67]

■

In view of the findings as recorded above in respect of Issue 3, it is found that the ICC proceedings instituted in the aggrieved woman's department can be considered the first-stage of inquiry which carries out a preliminary / fact-finding inquiry, after which the report of the ICC may be sent to the employer / department of the 'respondent'. Depending on the findings of the ICC (at the aggrieved woman's workplace) as the first stage, the 'employer' may then take a decision to initiate disciplinary proceedings under the applicable service rules and in such disciplinary proceedings, the ICC constituted at the workplace of the 'respondent' shall be the inquiring authority. While conducting the disciplinary proceedings against the 'respondent', the ICC at the workplace of the 'respondent' shall have reference to the report of the fact-finding inquiry by the ICC constituted at the workplace of the aggrieved woman. [Para 68]

■

The instant appeal originates out of the notice / order dated 13-6-2023 directing the appellant to appear before the ICC constituted at the workplace of the aggrieved woman after institution of proceedings and filing of complaint by the aggrieved woman under section 9 of the POSH Act. It is a challenge which was brought by the appellant at a preliminary stage. While issuing notice vide order dated 18-7-2023 in the instant appeal, it was directed by this Court that inquiry may continue but the final outcome of the inquiry shall be kept in a sealed cover. As mentioned above, a copy of the report of the ICC in sealed cover has been supplied and the same has been perused. [Para 69]

■

A concern was raised that since the appellant is an employee of a different department, the ICC at the aggrieved woman's workplace will not be privy to details about the employee's scope of duty, work and service records, etc. However, from a bare perusal of the report, it is found that the ICC at the aggrieved woman's workplace has communicated with the employer of the 'respondent', i.e., his Department and sought information with respect to the incident and scope of duty of the 'respondent', which the Department has provided. The duty of the employer to co-operate in the ICC proceedings is a statutory duty of the employer, which it has duly complied with. Apart from this, the 'respondent' has not been able to show that any prejudice has been caused to him due to the proceedings being carried out by the ICC constituted at the workplace of the aggrieved woman. In any case, the right and remedy of the aggrieved woman to bring a complaint under the POSH Act must be juxtaposed and balanced with the sacrosanct right of the 'respondent' to be heard and for application of mind before imposing of any punishment. As held above, after the conduct of a fact-finding / preliminary inquiry by the ICC constituted at the workplace of the aggrieved woman under the POSH Act, its recommendations shall be sent to the Department being the 'employer' of the 'respondent', at which stage the employer will take a decision about initiation of disciplinary proceedings under the provisions of the CCS CCA Rules, 1965. The fact that there might be administrative lethargy resulting in delay of the ICC proceedings if the workplace of the 'respondent' fails to co-operate with the factual inquiry being conducted by the ICC at the aggrieved woman's workplace, even though in the facts of this case, the employer has duly complied with requests from the aggrieved woman's workplace. However, in that respect, it will suffice to say that cooperating with the ICC in conduct of inquiry is a statutory duty of the employer under section 19(f) of the POSH Act, which shall be complied with. [Para 70]

PROTECTION OF EMPLOYEES DURING INVESTIGATION

An employee of company who has disclosed information during investigation is protected against dismissal, discharge or removal or change in terms of his employment to his disadvantage, during investigation, without permission of NCLT [earlier CLB upto 1-6-2016]

Company should give intimation of proposed action to NCLT and if no reply is received within 30 days, proposed action can be taken [section 218(2) of Companies Act, 2013] [corresponding to section 635B(2) of the 1956 Act]

If company is not satisfied with order of NCLT, it can file appeal in NCLAT within 30 days - section 218(3) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 635B(3) of the 1956 Act]

Such removal or change in terms of employment is subject to other laws also - section 218(5) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 635B(5) of the 1956 Act]

39.5-1 Protection to legal advisers and Bankers

A legal adviser cannot be compelled to supply privileged communication except name and address of his client. A banker has to disclose information about the company or the person under investigation but not of any other customer - section 227 of Companies Act, 2013. [corresponding to section 251 of the 1956 Act].

39.5-2 Freezing of assets of company on inquiry and investigation

Central Government can make application to NCLT for freezing of assets, funds and properties of the company, if there is reasonable ground to believe that removal or transfer or disposal of funds, assets or properties of company is likely to take place in manner prejudicial to interests of company or its shareholders or creditors or in public interest. Such order can be for period upto three years - section 221(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

If despite such order, there is removal or transfer of disposal of assets, company as well as every officer who is in default is liable for punishment of fine and imprisonment - section 221(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

The section 221 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and is effective from 1-6-2016.

39.5-3 Source of information need not be disclosed

Often investigation is carried out on basis of some secret information. To protect the informant, it has been provided that Registrar or officer of Government or any other person shall not be compelled to disclose to Court, Tribunal or other authority, where he got information which has led Central Government to order special audit or order an investigation - section 457 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 635AA of the 1956 Act].

The process of criminal law including the trial, appeal and revision is a protracted one and it is difficult to visualise a situation where the Settlement Commission in a particular case shall take such a long time for disposing of the application and in granting immunity from criminal prosecution that the accused shall have lost all opportunities to take benefit of such an order granting immunity even before the appellate or the revisional Court. It is not possible to take the view that the Settlement Commission while exercising its exclusive jurisdiction under section 245F(2) may exercise the power of an income-tax authority and stay the prosecution and, hence, in the interest of justice and to obviate anamolous situation being created it is just and proper to stay the criminal prosecution. The Settlement Commission has no such jurisdiction. This is so for the reason that once a criminal proceeding has been validly instituted for committing any offence under Chapter XXII, no income-tax authority under the Act has been vested with the jurisdiction to stay the proceedings before the criminal court. Section 279(2) provides that any offence under this Chapter may either before or after the institution of the proceeding be compounded by the Commissioner or a Director General. Once the offence is compounded, the proceeding before the Criminal Court comes to an end and the question of stay of criminal proceeding does not arise. Criminal proceedings are proceedings independent of assessment proceedings. The question of either grant of sanction for prosecution or compounding the offence under section 279(1) and (2) is not before the Settlement Commission and, hence, keeping in view the provision of section245F(4), in the absence of any express direction of the Settlement Commission to the contrary, the income-tax authority can exercise its power under section 279(1) and (2) even after the Settlement Commission has allowed the application to be proceeded with and section 245F(2) cames into play. Be that as it may, the fact remained that since no income-tax authority under the Act has the authority to stay the criminal proceeding, the Settlement Commission has no such jurisdiction, either exclusive or concurrent.

The stay of criminal proceeding in all cases in which the Settlement Commission has allowed the application to be proceeded with also does not appear necessary for saving the provisions of section 245H from being rendered rendundant. If the criminal proceeding is allowed to continue and the accused is held not guilty and acquitted, the matter comes to an end. If the accused is convicted and immunity from criminal prosecution is subsequently granted by the Settlement Commissioner after recording necessary satisfaction under section 245H or the Commission simply passes favourable orders without granting immunity from such criminal prosecution, it should be open to the accused to challenge his conviction on such grounds either in appeal or revision or special leave to appeal under article 136 of the Constitution of India. Also, a favourable finding recorded by the Settlement Commission even in a case in which grant of immunity from criminal prosecution is refused is required to be considered by the criminal court when brought to its knowledge provided such a finding has a bearing on the merits of the case before the Court. For that matter even in cases where the criminal prosecution has been launched before the date of filing of the application before the Settlement Commission and the Commission has no jurisdiction to grant immunity from criminal prosecution, favourable orders can be passed by the Commission in favour of the assessee and such favourable orders need be given due regard by the criminal court.

Thus, just as pendency of an application before the Settlement Commission at any stage, i.e., even after the application has not been rejected and has been allowed to be proceeded with, is no ground for quashing criminal prosecution, its pendency is also not a good ground for staying the criminal proceeding. However, if the decision in a proceeding before any income-tax authority or the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal or the Settlement Commission having a bearing on the fate of the criminal prosecution is imminent, the criminal court can in an appropriate case stay the proceeding under section 309 of Code. However, such exercise of discretion on the part of the criminal court in an appropriate case would depend on the facts of each case and it is not possible to lay down any proposition that if the Settlement Commission has allowed an application to be proceeded with, an order refusing to stay the criminal proceeding by the trial court under section 309 of the Code on that ground will amount to an abuse of the process of the Court to make it a fit case for interference by the High Court in the exercise of its inherent powers under section 482 of the Code.

Hence, the petitioners had failed to make out any case either for quashing of the criminal prosecution or for stay of the criminal proceedings. Therefore, the petitions, having no merit, were dismissed.

WHETHER THE DISMISSAL ORDER DATED 12.07.2017 WAS PASSED BY THE COMPETENT AUTHORITY ?

■

The Appellant has laid considerable emphasis on the fact that she was appointed by the Superintending Engineer but dismissed by the Executive Engineer. According to her, the dismissal order is invalid because it was passed by an authority lower than the appointing authority. [Para 30]

■

The courts below examined the applicable MSEDCL Employees Service Regulations and found that the Appellant was a Pay Grade-III employee. They further held that, under the relevant regulations and schedules governing disciplinary action, the Executive Engineer was competent to impose punishment on an employee belonging to that category. The High Court also considered the Appellant's reliance on the schedule relating to transfers and held that the said schedule did not govern dismissal from service. [Para 31]

■

The question of competence has to be determined with reference to the service regulations governing the employee. If the regulations empower a particular authority to impose punishment on a specified category of employees, the order cannot be set aside merely on a general proposition that the authority that passed the punishment order should not be below the authority that issued the appointment order. The Appellant has not established that the Executive Engineer was excluded from exercising the power of disciplinary authority under the applicable Regulations. [Para 32]

■

The broader principle is that a corporation or company having a legal personality distinct from the Government is not, merely because of Government ownership or control, is to be treated as a Government department for the purpose of Article 311. What is material is whether the employee holds a civil post under the Union or State or not. In the present case, it has not been established that the Appellant holds a civil post thus, entitled to the protection as envisaged in Article 311 of the Constitution. [Para 36]

■

Court therefore finds no error in the concurrent finding that the Executive Engineer was competent to pass the order of dismissal. [Para 37]

Court also finds no error in the concurrent finding that the Executive Engineer was competent under the applicable MSEDCL Employees Service Regulations to pass an order of punishment against the Appellant, who was a Pay Grade-III employee. The challenge to the dismissal order on the ground of lack of competence is therefore rejected. [Para 111.5]

WHETHER A FRESH SHOW-CAUSE NOTICE FOR PUNISHMENT WAS REQUIRED AFTER THE DE NOVO PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE LABOUR COURT?

■

The Appellant's principal submission is that the show-cause notice dated 25.04.2008 was issued on the basis of the domestic enquiry. That enquiry was thereafter found to be not fair. The Industrial Court, by order dated 14.08.2015, remanded the matter to the Labour Court and permitted the Respondent-management to establish the misconduct before the Labour Court. According to the Appellant, once misconduct was proved in the de novo proceedings before the Labour Court, the Respondent could not have mechanically acted upon the earlier show-cause notice issued based on the earlier domestic enquiry which was found to be defective. [Para 38]

■

The submission requires consideration in the light of Regulation 88(j) of the MSEDCL Service Regulations. Regulation 88(j), titled "Show Cause Notice", reads as follows: "After the enquiry is completed, the Competent Authority shall serve a notice on the employee communicating to him its findings and asking him to show cause within a specified time as to why the contemplated punishment involving dismissal, removal or reversion or withholding of increment/s should not be inflicted on him. The employee may be supplied with a copy of the findings of the Competent Authority or of those of the Enquiry Officer, as the case may be, or he may be given an opportunity to take a copy of such findings." [Para 39]

■

The language of Regulation 88(j) is significant. It contemplates a notice to be issued after the enquiry is completed. The purpose of such notice is not an empty formality. The employee must be informed of the findings based on which the competent authority proposes to impose punishment and must be given an opportunity to show cause why the contemplated punishment should not be inflicted. [Para 40]

■

Court is conscious that a second opportunity against proposed punishment is not a mandate in every disciplinary proceeding. However, where the applicable service regulation expressly provides for a post-enquiry notice communicating the findings and calling upon the employee to show cause against the contemplated punishment, the authority must comply with that regulation. In the present case, therefore, the issue arises not as an abstract constitutional requirement, but from the express language of Regulation 88(j). [Para 42]

In order to examine what the expression 'exemption of the sentence or order' occurring in section 389(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure means, one has to note that the criminal courts holding criminal trials not only pass orders of conviction and impose sentences but can pass diverse orders but which need not necessarily have a reference to the conviction. It is open for a criminal court to award costs or compensation for arresting persons without any sufficient ground These orders are not passed by the criminal courts only on the basis of recording of conviction. These are the kinds of orders which are contemplated by provisions of sub-section (1) of section 389 and the powers are conferred on the Appellate Court to suspend the execution not only of the sentence imposed or the conviction, but also the execution of the order which may bede hors of the conviction. The powers of the Appellate Court under section 389(1) cannot be construed with reference to the expression 'order' as suspending the order of conviction itself. The powers of the Appellate Court do not entitle such a court to direct that the order of conviction should stand suspended The conviction can only be set aside.

The contention that the expression 'order' covers even the order of conviction cannot be accepted because the expression used by the Legislature is 'execution of the sentence or order'. The section makes it clear that the appellate court can suspend the execution of the sentence or the execution of the order and in respect of the order of conviction, there is no question of execution and consequently suspension.

The Appellate Court exercising powers under sub-section (1) of section 389 is not concerned with the consequences which may flow from the order of conviction in regard to the provisions of some other statute. The Appellate Court which entertains appeal against the order of conviction is entitled to suspend the execution of the sentence or the orders which flow as a consequence of the judgment either of conviction or acquittal and such a Criminal Appellate Court is not concerned with the consequences in respect of some other statutes which are visited upon the person who is convicted by a Criminal Court. The submission that the order of conviction will have automatic impact with reference to some other statutes is devoid of any merit because the Legislature has taken sufficient precaution in respect of those other statutes to protect a person who has preferred an appeal against the order of conviction. As mentioned earlier, the recording of order of conviction against a director, will not automatically disqualify the director of a company from holding the post, in a case where appeal is preferred within the stipulated period of limitation or where the Central Government exempts such person or the company from disqualification. Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act provides that the disqualification shall not take effect until three months have elapsed from the date of conviction or, if an appeal or revision application against the order of conviction is preferred, then until that appeal or application is disposed of by the court. Section 11 of the Representation of the People Act confers power upon the Election Commission to remove any disqualification. It is, therefore, obvious that whenever the Legislature thought it fit, statutory provisions were made to lessen the rigour of the consequences of recording of conviction. The Legislature, in its wisdom, did not make any such provision under section 267 when conviction is recorded against the person who is a managing director. Therefore, it is not permissible for the appellate court which entertains the appeal against the order of conviction to suspend the order of conviction and the only power available under section 389(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is to suspend the execution of the sentence of the order, which expression does not include conviction. The mere fact that the order of conviction leads to some consequences in respect of provisions of other statutes is not sufficient for assuming powers which the Appellate Court does not possess under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The powers of the criminal court flow from the Code and it is not open for the criminal court to assume powers only because the convicted person is likely to suffer certain disqualification under the provisions of other statutes.

Res judicata - Issue estoppel and criminal proceedings

2.35 Issue estoppel is a branch of the law of res judicata applied to criminal proceedings. The binding nature of a finding arrived at between the parties in previous litigation, in a subsequent litigation between the same parties as applied to criminal proceedings is called “issue estoppel”. The effect of a verdict of acquittal pronounced by a competent Court on a lawful charge and after a lawful trial is not completely slated by saying that the person acquitted cannot be tried again for the same offence. To that it must be added that the verdict is binding as conclusive in all subsequent proceedings between the parties to the adjudication. The maxim res judicata pro vertiate accipitur is no less applicable to criminal than to civil proceedings.1 The principle of issue estoppel outside the scope of section 300 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to India.2 It applies not only in favour of the accused but also against him. But in all criminal proceedings, the principle of res judicata or issue estoppel may come in conflict with another principle, namely, that the prosecution must prove that the accused is guilty and unless this is done the accused is presumed to be innocent. The principle of issue estoppel cannot override the principle of presumption of innocence of the accused. Similarly, the following special features of the criminal proceedings would further modify the application of issue estoppel.

◆ First, in a criminal case, there is no duty on the accused to adduce evidence in defence while in a civil case adverse inference may be drawn from the refusal of a party to adduce evidence in his possession or power.

◆ Secondly, the burden of proof to prove the guilt of the accused is more on the prosecution in a criminal case as compared to the burden of proof on the plaintiff to prove his case against the defendant in a civil case.

◆ Thirdly, certain evidence such as confession in certain circumstances cannot be proved in a criminal case against the accused though there is no such restriction between the parties to a civil proceeding.

◆ Lastly, a finding of fact arrived at in a civil proceeding may not be binding in a criminal proceeding against the accused.

Generally speaking, the principle of issue estoppel is invoked to bar adducing of evidence to proved facts which have been already adjudicated upon in a previous proceeding between the parties. It is easier to obtain a finding of fact for a plaintiff against a defendant in a civil proceeding than for the prosecution to do so against the accused in a criminal proceeding. Therefore, the finding of fact given in a previous civil proceeding may not act as res judicata in a subsequent criminal proceeding. For the same reasons, a finding of fact in a criminal proceeding against an accused person should act as res judicata in a subsequent civil proceeding between the same parties. In Hollington v. F. Hewthorn & Co. Ltd.1, the Court of Appeal in England, however, did not accord the effect of res judicata to a summary conviction of the accused for a traffic offence in a subsequent civil proceeding in which the accused was sued for damages by the person who was injured by the negligence of the accused in driving a car. Similarly, in Anil Behari Ghosh v. Smt. Latika Bala Dassi2, the conviction by a Criminal Court of a person for the murder of his father was not regarded as conclusive in a subsequent proceeding for revocation of the grant of probate under section 263 of the Succession Act. These decisions apparently did not attach importance to the fact that the rules of procedure and evidence are more favourable to the accused in criminal proceeding and, therefore, there should be no objection to a finding against the accused in a criminal proceeding acting as res judicata in a subsequent civil proceeding.

The Supreme Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO3 observed:

“...In the criminal case all the ingredients of the offence in question have to be established in order to secure the conviction of the accused. The Criminal Court no doubt has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and in an appropriate case it may drop the proceedings in the light of an order passed under the Act. It does not, however, mean that the result of a proceeding under the Act would be binding on the Criminal Court. The Criminal Court has to judge the case independently on the evidence placed before it. Otherwise, there is a danger of a contention being advanced that whenever an assessee or any other person liable under the Act had failed to convince the authorities in the proceedings under the Act that he has not deliberately made any false statement or that he has not fabricated any material evidence, the conviction of such person should invariably follow in the criminal court. . .” (pp. 700, 701)

The human mind does not function in compartments. [Para 44]

■

When it receives impressions from different sources, it is the totality of the impressions, which goes into the making of the decision. It is not possible to analyse and dissect the impressions and predicate which impressions went into the making of the decision. Nor is it any easy exercise to erase the impression created by particular circumstances so as to exclude the influence of such impression in the decision-making process. [Para 45]

■

Therefore, where there is material before the District Magistrate, which is of the character as would have reasonable probability to influence the decision of a reasonable man, the Court would be reluctant to accept the ipse dixit of the District Magistrate that he was not so influenced and a fortiori, if such material is not disclosed to the detenu, the order of detention would be vitiated. The principle that the material that may influence the decision of a quasi-judicial authority to award a penalty, must be disclosed to the delinquent, was affirmed by the Apex Court in the case of Union of India v. Mohd. Ramzan Khan, (1991) 1 SCC 588. [Para 47]

The principles of natural justice require that the employee should have a fair opportunity to meet, explain and controvert it before he is condemned. It is negation of the tenets of justice and a denial of fair opportunity to the employee, to consider the findings recorded by a third party like an enquiry officer, without giving an opportunity to reply. ■

Although the disciplinary authority is required to arrive at its own findings on the basis of the evidence, but it is equally true that the disciplinary authority takes into consideration the findings recorded by the enquiry officer along with the evidence on record. In the circumstances, the findings of the enquiry officer do constitute an important material, which is likely to influence the conclusions of the disciplinary authority and therefore, the same must be made available to the employee. 13.2-3c Relevance of expression "Any matter arising out of or connected with such appeal and which is so pending" - Whether "any matter arising out of or connected with" covers even non-appealable orders in respect of which appeal lies to CIT(A)? For example, AO passes an order under section 171 as regards the partition of HUF. Then he makes an assessment based on his findings in section 171 order. Can appeals on both matters pending before CIT(A) be transferred to JCIT(A). These are obviously connected matters, but one of them (order under section 171) is a non-appealable order under section 246(1) and is appealable to CIT(A) under section 246A. It may be opined here that the non-obstante clause in sub-section (3) overrides both sub-sections (1) and (2). However, there is no non obstante clause in sub-section (2). If intent was connected matters which are not appealable orders under section 246(1) can also be transferred, then there was no reason why Parliament could not have provided a non obstante clause in sub-section (2) overriding sub-section(1) as has been done in sub-section (3).

Thus, in this example, the order under section 171 cannot be transferred from CIT(A) to JCIT(A)

13.2-3d Whether appeal fully heard and on which decision has been reserved by CIT(A) and is yet to be delivered as of 1-4-2023 is a pending appeal which can be transferred from CIT(A) to JCIT(A)? - It is a pending appeal as it is undecided though fully heard. Technically, it 'may' be transferred. However, the discretion is to be exercised judicially by Board or authorised authority and should not be exercised arbitrarily. It is in no one's interest that a matter fully heard be transferred as it will involve the rigours of rehearing the case by JCIT (Appeals). However, if too much time has elapsed after completing the hearings and the matter is still pending for decision, it may be in assessee's interests that the matter be transferred to JCIT (Appeals) and decided expeditiously after a rehearing by JCIT (Appeals). The Supreme Court was conscious of possible prejudice to parties where Court reserves its judgment and takes a long time to pronounce the judgment without rehearing.

In R.C. Sharma v. UOI [1976] (3) SCC 574, the Supreme Court observed that "Nevertheless an unreasonable delay between hearing of arguments and delivery of judgment, unless explained by exceptional or extraordinary circumstances, is highly undesirable even when written arguments are submitted. It is not unlikely that some points which the litigant considers important may have escaped notice. But, what is more important is that litigants must have complete confidence in the results of litigation. This confidence tends to be shaken if there is an excessive delay between hearing of arguments and delivery of judgments."

In Anil Rai v. State of Bihar (Judgment dated 6-8-2001), the Supreme Court held as under:

(a)

Where a judgment is not pronounced within three months from the date of reserving judgment, any of the parties in the case is permitted to file an application in the High Court with prayer for early judgment. Such application, as and when filed, shall be listed before the Bench concerned within two days, excluding the intervening holidays.

(b)

If the judgment, for any reason, is not pronounced within a period of six months, any of the parties of the said list shall be entitled to move an application before the Chief Justice of the High Court with a prayer to withdraw the said case and to make it over to any other Bench for fresh arguments. It is open to the Chief Justice to grant the said prayer or to pass any other order as he deems fit in the circumstances.

So, factors such as the following must weigh with CBDT or authorised authority in exercising discretion to transfer cases "fully heard but the decision of CIT(A) pending" to JCIT(A)

(a)

Length of time for which decision by CIT(A) is pending though the matter fully heard.

(b)

Whether assessee moved any application before CIT(A) for expediting judgment after matter was fully heard.

(c)

Whether assessee has raised any objection to transfer from CIT(A) to JCIT(A) when afforded the mandatory opportunity of being heard before the transfer.

Introduction

1. Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated Jan. 1, 2013 has mandated the initiation of recovery proceedings thirty days after the filing of an appeal, if no stay is granted.

Important situations

2. Important situations and directions for recovery have been tabulated as follows:- 3. Judicial precedents

3.1 Case of M/s. Symrise Pvt. Ltd. v. UOI - The Madras High Court in the case of Symrise (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [W.P. Nos. 1509 & 1510 of 2013, dated 21-1-2013] stayed the application of the circular stating that it overreaches the provisions of the Customs Act.

The Circular (supra) mandates that steps for recovery must be initiated within a specified period after the filing of the appeal if no stay is granted. There may be a situation where the Commissioner (Appeals) or the CESTAT is unable to decide the application for stay within specified period. Administrative reasons, including the lack of adequate infrastructure, the unavailability of the officer concerned before whom the stay application has been filed, the absence of a Bench before the CESTAT for the decision of an application for stay or the sheer volume of work are some of the causes due to which applications for stay remain pending.

In a situation where an assessee has done everything within his control by moving an application for stay and which remains pending because of the inability of the Commissioner (Appeals) or the CESTAT to dispose of the application within specified period, it would be against justice, if recovery proceedings are allowed to be initiated in the meantime.

3.2 Case of CC&CE v. Kumar Cotton Mills (P.) Ltd. - The protection of the revenue has to be necessarily balanced with fairness to the assessees. That was why, even though a specific statutory provision came to be introduced by the Parliament in section 35C(2A) to the effect that an order of stay would stand vacated where the appeal before the Tribunal was not disposed of within 180 days, yet the Supreme Court in the case of CC&CE v. Kumar Cotton Mills (P.) Ltd. 2005 (180) ELT 434 held that this would not apply to a situation where the appeal has remained pending for reasons not attributable to the assessee.

3.3 Case of L&T v. UOI - L&T was engaged in providing services of commission agents in India and Nepal for all kinds of earth moving equipments and other machines, including accessories and spares manufactured by L&T Komatsu Limited. The Department demanded service tax thereon for the period from July, 2003 to March, 2005 under the heading 'clearing and forwarding agent's services'. L&T filed an appeal before the Tribunal along with an application for stay of demand, which was pending. A hearing was granted to L&T in matter of stay application, but it was adjourned due to non-availability of the Tribunal Bench. Pending such application, the Department initiated recovery proceedings and allegedly threatened to take coercive action for recovery relying on CBEC's Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1-1-2013. L&T challenged the circular as invalid.

The application of the same circular (supra) came up for adjudication before the Bombay High Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. Union of India [2013] 38 STT 684/30 taxmann.com 363, the Bombay High Court held as under :

"We have come to conclusion that the provisions contained in the impugned Circular, dated 1 January, 2013, mandating the initiation of recovery proceedings thirty days after the filing of an appeal, if no stay is granted, cannot be applied to an assessee who has filed an application of stay, which has remained pending for reasons beyond the control of the assessee. Where, however, an application for stay has remained pending for more than a reasonable period, for reasons having a bearing on the default or the improper conduct of an assessee, recovery proceedings can well be initiated."

Concluding remark

4. There can be no coercive recovery pending stay application before the appellate authorities/Court, if such pendency is for a reason not attributable to the assessee.

Applicant was Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of ICICI Bank.

During her employment with ICICI Bank applicant had signed in acceptance various policies of ICICI Bank which included Code of Conduct, Framework for dealing with conflict of interest, Deeds for Covenants and Clawback agreement. Applicant was also required to make various disclosures in compliance of the Companies Act, 1956, the Companies Act, 2013, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the SEBI (Listing Obligation and Disclosure) Regulations, 2015, RBI Master Circular on Loans and Advances and RBI Guidelines on Compensation of Whole Time Directors/CEOs.

The applicant was granted Employee Stock Options (ESOPs) was based on performance, continued good conduct and the representations/disclosures made by applicant to ICICI Bank at such time.

There were news articles which contained allegations of nepotism against applicant with regard to grant of loans to companies affiliated with Videocon Group 'Venugopal Dhoot' as a quid pro quo for investments by 'Venugopal Dhoot' or his affiliates in NuPower Renewables, a company promoted by the husband of applicant.

ICICI Bank appointed a reputed law firm to conduct independent enquiry into the allegations appearing in these news articles.

Applicant and her husband in the aforementioned enquiry had provided information and documents indicating that there were no investments made by 'Venugopal Dhoot' and his affiliates in NRPL. Based on the information submitted by applicant and her husband, the law firm submitted its report with ICICI Bank stating that there was no merit in the allegations.

Later on, ICICI Bank received whistleblower letters primarily alleging abuse of position by applicant and the business dealings between Videocon Group and husband of applicant.

The Board of Directors of ICICI Bank decided to conduct an enquiry into the allegations against applicant in accordance with the Terms of Reference. Relevant filings were also made by ICICI Bank with the stock exchanges.

Justice B.N. Srikrishna (Retired Judge of the Supreme Court) was appointed by Audit Committee of ICICI Bank to conduct an independent enquiry into the allegations against applicant.

At a Board meeting of ICICI applicant communicated her decision to go on leave until the said enquiry was completed. The Board in good faith accepted her decision and made necessary disclosures to the stock exchange.

While the enquiry was still pending applicant addressed a letter requesting the Board of Directors of ICICI Bank to grant her early retirement.

ICICI Bank, intimated the Board's approval and referred to benefits under the Early Retirement Scheme ('ERS').

Pending the completion of the Enquiry, applicant exercised 6,90,000 ESOPs and received other benefits.

Justice Srikrishna (Retired) submitted Enquiry Report to ICICI Bank wherein the conduct of applicant had been highlighted. The Enquiry Report had held that applicant had committed 'Gross/Serious Violations' of the Code of Conduct for extended periods of time.

The Board of Directors of ICICI Bank at their meeting considered and deliberated on the findings of the Enquiry Report and conclusion therein. In the light of the findings on serious violations by applicant having coming to the knowledge of the Board it was unanimously resolved to treat the separation of applicant from ICICI Bank as termination for cause under the ICICI Bank's internal policies, schemes and the Code of Conduct with all attendant consequences (including revocation of all her existing and future entitlements such as any unpaid amounts, unpaid bonuses or increments, vested and unvested and unexercised stock options and medical benefits) and claw back all bonuses paid and to take further actions as warranted (including notifying or securing regulatory approvals as required). Disclosures to the stock exchanges was also made by ICICI Bank in this regard and the RBI was also immediately informed about the findings.

Applicant filed writ petition claiming that once the Board had accepted her early retirement, the relationship of employer and employee between ICICI Bank and applicant ended and bank could not thereafter take any disciplinary action against applicant or revoke retirement benefits.

Section 14(2) states that a person aggrieved by an order pertaining to any service matter may make an application to the Tribunal. The application, therefore, lies against an "order". A show cause notice issued to the petitioner cannot, by any stretch of imagination, be treated as an "order". The order would follow the show cause notice, after the noticee tenders his response thereto, and the response is considered by the competent authority. [Para 25]

■ Thus, Section 14(2) clearly does not render a show cause notice issued to an officer amenable to challenge before the Tribunal. This position is also fortified when one refers to Section 3(o) to which Mr. Bhandari himself drew attention. Clause (iii) of Section 3(o) includes, within the meaning of "service matters", "summary disposal and trial where the punishment of dismissal is awarded". Thus, prior to the awarding of any punishment to the officer concerned, it cannot even be said that his grievance constitutes a "service matter". [Para 27]

■

Thus, the provisions of the AFT Act, too, do not support Mr. Bhandari's contention that the show cause notice was answerable to the Tribunal or that any appeal, against the recommendations of the ICC, would lie before the Tribunal so as to enable the petitioner to bypass the requirement of responding to the show cause notice. [Para 28]

■

Thus, the Supreme Court has clearly laid down the protocol to be followed in a case where there is an allegation of sexual harassment by an officer at the workplace. Briefly stated, the matter has to be referred to an ICC. However, the recommendations of the ICC do not put a full stop to the proceedings. If the ICC exonerates the officer, the matter may rest there. However, if the findings of the ICC are against the officer, of which the ICC finds the officer complicit, it constitutes actionable misconduct under the service rules, and disciplinary action has to follow. [Para 30]

■

The Supreme Court has, in its decision in Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India (2013) 1 SCC 311, modified the directions in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) 6 SCC 241 by clarifying that the findings of the ICC would constitute an inquiry report as envisaged in the service rules applicable to the officer and that, therefore, once the ICC rendered its findings, the ball would, so to speak, be in the Court of the disciplinary authority. It would be for the officer concerned to respond to the findings of the ICC, before the disciplinary authority, which would then take a conscious decision as to whether to exonerate the officer or, if the officer is found guilty, to punish him appropriately. [Para 31]

■

It is this exercise which has been initiated by the show cause notice dated 5 March 2025, the proceedings in which the petitioner has successfully managed to stultify till now. [Para 32]

■

The Court is of the opinion that any further delay in these proceedings would completely defeat the very philosophy behind the decision in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (supra). [Para 33]

■

In exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, the Court is of the opinion that no case has been made out to interfere with the decision of the Tribunal or even to issue notice in this writ petition. If this petition were to remain pending before this Court, it would result in further protraction of the proceedings against the petitioner which, the Court is clear in its view, would be completely unfair as well as unjust to all parties concerned. [Para 37]

In that view of the matter, notice is declined in the writ petition which is, accordingly dismissed. The Court would have been inclined to award costs; however, as notice is not being issued in the writ petition, the Court refrains from doing so. [Para 38]

The writ petition is, accordingly, dismissed in limine. [Para 39]

HEADNOTE: Section 276C, read with sections 277 and 278 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Offences and prosecutions - Wilful attempt to evade tax - Assessment year 1981-82 - Whether, in case of an assessee who has filed a petition in High Court against order of Tribunal refusing to refer case and such petition has been admitted for hearing, prosecution proceedings separately initiated can be quashed - Held, no - Whether a mere expectation of success in some proceeding in appeal or reference under Act cannot come in way of institution of criminal proceedings under sections 276C and 277 - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1981-82, petitioner-firm, with three other petitioners as partners, submitted return of income disclosing a loss of Rs. 22,198. They also showed the payment of interest to a firm 'MK' to the tune of Rs. 34,721 and further disclosed that they had received loan from 'BKL' to the tune of Rs. 21,000. The ITO did not accept this contention. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted petitioner's appeal. The Tribunal, however, accepted appeal by department and found that loss shown as above and the loan from 'BKL' was not correct. The petitioner's reference application was dismissed by the Tribunal. Thereafter, they filed a petition in the High Court which had been admitted for hearing. During the pendency of these proceedings the ITO filed a criminal case against the petitioner under sections 276C, 277 and 278. The Court recorded the evidence and framed charges. The petitioner's revision against the framing of charges had been dismissed by Addl. Sessions Judge.

On petition under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 for quashing the proceedings, it was contended by the petitioner that the continuance of two separate proceedings would be unjust and that the petitioner would be put to double jeopardy. On the other hand, the respondent contended that merely because petitioner was contesting the assessment order or appellate order, it could not be said that prosecution was wholly baseless.

HELD: Civil Court decision or a decision of the civil proceedings is relevant in a criminal prosecution, but criminal courts are required to reach an independent finding and conclusion. There is no provision in law which provides that the prosecution for the offences cannot be launched until the assessment proceedings initiated against the assessee are completed. Further, a mere expectation of success is some proceedings in appeal or reference under the Act cannot come in the way of the institution of the criminal proceedings under sections 276C and section 277. In the criminal case all the ingredients of the offence in question have to be established in order to secure the conviction of the accused. The criminal court, no doubt, has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and in an appropriate case it may drop the proceedings in the light of an order passed under the Act. It does not, however, mean that the result of a proceeding under the Act would be binding on the Criminal Court. In view of the above opinion expressed by the Apex Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO [1984] 149 ITR 696, it could not be said, in the instant case, that merely because a proceeding under the Act was pending, the prosecution under sections 276 and 277 could not be started or that the proceedings in any way deserved to be quashed. Since the two proceedings are different and the standard of proof in both the proceedings are also different, it would not be proper to quash the criminal prosecution, merely because proceedings under the Act in appeal or reference were pending.

Accordingly, the petition was dismissed.

Further, if an allegation of contention is not proved, would it still be considered an offence? Whether it shall be regarded as an offence only after all the legal remedies available at the disposal of the assessee have been exhausted? In this regard, it is essential to consider the 'Presumption of Innocence', which provides that "everyone charged with an offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law". The Supreme Court held that presumption of innocence is a human right [See Narender Singh & Anr. v. State of M.P. (2004) 10 SCC 699, Ranjitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma v. State of Maharashtra and Anr. Parliamentary Standing Committee under the chairmanship of by Mr. Jayant Sinha, Former Minister of State of Finance in its report submitted on March 2020.6 The committee rendered its opinion in favour of incorporation of Section 32A into the Code with a view to safeguard the position of the resolution applicant from the offence the former promoters. Such an observation keeping in mind the necessity of cleansed entity where the change in management of the corporate debtor has taken place.

Pre-Condition to the Applicability of Section 32A

In order to discourage the abuse of this provision, safeguard has been introduced by way of pre-condition which need to be satisfied before resorting to Section 32A are:-

The resolution applicant is not involved or related party to promoter group,

The resolution plan results in control of corporate debtor or change in the management.

Liability for the Offence Committed Prior to the Commencement of CIRP

As a result of incorporation of Section 32A of the Code, the corporate debtor shall cease to responsible for the offence committed prior to the commencement of CIRP and the property of corporate debtor which are part of resolution plan, no action can be taken against those property.

However, it is clarified the ambit of the Section 32A is very limited in terms of liability and it doesn't immune or absolve the person who are:-

responsible for the activities of the corporate debtor in conduct of business,

officer in default

directly or indirectly involved in the commission of the offence

All the above mentioned person shall continue to remain liable for the offence committed prior to the commencement of the CIRP. Furthermore there is also no bar against the property other than property of corporate debtor and the person who has acquired that property under the liquidation or CIRP, as the case may be.

Conundrum Continues

Promulgation of Section 32A in the Code has lot of implication and its position is not very in this regard. Various relevant legal issues time and again has come before the Appellate Tribunal and High Courts for consideration and these issues need to be redressed as they core to the application of Section 32A.

The question of interpretation of Section 32A came up before the Appellate tribunal in the case of JSW Steel Ltd. v. Mahendra Kumar Khandelwal., 7 wherein the Appellate tribunal held that the Section 32A is retrospectively applicable and also set aside all the attachments of the corporate debtor made by Enforcement Department under PMLA. However, it wasn't clarified whether it is also applicable to the proceedings which have already been concluded and no adjudication is pending w.r.t. corporate debtor however they satisfies the parameters laid down in the Section 32A of the Code.

In the case of Tata Steel BSL Ltd v. Union of India,8 wherein summon issued before the incorporation of Section32A into the Code by the Investigating officer was under challenge. The Delhi HC ruled that the petitioner is entitled to the benefit under section 32A of the Code as the instant case falls within the clear language used in Section 32A and hence corporate debtor cannot be made responsible for the offence committed prior to commencement of CIRP even when the resolution plan has been approved by the Adjudicating Authority, when it is expressly prohibited by the provision. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner was upheld and liable to be discharged in the merits of the case.

As understood, an offence occurs upon a violation or breach of law, which is punishable. In this regard, a question arises as to whether the same would be regarded as an offence until it is proved? Further, if an allegation of contention is not proved, would it still be considered an offence? Whether it shall be regarded as an offence only after all the legal remedies available at the disposal of the assessee have been exhausted? In this regard, it is essential to consider the 'Presumption of Innocence', which provides that "everyone charged with an offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law". The Supreme Court held that presumption of innocence is a human right [See Narender Singh & Anr. v. State of M.P. (2004) 10 SCC 699, Ranjitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma v. State of Maharashtra and Anr. (2005) 5 SCC 294]. The Supreme Court also held that once the accused has been convicted by the learned trial court, there shall not be any presumption of innocence thereafter [Shakuntala Shukla v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Another Criminal Appeal No. 876 of 2021].

Based on the above, it can be concluded that the expenditure incurred by an assessee for any purpose, which is an offence, should not be allowed, provided it has been upheld as an offence by any court or regulatory authority. The same shall not change even if the right to appeal against the decision of the court or authority is available.

However, the expenses incurred in defending the same should be allowable, irrespective of the outcome of the contention [See Sree Meenakshi Mills Ltd v. CIT [1967] 63 ITR 207(SC), reaffirmed in CIT v. Birla Cotton Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd.[1971] 82 ITR 166 (SC)]. Further, the charges paid for an offence which are compensatory in nature should not be disallowed under Section 37(1). Only the expenditures incurred for an offence which are penal in nature should be disallowed [See Ocean Agro (India) Ltd. v. Dy. Res judicata - Issue estoppel and criminal proceedings 2.35 Issue estoppel is a branch of the law of res judicata applied to criminal proceedings. The binding nature of a finding arrived at between the parties in previous litigation, in a subsequent litigation between the same parties as applied to criminal proceedings is called “issue estoppel”. The effect of a verdict of acquittal pronounced by a competent Court on a lawful charge and after a lawful trial is not completely slated by saying that the person acquitted cannot be tried again for the same offence. To that it must be added that the verdict is binding as conclusive in all subsequent proceedings between the parties to the adjudication. The maxim res judicata pro vertiate accipitur is no less applicable to criminal than to civil proceedings.1 The principle of issue estoppel outside the scope of section 300 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to India.2 It applies not only in favour of the accused but also against him. But in all criminal proceedings, the principle of res judicata or issue estoppel may come in conflict with another principle, namely, that the prosecution must prove that the accused is guilty and unless this is done the accused is presumed to be innocent. The principle of issue estoppel cannot override the principle of presumption of innocence of the accused. Similarly, the following special features of the criminal proceedings would further modify the application of issue estoppel.

◆ First, in a criminal case, there is no duty on the accused to adduce evidence in defence while in a civil case adverse inference may be drawn from the refusal of a party to adduce evidence in his possession or power.

◆ Secondly, the burden of proof to prove the guilt of the accused is more on the prosecution in a criminal case as compared to the burden of proof on the plaintiff to prove his case against the defendant in a civil case.

◆ Thirdly, certain evidence such as confession in certain circumstances cannot be proved in a criminal case against the accused though there is no such restriction between the parties to a civil proceeding.

◆ Lastly, a finding of fact arrived at in a civil proceeding may not be binding in a criminal proceeding against the accused.

Generally speaking, the principle of issue estoppel is invoked to bar adducing of evidence to proved facts which have been already adjudicated upon in a previous proceeding between the parties. It is easier to obtain a finding of fact for a plaintiff against a defendant in a civil proceeding than for the prosecution to do so against the accused in a criminal proceeding. Therefore, the finding of fact given in a previous civil proceeding may not act as res judicata in a subsequent criminal proceeding. For the same reasons, a finding of fact in a criminal proceeding against an accused person should act as res judicata in a subsequent civil proceeding between the same parties. In Hollington v. F. Hewthorn & Co. Ltd.1, the Court of Appeal in England, however, did not accord the effect of res judicata to a summary conviction of the accused for a traffic offence in a subsequent civil proceeding in which the accused was sued for damages by the person who was injured by the negligence of the accused in driving a car. Similarly, in Anil Behari Ghosh v. Smt. Latika Bala Dassi2, the conviction by a Criminal Court of a person for the murder of his father was not regarded as conclusive in a subsequent proceeding for revocation of the grant of probate under section 263 of the Succession Act. These decisions apparently did not attach importance to the fact that the rules of procedure and evidence are more favourable to the accused in criminal proceeding and, therefore, there should be no objection to a finding against the accused in a criminal proceeding acting as res judicata in a subsequent civil proceeding.

The Supreme Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO3 observed:

“...In the criminal case all the ingredients of the offence in question have to be established in order to secure the conviction of the accused. The Criminal Court no doubt has to give due regard to the result of any proceeding under the Act having a bearing on the question in issue and in an appropriate case it may drop the proceedings in the light of an order passed under the Act. It does not, however, mean that the result of a proceeding under the Act would be binding on the Criminal Court. The Criminal Court has to judge the case independently on the evidence placed before it. Otherwise, there is a danger of a contention being advanced that whenever an assessee or any other person liable under the Act had failed to convince the authorities in the proceedings under the Act that he has not deliberately made any false statement or that he has not fabricated any material evidence, the conviction of such person should invariably follow in the criminal court. . .” (pp. 700, 701)

Rashmi Metaliks Limited v. Enforcement Directorate [2022] SCC OnLine Cal 2316]

A Single Bench of the Hon'ble High Court of Calcutta came to the rescue of the Accused and stayed the two orders of freezing of the accounts of the accused dated July 13, 2022.

The ED had claimed that the company made a wrongful declaration to avail benefits of the Indian Railways' dual freight policy of 2009. The Accused's challenge to the Show cause notice issued by the Railways & Civil Suit filed by the Union of India against the accused was stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 2015.

With freezing orders passed by ED in 2022, i.e. after seven (7) years from the date on which all pending proceedings were stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, and also the summons under the Act were issued prior to the stay order, it was held that the ED could not have initiated any action against the petitioners during the subsistence of the order of stay of the pending proceedings against the accused by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 2015.

Taking consideartion of the exception carved out in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra) for a person named in the criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence being absolved by a Court of competent jurisdiction, interestingly, the Court has drawn an analogy to the present facts where the proceedings have only been stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court & no discharge or no acquittal have been made while restraining the ED from proceeding ahead with its action against the accused.
