The genesis in the cited case rested with the ED registering ECIR on the basis of three (3) FIRs. Out of the three (3) FIRs, one (1) was quashed & the remaining two (2) were stayed till further orders.

Before the Division Bench of the Hon'ble High Court of Madras the primary question was about the implication of quashing & staying of FIRs on the proceedings initiated by the ED under the PMLA.

In line with the directions passed in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra), the ED fairly conceded that in so far as the quashed FIR is concerned, the department cannot proceed ahead under the Act. However, it was strenuously contended by them that the accused cannot take benefit of the stayed proceedings and plea before the court that proceedings under PMLA for the remaining two (2) FIRs too be quashed.

On the other hand, the petitioners refuted the said contention of the department, and relied upon the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Calcutta in Rashmi Metaliks Ltd. (Supra).

The Division Bench in its judgment discarded the contentions of the Department and answered in negative to the question whether the ECIR, which is also pursuant to the FIRs which have been stayed by the High Court, can be proceeded with or not.

Placing reliance on precedents on 'jurisdictional fact to be taken into account by a Court before assuming jurisdiction over a particular matter', the court opined that the existence of jurisdictional fact is a condition precedent for the exercise of power by a Court of limited jurisdiction. Therefore, in present matter, when there is no cause of action, since the proceeding in one (1) of the cases was quashed, and the proceedings in two (2) other cases have been stayed by the Court, there was no jurisdictional fact or cause of action for the respondent/department to initiate any proceedings during the period of order of stay operating against the two FIRs.

Finally, in its conclusion, the Hon'ble High Court opined that in view of the quashing of the proceedings in one (1) of the FIR and staying of the proceedings in the remaining two (2) FIRs, the scheduled offence was eclipsed, suspended or stop operating during the period of stay. Therefore, the Department has to await the finality of the said proceedings. In case, if the other two (2) remaining FIRs also get quashed pursuant to the orders in the applications filed by the respective accused to quash the proceedings, in which event, the Department cannot step in or initiate any proceedings under the PMLA, as held in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (Supra).

Is Commission of a Scheduled Offence a Sine Qua Non for Proceedings under PMLA

In light of the conflicting interpretation amongst various High Courts in India on the issue whether money-laundering is a standalone offence or dependent on the scheduled offence, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has now put to rest the divergent views by affirming that "if the person is finally discharged/acquitted of the scheduled offence or the criminal case against him is quashed by the Court of competent jurisdiction, there can be no offence of money laundering against him or any one claiming such property being the property linked to stated scheduled offences through him."

Some of the recent notable judgments on the aforesaid issue are as hereunder:

. The court unless proven otherwise, shall presume that the proceed of crime is involved in money laundering.

APPEAL & REVISION

Section 47 provides an opportunity to an aggrieved party on account of orders passed by the special court to either prefer an appeal or a revision before the jurisdictional Hon'ble High Court. Chapter XXIX (Appeal) and XXX (Revision) under CrPC shall govern the power and procedure of appeal and revision, respectively before the Hon'ble High Court. EEFECT OF ACQUITTAL IN SCHEDULED OFFENCE ON TRIAL OF OFFENCE OF MONEY LAUNDERING

The prosecution under the PMLA for offence of money laundering and the trial for scheduled offences are inter-linked to each other. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the landmark judgment of Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India2 has inter-alia held hereinbelow:-

"187. …….(d) The offence under Section 3 of the 2002 Act is dependent on illegal gain of property as a result of criminal activity relating to a scheduled offence. It is concerning the process or activity connected with such property, which constitutes the offence of money-laundering. The Authorities under the 2002 Act cannot prosecute any person on notional basis or on the assumption that a scheduled offence has been committed, unless it is so registered with the jurisdictional police and/or pending enquiry/trial including by way of criminal complaint before the competent forum. If the person is finally discharged/acquitted of the scheduled offence or the criminal case against him is quashed by the Court of competent jurisdiction, there can be no offence of money laundering against him or any one claiming such property being the property linked to stated scheduled offence through him."

The aforesaid principle of Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (supra) was relied by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in another matter of Parvathi Kollur v. State by Directorate of Enforcement3 whereby on account of acquittal by a trial court in relation to the scheduled offence, the accused was discharged for offence of money laundering as well.

CONCLUSION

The PMLA is a cardinal legislation to support the financial ecosystem of the nation by combating to the offence of money laundering. The Act is a result of a world-wide effort under the aegis of United Nations which later on was reiterated by Indian Parliament in the form of legislation.

The recognition of money laundering as an offences has provided ample scope to the agencies to not only recover the proceeds of crime under the adjudication proceedings but also initiating prosecution proceedings for commission of the offences of money laundering. Such recognition of money laundering as a criminal offence shall benefit the society at large by deterring other similar minded people.

Reliance on the Supreme Court decision

3. The Circular draws reference to the decision of the Apex Court in the case of Collector of Customs, Bombay v. Krishna Sales (P) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The Apex Court observed that "As is well known, mere filing of an Appeal does not operate as a stay or suspension of the Order appealed against". It should be noted that this decision of the Apex Court was somewhat in a different context and was issued when the service tax was not even in force. In fact, the decision was passed by the Apex Court in favour of the assessee.

The appeal before the Apex Court was preferred by the Collector of Customs against the judgment of the Delhi Tribunal. The assessee, Krishna Sales (P) Ltd., imported machinery and classified as a 'Bevel Gear Generator'. The Customs authorities raised an objection and classified the machinery as 'Bevel Gear Planer', thereby confiscating the machinery.

The assessee was given an option to pay a redemption fine of Rs. 70,000/- and penalty of Rs. 10,000/- and clear the goods. Assessee filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The appeal was allowed by the Tribunal which agreed with the classification claimed by the assessee. The counsel for the assessee requested that the customs authorities may be directed to issue a detention certificate for the entire period during which the goods were detained till the date of issuance of the detention certificate.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee by virtue of which the respondent was entitled to clear the machinery without payment of any duty. But the respondent required a detention certificate to clear the machinery. Evidently, in view of this problem, the Apex Court made the following interim order:

"Having heard Ld. Counsel for the Collector of Customs, Bombay and M/s. Krishna Sales (P) Ltd., we direct that the application made by the latter for a detention certificate should not be rejected on the ground that the Appeal is pending in this Court against the Order of the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi."

However,when the assessee applied for issuance of a detention certificate, no such certificate was issued. The assessee submitted that the action of the authorities is relatable to and influenced by the public notice issued by the Collector of Customs, Bombay on July 25, 1985. So far as the detention certificate for a period exceeding six months is concerned, it can be issued only with the approval of and under the signature of the Collector. Para 4 of the public notice deals with issue of detention certificates to the parties succeeding in appeals and read as follows:

"Detention Certificate, as a rule, will be issued by the concerned competent Customs Authority to the Appellants succeeding in Appeals on receipt of the copies of such Orders which the latter making formal application for issue of Detention Certificates. However, in cases where the Customs House decides to go in second Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, the issue of Detention Certificate will be considered only after such second appeal is finally disposed of in favour of the parties."

The Apex Court held as follows:

"6. According to the above mentioned para 4, the goods will not be released even where the party succeeds in cases where the Customs Authorities decide to go in Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court. They will consider the issuance of such certificate only after the decision of the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, as the case may be. The Counsel for the assessee characterised the direction as arbitrary and contrary to law. We see the force in his submission. If the authorities are of the opinion that the goods ought not to be released pending the Appeal, the straight forward course for them is to obtain an Order of Stay or other appropriate direction from the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, as the case may be. Without obtaining such an Order they cannot refuse to implement the Order under Appeal. As is well-known, mere filing of an Appeal does not operate as a Stay or suspension of the Order appealed against. Moreover, such detention is likely to create several complications relating to the demurrage charges besides the possible deterioration of the machinery and goods. We hope and trust that the Collector of Custom Bombay shall appropriately revise the said public notice in the light of the observations made herein. If he does not do so, there is a likelihood of the Customs Authorities being themselves made liable for demurrage charges in appropriate cases.

There are numbers of questionsrelating to withholding of refundswhich arise in the mind of professionals which are as under:-

Q1: Whether issue of a notice can be said to be pending assessment?

Ans. The expression "pending" means "something not concluded" or "undecided" and the expression "to issue" means to send out.

The Hon'ble ITAT Lucknow in the case of Kailash Auto Finance Ltd v. Asstt. CIT [2009] 32 SOT 80 held that and action is considered pending as soon as it is commenced and until it is concluded. An assessment proceeding would commence and be pending when notice of assessment is issued.

The Hon'ble ITAT Bangalore in the case of Himalaya Drug Co. v. Dy. CIT [2014] 48 taxmann.com 65 held that the expression "to issue" means to send out so that the officer concerned has lost control over the order so that he is not in a position to tamper/alter the same.

To conclude, if the AO has dispatched the notice and lost control over it, it may be said that the notice is issued, and the proceedings for assessment or reassessment are pending.

Q2 Can Section 143(1) intimation be treated as an assessment order or initiation of assessment proceeding?

Ans. The intimation received by the taxpayer, though appealable, cannot be considered as an order of assessment. When a taxpayer receives an intimation then it is not a notice for assessment or reassessment.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Rajesh Jhaveri Stock Brokers (P.) Ltd. [2007] 161 Taxman 316/291 ITR 500 held that Section 143(1) intimation received by the taxpayer, though appealable, cannot be considered as an order of assessment. Also, the said intimation, unlike a notice under Section 143(2), cannot be said to initiate assessment proceedings.

Thus, when a taxpayer receives an intimation but not any notice for assessment/reassessment, it cannot be said the assessment proceedings are pending and it does not authorise the AO to withhold the refund.

Q3 Whether issue of notice under Section 142(1) amount to "assessment is pending"?

Ans. Issue of notice u/s 142(1) does not mean that "assessment is pending. "

Issuance of notice u/s 142(1) itself does not amount to initiation of assessment proceedings and an assessment proceeding is deemed to be initiated when a notice of assessment is issued to the assessee. Notice u/s 142(1) is served for the purpose of making an assessment under the Income Tax Act. The information, documents, return or accounts furnished in response to notice u/s 142(1) or non-compliance in regard to such notice may be ground for initiation of assessment proceedings but it does not mean that assessment is pending.

Q4 Whether conducting an enquiry under Section 148A amount to "assessment is pending"?

Ans. As per Section 148A before issuing a notice under Section 148, the AO shall conduct enquiries, if required, and provide an opportunity of being heard to the assessee. After considering his reply, the AO shall decide, after passing an order, whether it is a fit case for the issue of notice under Section 148 and serve a copy of such order along with such notice on the assessee.

4.5 Illegality of Strikes and Lockouts:

A strike or lock-out must be considered illegal if it is commenced or declared in contravention of Section 22 or 23 of the Act.

4.5-1. When continuation of a strike or lock-out is not deemed illegal If a strike or lock-out relating to an industrial dispute has already commenced and is in existence at the time of reference of the dispute to the Board, a labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal, its continuance shall not be deemed illegal. The only condition is that the strike or lock-out was legal when it began and has not been prohibited.

4.5-2. Legality of strikes or lock-outs declared in consequence of illegality

A lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike or a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out must not be considered illegal.

4.5-2-1 Whether a lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike is automatically illegal?

The Supreme Court in Indian Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. & Another v. Their Workmen (1958 AIR 130, 1958 SCR 667), noted that a lock-out was declared in consequence of repeated illegal strikes by the workmen. The Supreme Court held that the lockout was lawful and that the lockout notice, stating that employees' services "shall be deemed to be discharged," meant a temporary refusal to employ, not a permanent dismissal.

The intention was not termination, but rather the suspension of services due to work disruption. Workers who reported within an extended period retained the right to resume work unconditionally. Further, the Court emphasised that Industrial Tribunals have limited scope to interfere in disciplinary actions and may intervene only where the action is malafide, constitutes unfair labour practice, violates principles of natural justice or is based on findings not supported by material.

Conclusion:-

Under PMLA 2002 civil proceedings for attachment of properties representing 'proceeds of crime' generally commence first , followed by prosecution proceedings for trial of the accused. Release or otherwise of the properties under attachment is subject to outcome of prosecution case. , as attachment of properties also form part of the prosecution case. DOCTRINE OF MERGER

In tax matters, the Commissioner is having power to review the order-in-original passed by the adjudicating authority subordinate to the Commissioner if he is not, satisfied with the order-in-original. For this purpose the Commissioner is required to issue show-cause notice to the assessee and pass order after giving the assessee, a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The Commissioner is not having power to review if the subject-matter of the review is already decided in the appeal by the appellate authority since the order-in-original merges with the order-in-appeal which is called as doctrine of merger. In this article, the concept of ‘doctrine of merger’ is discussed in detail and the applicability of the said doctrine in respect of service tax matters is also discussed.

Introduction

1. Section 83A of the Finance Act, 1994 (‘the Act’) gives the powers of adjudication to the Central Excise Officers. Section 84 of the Act gives powers of revision of orders by the Commissioner of Central Excise. Section 84 provides that the Commissioner of Central Excise may call for the record of a proceeding in which an adjudicating authority subordinate to him passed any decision or order and may make such inquiry or cause such inquiry to be made and, subject to the provisions of service tax, pass such order thereon as he thinks fit, after giving the assessee a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The section further provides that no order shall be passed by the Commissioner of Central Excise in respect of any issue if an appeal against such issue is pending before the Commissioner (Appeals). Likewise if any issue is decided by the appellate authorities, the review power could not be exercised by the authority according to the doctrine of merger.

2. Doctrine of merger

(i )Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala 2001 (129) ELT 11 (SC) : The Supreme Court held that where an appeal or revision is provided against an order passed by a Court, Tribunal or any other authority before superior forum and such superior forum modifies, reverse or affirms the decision put in issue before it, the decision by the subordinate forum merges in the decision by the superior forum and it is the latter which subsists, that remain operative and is capable of enforcement in the eyes of law.

The doctrine of merger is not a doctrine of universal or unlimited application. It will depend on the nature of jurisdiction exercised by the superior forum and the content or subject-matter of challenge laid or capable of being laid shall be determinative of the applicability of merger. The superior jurisdiction should be capable of reversing, modifying or affirming the order put in issue before it. Under article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court may reverse, modify or affirm the judgment-decree or order appealed against while exercising its appellate jurisdiction and not while exercising the discretionary jurisdiction disposing of petition for special leave to appeal. The doctrine of merger can, therefore, be applied to the former and not to the latter.

(ii) CCE v. Chellapandi Match Works 2006 (197) ELT 272 (Trib. - Chennai). - The Tribunal held that long before the Collector reviewed the Assistant Collector’s order-in-original, the Assistant Collector’s order had merged with the order in appeal dated November 4, 1993. The review order was passed on January 24, 1994 and that, on account of the merger, there was no order of the Assistant Collector to be reviewed on January 24, 1994, and, consequently, the review was held to be not maintainable. The Tribunal further held that the reviewing authority could have preferred an appeal against the order-in-appeal instead of resorting to review an order, which was non est on the date of issuance of show-cause notice. The Tribunal set aside the order of the Commissioner.

Impact of Notifications and Circulars vis-a-vis Judicial Decisions 7. Notifications are issued by competent authorities in exercise of their powers conferred under the relevant statute. Notifications supplement the primary and subordinate legislation, i.e., the Act and Rules, by filling up certain gaps in the law, which are required to be notified from time to time, as and when necessary. Notifications, thus, originate from and get merged with the main law. Circulars, on the other hand, are issued by competent bodies, in exercise of their general administrative powers, to elucidate, clarify or amplify any provision, or to remove any anomaly in its practical implementation. The Circular, however, does not supplement the law, it must complement it.

It has been held that it would be proper on the part of the authorities to ensure that neither the statutory provision nor the notification which forms part of the statute are paid scanty regard. [ITC Ltd. v. Commr. of Cus. (Port), Kolkata 2007 (6) STR 405 (Trib. - Kol.)]. As regards circulars in CCE v. H.M. Polycontainers Ltd. [2007] 9 STT 96 (Mum. - CESTAT), it has been observed that Board’s Circulars are not binding on Commissioner (Appeals). However, in judicial discipline, the Commissioner (Appeals) is bound by the decision of the higher Tribunal.

Essence of Appellate Power

8. Appeal implies in its natural and ordinary meaning the removal of cause from any inferior Court or Tribunal to a superior one for the purpose of testing the soundness or correctness of the decision and proceedings of the inferior Court or Tribunal. The superior forum shall have jurisdiction to reverse, confirm, annul or modify the order of the forum appealed against and in the event of remand the lower forum shall have to re-hear the matter and comply with such directions as may accompany the order of removal. The appellate jurisdiction inherently carries with it a power to issue corrective directions binding on the forum below and failure on the part of the latter to carry out such directions or show disrespect to or to question the propriety of such direction would be destructive of the hierarchial system in the administration of justice. Seekers of justice would lose faith in both and would only knock the doors of the High Courts under article 226 of the Constitution of India for correcting orders. [TVL Ragam Polymers v. CTO 2007 (6) STR 292 (Mad.)].

8.1 Impact of Stay in an Appeal - It is well-settled that during the appeal period or when the stay has been given to the appellants till further orders, the revenue authorities shall not make any recovery towards the demands made in the impugned orders. [Berger Paints India Ltd. v. CCE [Final Order No. 51 of 2006, dated 8-2-2006.]

When the Tribunal had already extended the stay granted to the appellants till further orders, the act of the concerned Assistant Commissioner to adjust the amount of duty without taking Tribunal’s order or any higher court’s order, was held completely irregular. If he had any grievances with the Tribunal’s order, he could have filed an appeal before any higher forum and since it had not been taken, he could have taken the Tribunal’s order before adjusting the amount which had also not been done. This was nothing but disregard shown to the Tribunal by the concerned Assistant Commissioner.

Conclusion

9. The importance of the doctrine of judicial discipline with regard to a statute has been reiterated and stressed upon time and again by various judicial fora. Ironically, the doctrine has been overlooked by the same (or similar) fora at several other occasions.

Service tax is a bubbly law, yet evolving and unsettled. It, thus, demands practice of judicial discipline with more sincerity. For aligned functioning and unanimity on interpretation of statute, it is immensely important that all members of the judiciary fraternity exercise their functions in strict observance of the principle of judicial discipline. Before rendering their own interpretation of the provisions of service tax law, which has today assumed ever growing significance both for the industry and the revenue, the courts must duly consider and follow the decisions given by higher authorities.

Parallel proceedings can survive: A civil suit for recovery and a complaint case under the NI Act are maintainable for the same cause of action.

When a cheque gets dishonoured, the Complainant runs from pillar to pillar to recover the money. Oftentimes, the payee of the cheque files and proceeds with a 138 NI complaint. However, the question arises whether another alternative route for recovery of the cheque amount is possible or not. The answer is positive. A Complainant can simultaneously opt for two routes, one being the complaint case under the NI Act, and the other being the filing of a recovery suit for the cheque amount under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Thus, the remedies under civil law for recovery with interest and remedies under criminal law for cheque dishonour offences are distinct in nature and can be pursued simultaneously without one barring the other. The Indian Courts have clarified that when both proceedings result in any relief, appropriate adjustments must be made. The civil court shall take into account any compensation paid or recovered under Section 138 proceedings, and conversely, the criminal court should consider amounts already decreed or recovered in the civil suit when imposing fines to ensure fairness and prevent double recovery.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in D. Purushotama Reddy & Ors v. K. Sateesh14, has opined that a suit for recovery of money due from a borrower is maintainable at the instance of the creditor. It is furthermore beyond any doubt or dispute that for the same cause of action, a complaint petition under the terms of Section 138 of the Act would also be maintainable. Furthermore, in Vishnu Dutt Sharma v. Daya Sapra15, which elaborated on the relationship between civil and criminal proceedings, and clarified that findings in a criminal proceeding are generally not binding in a civil proceeding, and vice versa, except for limited purposes. It also reaffirmed that criminal matters often take precedence when both are pending.

Recently, the High Court of Delhi in Smt. Rama Oberoi v. State of NCT of Delhi and Anr16, while dismissing a quashing petition challenging the summoning order on the ground that a civil suit for recovery is already pending for the same transaction for which the cheques were issued, thus, the NI Complaint is not maintainable. While dismissing the petition with a cost of Rs. 10,000/-. The High Court opined that;

"4. It is trite that where both a civil remedy as well as a criminal remedy for any transaction are available, the aggrieved person can avail both the remedies. What has been filed by the present respondent through civil suit is a civil remedy pertaining to civil liability of the petitioner to pay the outstanding amount. The complaint case filed by the present respondent pertains to criminal liability where despite being served with a statutory notice after dishonour of cheque, the petitioner/accused opted not to pay. The goal of the civil suit is the decree of the suit amount while the goal of the criminal proceedings is imposition of punishment, which can be imprisonment as well. There is no bar on the respondent proceeding with both remedies simultaneously."

1.6-1a Effect of conviction for concealment - Section 95(i)(a) of the Finance Act, apart from the above restrictions, also provides that a person who has been convicted for concealment on or before filing of declaration, the provisions of the Scheme would not apply, in respect of Tax arrear under any Direct tax enactment. It may be noted that where a prosecution is instituted, the bar is against Tax arrear in respect of the assessment year concerned. However, where the person has been convicted, it appears that, he would not be in a position to make any declaration under the Scheme. The manner in which the provision is drafted creates such ambiguity; but, the intention appears to be otherwise. The other view, is that the bar is against only in respect of Tax arrear for which he has been convicted, which cannot be ruled out and seems to be a more appropriate view. This view is based on reading the provision as follows :

“The provisions of this Scheme shall not apply—

(i) in respect of Tax arrear under any Direct tax enactment,—

(a) . . .; or in respect of a person who is convicted for concealment. . . .”.

Thus, for non-application of the Scheme, the primary requisite is that there should be a Tax arrear and further the person concerned ought to have been convicted. Had the intention been otherwise, possibly, such a provision would have been made in section 95(iii), which totally prohibits a person from making any declaration.

Accordingly, the second view is preferable.

(3) Does non-timely execution of Resolution Plan result in liquidation

Once the NCLT approves the Resolution Plan, but the same remains unimplemented by SRA for certain reasons, for no fault of the creditors and other stakeholders of CD, the same ought not to necessarily result in liquidation of CD. The rationale being that object of IBC is to resolve debtor-in-distress and also realise the dues owed by CD. Thus, liquidation ought to be resorted, as last resort.

(4) Priority of payments under Resolution Plan

That at the relevant time when the Plan was submitted in 2017, it complied with the then provisions of IBC and CIRP Regulations that required the Plan to make payments of at least the liquidation value to OCs (under unamended Regulation 38). Subsequently, through 2019 Amendment to Regulation 38, the priority of payments to OCs under resolution plan, was introduced. The subsequent amendment to law would not have an effect on the already approved Plan(s).

(5) Whether EBITDA is payable to creditors of CD

As held by SC in COC of Essar Steel v. Satish Kumar Gupta (supra), the distribution of profits generated during CIRP would not go towards payment of dues to creditors of CD. Rule 29 - The words 'for any other substantial cause' must be read with the word 'requires' in the beginning of the sentence and it is only where the appellate court requires any document to be produced or any witness to be examined that this rule will apply. The discretion to receive additional evidence is to be exercised only when any point is required to be cleared up in the interests of justice. This power given to the Tribunal has to be exercised cautiously and sparingly in order to advance the interests of justice. Rule 29 is not intended to allow an assessee who has been unsuccessful throughout to patch up the weak parts of his case or to fill up omissions [A. K. Babu Khan v. CWT[1976] 102 Taxman 757 (AP)].

Though the omission to record the reasons for admitting additional evidence under Rule 29 is a serious defect, the rule not being mandatory, such omission will not vitiate the Tribunal's order [CIT v. Motilal Hirabhai Spg. & Wvg. Co. Ltd. [1978] 113 ITR 173 (Guj.)].

Rule 29 does not enable the assessee or the department to tender fresh evidence to support a new point or to make out a new case [CIT v. Babulal Nim [1963] 47 ITR 864 (MP)].

If an application is pending under Rule 29, Tribunal should first dispose of such application on merits and thereafter proceed to dispose of appeal on merits [Jyotsna Suri v. ITAT [2003] 128 Taxman 33 (SC)].

14.8 Revision of orders prejudicial to revenue [Section 377 of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 263 of the ITA 1961)]

Section 263 of the ITA 1961 specifies that where the PCCIT, CCIT, PCIT or CIT considers that an order passed by the AO or TPO in a proceeding is prejudicial to the interest of the revenue, he may pass a revisionary order. The order for revision shall be made within two years from the end of the financial year in which the order sought to be revised was passed. However, an order can be revised at any time if it has been passed in consequence of any finding or to give effect to the direction contained in the order of the Appellate Tribunal, the High Court or the Supreme Court. While computing the limitation period, the following period shall be excluded:

(a)

Time taken in providing an opportunity of rehearing to the assessee, where an assessing officer ceases to exercise jurisdiction and is succeeded by another assessing officer; and

(b)

The period commencing on the date on which a stay on any proceeding under this section has been granted by an order or injunction of any court and ending on the date on which the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner receives a certified copy of the order or injunction vacating the stay.

In the ITA 2025, a new sub-section (7) has been introduced in section 377 (corresponding to Section 263 of the ITA 1961), stating that if, after the exclusion of the period mentioned above, the remaining time limit for completing the revision is less than sixty days, such remaining period shall be extended to 60 days, and such period of limitation shall be deemed to have been extended accordingly.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

14.9 Revision of other orders [Section 378 of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 264 of the ITA 1961)]

Section 264 of the ITA 1961 specifies that the PCCIT, CCIT, PCIT or CIT, either on his own motion or on an application filed by the assessee, may call for and examine the records of any proceedings in which an order is passed by any authority subordinate to him. The Commissioner can pass such an order which is not prejudicial to the interest of the assessee. Where any revisionary order could be prejudicial to the assessee, the commissioner has to exercise his revisionary power under section 263.

The Commissioner is required to pass an order within 1 year from the end of the financial year in which the application is made for revision. If the Commissioner acts suo motu, he must revise the order within one year from the date of the original order. However, an order can be revised at any time if it has been passed in consequence of any finding or to give effect to the direction contained in the order of the Appellate Tribunal, the High Court or the Supreme Court.

While computing the limitation period, the following period shall be excluded:

(a)

Time taken in providing an opportunity of rehearing to the assessee, where an assessing officer ceases to exercise jurisdiction and is succeeded by another assessing officer; and

(b)

The period commencing on the date on which a stay on any proceeding under this section has been granted by an order or injunction of any court and ending on the date on which the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner receives a certified copy of the order or injunction vacating the stay.

In the ITA 2025, a new sub-section (9) has been introduced in section 378 (corresponding to Section 264 of the ITA 1961), stating that if, after the exclusion of the period mentioned above, the remaining time limit for completing the revision is less than sixty days, such remaining period shall be extended to 60 days, and such period of limitation shall be deemed to have been extended accordingly.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

Annapurna Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. & Ors v. SORIL Infra Resources Limited (CP No. (IB)-22(PB)/2017] - Principal Bench, New Delhi

Date of Order: 24st March 2017

Facts of the Case:

Annapurna Infrastructure Private Ltd i.e. Operational Creditor have filed an application u/s 9 of the Code before the NCLT to initiate CIRP of SORIL Infra Resources Limited i.e. Corporate Debtor. Pursuant to an arbitration award dated 09.09.2016 passed by an arbitrator certain claims of the Operational Creditors have arisen against the Corporate Debtor. Corporate Debtor has filed further appeal u/s 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 ('Arbitration Act') for set-aside of the said arbitration award. However appeal u/s 34 of the Arbitration Act for setting aside the award has been dismissed by the arbitral tribunal vide its order dated 19.12.2016.

Subsequent to dismissal of appeal u/s 34 of the Arbitration Act, Operational Creditor has served a demand notice dated 16.01.2017 to Corporate Debtor u/s 8 of the Code for recovery of the claim as envisaged under arbitration award. In response to demand notice Corporate Debtor replied that a further appeal u/s 37 of the Arbitration Act have been filed before the Hon'ble High Court which is pending for adjudication and till the disposal of appeal Corporate Debtor is not liable for payment of any claim.

Objections and arguments of the parties:

Operation Creditor argued that appeal u/s 37 of the Arbitration Act cannot be regarded as continuation of arbitration proceeding because the arbitrator is the final judge of the facts and the High Court while hearing objections u/s 37 is not expected to scrutinize the award as an appellate forum1.

However, Corporate Debtor argued that arbitration proceeding do not come to an end on the announcement of arbitration award and the aggrieved party have a right for further appeal2 u/s 34 and 37 of the Arbitration Act.

NCLT Ruling:

(a)

Definition of Dispute is not exhaustive but illustrative:

NCLT held that conjoint reading of section 5(6) and section 8 makes it clear that corporate debtor has two option available under section 8(2) of the Code i.e. either disclosing existence of a dispute or pay the unpaid debt to the operational creditor. Further, definition of the word 'dispute' as provided u/s 5(6) of the Code, is not exhaustive but is, in fact illustrative. In other words a corporate debtor is not left with the only option of showing the existence of dispute by way of a pending suit, arbitration or to show the breach of representation or warranty. Corporate Debtor would be well within his right to show that goods and services were not supplied at all or the supply was far from satisfactory in case of demand raised by an operational creditor.

Further, NCLT observed that, it cannot be said that arbitration proceedings have come to an end merely on the dismissal of application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act as the proceedings are yet to attain finality as appeal under section 37 of the Arbitration Act is pending.

"The other judgment that no proceedings were pending on the date of issuance of demand notice in terms of section 8(1) of the Code is equally falicious. Admittedly appeal under section 37 of the Arbitration Act could be preferred within 30 days against an order passed under section 34 of the Arbitration Act. Merely because no appeal was pending on 16.1.2017 when the respondent have time to prefer the appeal would not entitle the applicant to invoke section 9 of the Code. If that view is taken then extreme technicality would result in nullifying the remedy of appeal within 30 days provided by section 37 of the Arbitration Act. No reasonable person would take such a view. Thus the argument is wholly devoid of merit and therefore we have no hesitation to reject the same"

(b)

Prohibition on forum shopping:

NCLT further held that, it is fundamental principles of judicial administration to allow only one remedy at one point of time and the same principal is evident from section 10 of the Civil Procedure Code. Therefore, where an issue is already pending adjudication in a Court having jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the same, a subsequently instituted suit on the same issue between the same parties, cannot be allowed to proceed.

Accordingly, based on the above finding NCLT dismissed application of operational creditor for initiation of CIRP with cost of INR 1,00,000/-

The payment must be made on or before the due date to file the TCS statement related to such pay-ment.

The Supreme Court examined the interplay between proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and criminal prosecution under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The respondent had filed a complaint under section 138 against the appellants for dishonour of cheques due to insufficiency of funds. During the pendency of the criminal proceedings, the appellants filed an application under section 94 before the NCLT seeking initiation of personal insolvency, which was pending adjudication.

Relying on the pendency of the section 94 application and the interim moratorium contemplated under section 96 of the Code, the appellants sought adjournment of the section 138 proceedings sine die. The Trial Court rejected the application, leading to the issue before the Supreme Court.

The Court held that while the legislative intent behind the IBC is to provide a protective shield to debtors during the insolvency process, the scope and nature of proceedings under the Code may result in restructuring or even extinguishment of debt through liquidation, but such extinguishment does not absolve directors or individuals from criminal liability. The Court further held that permitting debtors to evade prosecution under section 138 by invoking insolvency proceedings would defeat the very object of the Negotiable Instruments Act, which is to maintain the integrity and credibility of commercial transactions.

It was held that personal responsibility for offences under section 138 persists irrespective of insolvency proceedings and their outcome. Accordingly, the prayer of the appellants to stay the prosecution under section 138 on the basis of the interim moratorium under section 96 was held to be untenable, and the rejection of their application by the Trial Court was upheld.

2. Jurisdiction of Writ Courts:

On perusal of the provisions contained in the earlier act, it may be noted that an exemption was granted to cases pending before High Courts or Supreme Court, but no such exemption has been provided for under the IBC. The issue was discussed in Canara Bank v. Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd.9. The appellant (i.e. the creditor) submitted that the adjudicating authority cannot exclude any court from the purview of moratorium for the purpose of recovery of amount or execution of any judgment or decree, including the proceeding, if any, pending before the High Courts and the Supreme Court of India against a corporate debtor.

The NCLAT acknowledged that clause (a) of Section 14(1) specifically does not exclude any Court, including the High Courts or even the Apex Court. However, the Hon'ble Bench there are certain constitutional provisions which must be considered. There is no provision to file any money suit or suit for recovery before the Supreme Court except under Article 131 of the Constitution; some High Courts have original jurisdiction to entertain the suits, which may include money suit or suit for recovery of money. However, the writ jurisdiction conferred on the Supreme Court and the High Court under Article 32 and Article 226 of Constitution of India, being a constitutional power, cannot be curtailed by any provision of an Act or court. Therefore, 'moratorium' will not affect any suit or case pending under Article 32 or 226. However, so far as suit, if filed before any High Court under original jurisdiction which is a money suit or suit for recovery, against the corporate debtor such suit will be covered by the bar imposed under Section 33(5).

3. Criminal Proceedings:

In criminal proceedings, particularly in the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the directors or officers in default, as the case may be, are generally held personally liable, as against the civil liability of the company. The company and its directors cannot shirk their criminal liability merely on the ground that the company was already wound up and the liquidator had taken charge of the affairs of the company.

Upholding the principle laid down by the Kerala High Court in Jose Antony Kakkad v. Official Liquidator10, in Counter Point Advt. P. Ltd., Rep. by its Director, Mr. Naresh Purushotham v. Harita Finance Limited, Rep. by its Special Legal Assistant, Miss. Gulzar Sayeeda [2006] 133 Comp Cas 435 (Mad.)11, the Madras High Court observed that:

"Though the words 'legal proceedings' in Section 446 of the Companies Act is wide enough to be taken in criminal proceedings also, such criminal proceedings must be in relation to the assets of the company. Criminal proceedings which are not in respect of the assets of the company but which end in the conviction or acquittal of the accused, cannot be stayed under Section 446 of the Companies Act. Proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, can end only in the conviction or acquittal of the accused in the case and no recovery of any amount covered by the dishonoured cheques can be made in the criminal proceedings. As the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are not in respect of the assets of the company, the proceedings pending in the criminal Courts cannot be stayed under Section 446 of the Companies Act."

This does not make a difference to the distinction drawn. These are concurrent remedies and the invocation of one does not necessarily dispense with, obviate or oust the other. The imposition of penalties under the Act by the authorities, and the conviction in a Court of law for an offence created by the Act, do not attract the principle of double jeopardy either. Ordinarily, the decision to prosecute an assessee or a person, who may be deemed to be an assessee under the various penal provisions of the Act, is a decision taken by the officer empowered to initiate action on being satisfied on the objective material before him that there is a case for prosecution without judicial determination under the Act, as to taxability, quantification of liability, or liability to any penalty, etc.

The view that the proceedings entailing penalty under the Income-tax Act are to be equated to the prosecution attracting the punishments is not correct as no conviction for any offence is involved in the imposition of penalty. From a reading of the provision of article 20(1) of the Constitution, it is evident that the first limit and the second limit are interlinked and have to be read together, and that while the first limit refers to a conviction for an offence, the second limit refers to the punishment that has to be inflicted with regard to an offence. Penalty is, on the other hand, levied for an act or omission of the assessee, not because it is an offence but because it is an attempt at evasion in the payment of the tax. In such a situation, article 20(1) of the Constitution is not attracted.1

There are a large number of cases where criminal law and civil law can run side by side. The object of the criminal law is to punish an offender who commits an offence against a person, property or the State for which the accused, on proof of the offence, is deprived of his liberty and in some cases even his life. This does not, however, affect the civil remedies at all for suing the wrongdoer in cases like arson, accident, etc. It is an anathema to suppose that when a civil remedy is available, criminal prosecution is completely barred. The two types of actions are quite different in content, scope and import.2

Article 20 and constitutional validity of criminal prosecution and levy of penalty for the same offence

3.8 Article 20 of the Constitution states that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of commission of the offence, and no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

The Supreme Court in Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay1 observed:

“Article 20(2) incorporates within its scope the plea of ‘autrefois convict’ as known to the British Jurisprudence or the plea of double jeopardy as known to the American Constitution, but circumscribes it by providing that there should be not only a prosecution but also a punishment in the first instance in order to operate as a bar to a second prosecution and punishment for the same offence.” (p. 325)

Article 20(2) contemplates proceedings of criminal nature and the prosecution in this context means an initiation of proceedings of criminal nature. The first part of article 20(1) prohibits a conviction while the second part deals with penalty that may be inflicted on conviction. The word ‘penalty’ has been used to denote the sentence or punishment. Like clause (2), clause (1) also contemplates proceedings of criminal nature.

A criminal proceeding may be defined as one, which if carried to its conclusion, may result in imposition of sentence such as death, imprisonment, fine or forfeiture of property. It also includes proceedings in which, in the larger interests of the State, orders to prevent apprehended breach of the peace, orders to bind down persons who are a danger to the maintenance of peace and orders aimed at preventing vagrancy are contemplated to be passed.

For instance, the imposition of penalty under the Income-tax Act is neither a prosecution nor a punishment for any offence and, therefore, the accused is not exposed to any double jeopardy. The proceedings, for the imposition of penalty, taken against an assessee under Income-tax Act are distinct from the criminal complaints filed against him. They can, therefore, continue simultaneously. The offences punishable under section 277 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961, and section 193 of the Indian Penal Code may be somewhat similar, but they are not identical.1 There is no legal bar on the prosecution of the accused for both these offences in view of section 26 of the General Clauses Act.

Introduction

1. Timely disclosure of material events is one of the keys to corporate governance in listed companies. Clause 36 of the erstwhile Listing Agreement and Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (LODR) mandate listed companies to intimate material event to the stock exchange immediately. SEBI has also rolled out guidance note1 with respect to intimation of material event.

Schedule III of LODR lists out events which are deemed to be material and list of events whose materiality is to be determined by the authorized key managerial personnel for such purposes.

Also, listed companies are mandatorily required to have a policy for determination of materiality in place listing out events and the criteria for determination of materiality, timing of disclosure to stock exchange, KMPs authorized to take decision on materiality, etc.

Non-disclosure of material events to the stock exchange is taken as serious non-compliance by the capital market watchdog and also the Appellate Authority.

Recently, in its order2 dated 7.8.2019, in the case of NDTV v. SEBI, SAT has upheld the order of SEBI insofar as SEBI has imposed penalty on the listed company for non-disclosure of the fact of a high pitched assessment order issued against it having the ability to eat away the net worth of the company.

Since the matter in question dates back to pre-LODR era, the default is with respect to clause 36 of Listing Agreement. However, the same is surely relevant since the corresponding provision is contained in Reg 30 of LODR.

The ratio decidendi that emerges out of the SAT order are as follows:

Event having impact on financials – surely material

2. The decisive factor to disclose any material events/information under clause 36 of the Listing Agreement with respect to any dispute/litigation was the 'material impact' of such event/information on its present or future operations or its profitability or financials.

Events like assessment order from tax department, which is huge enough to erode the entire networth of the company, is without any doubt, a material event and should be disclosed to the stock exchange immediately.

In the given case, SAT observed the following:

"It has come on record that the networth of the company was Rs. 365 crores and a demand of Rs. 450 crores was made in the assessment order. Such demand which eats away the networth of the company is in our opinion a material event and the assessment order had a "material impact" which the company was required to report to the Exchange "promptly" and which was required to be made public "immediately".

In the current LODR regime, Reg 30 lists down criteria for determination of materiality of the event which is elaborated in the materiality policy of the company.

Conclusiveness of an adverse order is not important for determining materiality of an event

3. That an adverse order is put to appeal and not conclusive and therefore not material – does not hold good. The management can surely take a view to appeal for the adverse order. However, the limited disclosure with respect to the event of receiving an adverse order which has material impact on the financials of the company is required to be made immediately without any delay.

The Guidance Note issued by Stock Exchange on clause 36 also requires the listed companies to consider the impact of such disclosure on legal/court proceeding while making the disclosure and require them to continue to inform the Stock Exchange till the conclusion of the dispute.

Not only this, the listed entity is also required to disclose the details of litigation/dispute to which company's key management personnel or its promoter/ultimate person in control has become party to a dispute and where the disclosure is not in the interest of company, the details of pending litigation may be limited to the extent of stating the occurrence of the event.

Accordingly, in the case in hand, the Hon'ble SAT observed that filing an appeal against the order of AO will not diminish the event's materiality and, therefore, hold non-disclosure to stock exchange, as non-compliance as per clause 36 of listing Agreement.

Material information to be disclosed "immediately"

4. The word "immediately" refers to "without any delay or lapse of time", "forthwith". SAT, in the instant matter opines that material information is required to be given to the Stock Exchange at the earliest without any undue delay.

It is to be noted that as per Reg 30 of LODR, material event is required to be intimated to stock exchange immediately, i.e., as soon as possible but not later than 24 hours from the occurrence of the minutes.

5.14

Case Studies

1. The Company has received a Show Cause Notice during the year 2022-23 from Initiating Officer for holding a benami property and alleging that company is only a shell company and its properties are held by it as benamidar for the real person controlling the company who has channeled his ill gotten funds into the company as share capital through a network of benami shell companies. The alleged benami properties were acquired prior to 25-10-2016. The Company contends that auditor need not report on this as company has sent reply with all details and, in view of Supreme Court judgment in Ganapati Dealcom, the IO will drop proceedings. Proceedings have not been dropped at the time of audit reporting. Company also contends that ARI disclosures are not required in view of the Supreme Court decision. How will you as auditor deal with this?

Auditor is not to sit in judgment on the merits of the case. For auditor, all that matters is that the proceedings are initiated during the year and are pending as of the date of audit report. Therefore, he needs to report the fact of initiation and pendency of the same. Company may disclose its opinion on the merits of the case in notes to financial statements while giving required ARI disclosures.

2. If in Case Study 1, what if, prior to date of audit report, the proceedings are dropped by IO after considering the reply of the Company ?

In that case also, auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings were initiated and subsequently dropped. The wordings in clause 3(i)(e) are "proceedings have been initiated or are pending against the company". Therefore, in view of the word "or" separating the words "initiated" and "are pending", auditor will have to report the fact that proceedings have been initiated during year and dropped after the year-end but prior to date of audit reporting.

3. What if show cause notice dated 1st April 2023 from Initiating Officer is received on 5th April 2023 and audit report is being signed on 30th April 2023? Will auditor have to report it in audit report for FY 2022-23?

No. Auditor will not report this in Audit report for the year under audit i.e. FY 2022-23. Auditor will report it in his report for FY 2023-24.

Audit report for the year is on events during the year. Post-balance sheet date developments in respect of such events which have occurred during the year will be considered. It is one thing that Show Cause Notice is issued during the year and there are further developments after the year-end in the matter which will have to be considered.

It is entirely a different matter that Show Cause Notice is issued and received after the year-end which has nothing to do with conditions existing as at the Balance sheet date. Auditor will not consider such post-balance sheet events in report for the year under audit.

AO performs a ministerial function - The AO, when he files the appeal under the direction of the Commissioner, performs merely a ministerial function. The expression 'AO' denotes an AO having jurisdiction over the assessee or the matter and not any AO. The officer selected must have some concern with the assessee against whom the appeal is filed by the Commissioner [CIT v. Anil Kumar Roy Chowdhury [1967] 66 ITR 367 (SC)].

Objection of Commissioner on order passed by CIT(A) - The objection of the Commissioner may cover not only the merits of the order passed by the CIT(A) but also what that officer had omitted to do in his order. The objection of the Commissioner for the purposes of maintainability of his appeal should, of course, be an order passed by the CIT(A). But the objection is not necessarily confined to what the order has stated but may extend to what the order has omitted to say. The appeal will not be held to be not maintainable only because the Tribunal might find that the CIT(A) himself had no jurisdiction to make a direction. That would be an order on the merits not affecting the maintainability of the appeal. Thus, the right is restricted to challenge the order u/s 250 and not to revert back to the assessment order and challenge those parts of the assessment order that were not the subject-matter of order [M. Ganapathi Asari v. CIT [1970] 75 ITR 296 (Mad.)].

ATTACHMENT OF CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY TO A CORPORATION

i. Strict Liability

Under this concept, a person shall be made legally responsible for the concerns of his acts even in the absence of guilty mind or criminal intention. Examples of some criminal offences which do not require mens rea are rape, murder, vehicular offences. In US, the rule followed is that whenever a particular legislation does not specify mens rea as an essential, it is deems that mental intent need not be prove in such offence, and hence treated it as strict liability.

In Indianapolis Water Co. v. American Strawboard Co.,27 court held that mere omission, irrespective of mens rea of defaulter, is sufficient to constitute crime.

ii. Vicarious Liability

The maxim qui facit per alium per se explains the concept better, which means, one who does an act through another is deemed to do it by himself. Similarly, under the concept of vicarious liability, one is made responsible for any act or omission of another. The reason here is the presumption that master is aware of what his servant is doing and that the servant is always deemed to act on behalf of and on the directions of the master. In Commonwealth,28 the court made the people acting on behalf of 3 companies liable for its activities by stating that CCL is necessarily vicarious because company is a legal fiction which is comprised of individuals alone.

Compounding of offences

Provisions of compounding have been introduced in customs law.

Section 137(3) of Customs Act provides that any offence under the Act can be compounded by Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioner of Customs. Such compounding can be done either before or after the institution of prosecution. Central Government is authorised to make Rules to provide for amount to be paid for compounding.

In Vinod Kumar Agarwal v. UOI (2008) 223 ELT 19 (Bom HC DB), it was held that compounding under Customs Act cannot result in discharge of offences under other Acts like IPC.

Awareness about provision of compounding should be enhances. People should be encouraged to compound offense. Disposal should be within six months - MF(DR) circular No. 15/2022-Cus dated 23-8-2022.

What is compounding ? - Fine and imprisonment can be imposed only by competent criminal Court. However, instead of going to Court, the offender may agree to pay composition amount. Order for paying composition money can be made by quasi-judicial authorities. This is called 'compounding of offences'.

'Compounding' is essentially a compromise arrangement between administrator of the enactment and person committing an offence. Compounding crime consists of receipt of some consideration (termed as compounding fees) in return for an agreement not to prosecute one who has committed an offence - Reliance Industries, In re - (1997) 24 CLA 214 (CLB).

'Compounding' means that the accused and the complainant have come to terms and the dispute between the parties has been settled amicably or adjusted by agreement and the complainant agrees not to prosecute the accused. If the case is pending, the accused and the complainant then make a joint application to the Court that the parties have come to terms and the case may not be proceeded with.

Thus, in compounding, there is a compromise or agreement, while in case of imposition of fine under provisions of an Act, there is no agreement as such. Section 320 of Criminal Procedure Code permits compounding of various offences under Indian Penal Code.

Such compounding can be done either before or after institution of prosecution. After payment of such composition amount, prosecution will not be launched, or if it was launched, it will be withdrawn.

Full and bona fide disclosure required for compounding of offence - In UOI v. Anil Chanana (2008) 4 SCC 175 = 222 ELT 481 (SC), it was held that compounding of offences is based on the principle of disclosure. If there are demonstrable contradictions or inconsistencies or incompleteness, application for compounding cannot be entertained. Applicant cannot hoodwink the authority. Applicant has to be a one-time evader. He has to make a clean breast of his affairs. Otherwise, offence should not be compounded. Compounding should be allowed only in case of doubtful benefit to the Revenue and to prevent needlessly proliferating litigation and holding up of collection.

Compounding means acquittal - As per section 320 of CrPC, composition will have the effect of acquittal of accused. It is not mere discharge. Thus, if offence is compounded, the person is deemed to be acquitted, and hence does not become ineligible to be appointed as a director [confirmed in circular No. 5/23 dated 28-4-1993 of Department of Company Affairs].

No penalty or prosecution after compounding - In P P Varkey v. STO (1999) 114 STC 251 (Ker HC), it was held that once offence is compounded, penalty or prosecution proceedings cannot be taken for same offence. In S Viswanathan v. State of Kerala (1999) 113 STC 182 (Ker HC DB), it was held that once the matter is compounded, neither department nor assessee can challenge the compounding order. Department cannot reopen the matter on the reason that actual suppression was much higher.

No appeal against order of composition - A person having agreed to the composition of offence is not entitled to challenge the said proceedings by filing appeal. - S V Bagi v. State of Karnataka (1992) 87 STC 138 = ILR 1992 Kar 1123 (Karn HC FB) - followed in Sakharia Bandhu v. ADCCT (1999) 112 STC 449 (Karn HC DB).

Appeal if application for compounding rejected - If authority rejects application for compounding, appeal can be filed before Tribunal - CCE v. Girish B Mishra (2016) 339 ELT 67 (Guj HC DB).

ITO cannot make use of statements recorded under FEMA - Income-tax proceedings are entirely different from and dissimilar to proceedings under FEMA. Therefore, ITO cannot make use of statements recorded by Enforcement Directorate (ED) for prosecuting deponents of those statements in a separate and independent proceeding under 1961 Act on the ground that deponents had retracted their statements given before ED [K. T. M. S. Mohammed v. UOI [1992] 65 Taxman 130 (SC)].

Judicial proceeding and Civil Court - For the purpose of investigation and enquiry, TRO is conferred with powers of a Civil Court and by virtue of their office and experience, TRO is an officer with trained judicial mind and, therefore, he can conduct enquiry as that of judicial proceedings [G. V. Films Ltd. v. S. Priyadarshan [2007] 163 Taxman 74 (Mad.)].

False evidence - Mere suppression of circumstances which would entitle assessee to an exemption under the 1961 Act will not amount to 'false evidence' within the meaning of section 193 of the IPC. Thus, assessee could not be convicted of an offence u/s 193 qua false statement made in verification clause of return of income [S. Harnam Singh Suri v. CBDT [1983] 15 Taxman 52 (Delhi)].

Cognizable offence - Section 136 makes a proceeding before the ITO a proceeding also u/s 228 of the Indian Penal Code and, thus, an interruption in his proceedings or an insult to him has become punishable under that section. It could not have been intended by the Legislature in enacting this provision that whereas an insult made to a public servant acting judicially, or interruption caused in his proceedings, would normally be cognizable only on the complaint of the public servant himself, the same offence if committed in respect of the proceedings before the ITO should be cognizable on the complaint of a private party. Thus, where the allegation was that a third party made a false statement on oath during the assessment proceedings of an assessee, the complaint against the offence would be cognizable only if it was filed by the ITO and not by the assessee [Lalji Haridas v. State of Maharashtra [1964] 52 ITR 423 (SC)].

Cross-examination - Though the proceedings before the income-tax authorities are not governed by the strict rules of evidence, before the income-tax authorities could rely upon a piece of evidence, they were bound to produce it before the assessee so that the assessee could controvert the statements contained in it by asking for an opportunity for cross-examination of the person with reference to the statements made by him [Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 4 Taxman 29 (SC)].

52. Stay granted by ITAT should not be vacated automatically after the expiry of 365 days

Section 254(2A) of the Act contains provisions for the disposal of appeals by the Tribunal. The first proviso to Section 254(2A) provides that if an assessee makes an application for the stay of proceedings, the Tribunal may, after considering the merits of the application, pass an order of stay for a period not exceeding 180 days from the date of the order. The Tribunal shall dispose of the proceedings within that period of stay.

Where the Tribunal does not dispose of the appeal within the original period of stay, and the delay is not attributable to the assessee, the Tribunal may extend the period of stay for a total period of 365 days (365 days including 180 days granted previously).

Further, the third proviso to Section 254(2A) provides that if the Tribunal does not dispose of the appeal within the period allowed (original plus extended), the order of stay shall stand vacated after the expiry of 365 days even if the delay in disposing of the appeal is not attributable to the assessee.

In Dy. CIT v. Pepsi Foods Ltd. [2021] 126 taxmann.com 69 (SC),the Supreme Court has held that the object of the third proviso to Section 254(2A) (i.e., automatic vacation of stay on completion of 365 days even if the assessee is not responsible for the delay) is discriminatory and is liable to be struck down as it violates Article 14 of the Constitution of India. The Apex Court further held that the third proviso should be read without the word "even" and "is not". Thus, any order of stay shall stand vacated after the expiry of the mentioned period only if the delay in disposing of the appeal is attributable to the assessee. After these words are struck down, the third proviso shall be read as under:

Provided also that if such appeal is not so disposed of within the period allowed under the first proviso or the period or periods extended or allowed under the second proviso, which shall not, in any case, exceed three hundred and sixty-five days, the order of stay shall stand vacated after the expiry of such period or periods, even if the delay in disposing of the appeal is not attributable to the assessee.

Thus, it is expected that the Govt. may bring an amendment in the third proviso to Section 254(2A) as held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the above case.

The Petitioner approached the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in a Writ Petition impugning the provisional attachment order dated December 29, 2017, issued by the ED.

It was observed that merely because a property used in commission of crime, the same cannot be construed as proceeds of that crime. In order to attach a property under the Act, it was necessary for the ED to have reasons to believe that the same was "derived or obtained" from any scheduled crime.

The Hon'ble Court found that the bedrock of the impugned order was that the Petitioner had obtained allocation of coal block on the basis of misrepresentation. There was not a whisper alleging that the Petitioner had derived benefits from the allocated coal block and nowhere the ED has indicated any reason, which could lead one to believe that the Petitioner had derived any other benefit from the allocation of the coal block in question.

Accordingly, the Petition was allowed and the impugned order along with the complaint under the Act was set aside.

In First Securities (P.) Ltd. v. CST [2008] 13 STT 199 (Bang. - CESTAT), the appellant was a registered stock broker. The revenue proceeded against the appellant for demand of service tax. The adjudicating authority in order-in-original demanded service tax and imposed penalty under section 76 and further penalty under section 78. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order-in-original. The appellant filed appeal against the order before the Tribunal and applied for stay petition. In the meantime, the Commissioner of Service Tax passed the impugned order-in-review by reviewing the order of the original authority. In the impugned order, the Commissioner enhanced the penalty heavily. The Tribunal held that in terms of section 84(4), the Commissioner of Central Excise is precluded from reviewing the order passed by the lower authority in respect of any issue if any appeal against such issue is pending before the Commissioner (Appeals). In the present case, after the order-in-original was passed, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order-in-original. In other words, the order-in-original had merged with the order-in-appeal. In such circumstances, there was no order-in-original existing for review by the Commissioner of Central Excise.

CCE [2008] 16 STT 87 (New Delhi - CESTAT), the Tribunal found that the Commissioner had interpreted the provisions of section 84(4) which stipulate that "no order under this section shall be passed by the Commissioner of Central Excise in respect of any issue if an appeal against such issue is pending before the Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals)" by holding that the issue was no longer pending before the Commissioner (Appeals) but had already been decided by the Commissioner (Appeals) and therefore, the revision was permissible. Editorial Team

Introduction

In 2025, courts across India delivered several landmark rulings that substantially shaped the interpretation and enforcement of Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) and banking laws, addressing critical issues of regulatory compliance, financial discipline, and economic governance. These decisions examined the scope of money-laundering offences, procedural safeguards in enforcement actions, priority of claims, recovery mechanisms, one-time settlements, and the extent of judicial review over actions of banks and financial institutions. This write-up aims to curate the Top Landmark FEMA and Banking Law Judgments of 2025, offering valuable insights for legal practitioners, compliance professionals, regulators, and academics seeking to understand the latest judicial trends influencing India's financial and regulatory framework.

1. Discharge rightly denied where accused aided co-accused in bank forms and cheques, knowing link to proceeds of crime: SC

K. Murali Krishna v. Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement [2025] 180 taxmann.com 462 (SC)

In the present case, the question before the Supreme Court was whether the petitioner was entitled to discharge under section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, in a prosecution for the offence of money laundering under section 3 read with section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.

The Supreme Court observed that, at the stage of considering a discharge application, the court is not expected to examine the truthfulness or sufficiency of the allegations, as such an exercise falls within the domain of trial. It was further noted that the scope of section 3 of the PMLA cannot be narrowly construed for the purpose of discharging an accused at the threshold.

The Court noted that the allegations against the petitioner indicated that he had indirectly assisted the main accused in filling up bank account opening forms and handling cheque leaves and was, therefore, alleged to be knowingly a party to activities connected with the proceeds of crime.

The Supreme Court held that since these allegations required appreciation of evidence and adjudication during trial, they could not be examined at the initial stage of discharge. Accordingly, it was held that there was no valid ground to interfere with the order of the High Court confirming rejection of the discharge application.

2. Attachment order under PMLA can be made without prior communication under Section 66(2): HC

Directorate of Enforcement v. Prakash Industries Ltd. [2025] 180 taxmann.com 189 (Delhi)

In the present case, the Supreme Court was called upon to examine the interplay between Section 3 read with Section 24 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002(offence of money laundering) and Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (discharge of accused).

The petitioner had filed an application under Section 227 Cr.P.C. before the Trial Court seeking discharge on the ground that he was not connected with the banking transactions underpinning the alleged money-laundering offence and had merely assisted Accused in filling bank account forms without knowledge of Accused's identity, contending he was wrongly implicated.

The Trial Court rejected this application. The High Court, in the impugned order, upheld that the scope of Section 3 of the PMLA is wide and cannot be narrowly circumscribed at the discharge stage.

The court further retreated that at the discharge stage under Section 227 Cr.P.C. is not to assess the truthfulness of allegations but only to determine whether prima facie a case is made out, leaving detailed factual inquiries for trial. It observed that, as per the complaint under Sections 44 and 45 of the PMLA, the petitioner was alleged to have "indirectly assisted" in filling account and cheque forms and was knowingly a party to activities connected with proceeds of crime — allegations which, if accepted, fall within the ambit of the offence under Section 3 read with the statutory presumption under Section 24 of the PMLA.

Therefore constituted prima facie material for trial, not a fit case for discharge. On this basis, the High Court confirmed the Trial Court's order, and the Supreme Court found no valid ground to interfere with the impugned order.

3. Once Recovery Certificate becomes final, Recovery Officer is bound to proceed in accordance with same: HC

Maharaji Educational Trust v. Housing and Urban Development Corporation Ltd. HUDCO

In the present case, the Delhi High Court examined whether the Recovery Officer could travel beyond a revised Recovery Certificate issued under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993, in recovery proceedings initiated by HUDCO against Maharaji Educational Trust.

In circumstances where CIRP is initiated or pursued as a strategic weapon to shield the Corporate Debtor from liabilities arising under special penal statutes such as the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. and to unlawfully derive the benefit of immunity contemplated under Section 32A of the Code, the invocation of Section 60(5) becomes indispensable. The Tribunal, in such cases, is not only empowered but duty-bound to scrutinize whether the insolvency process is being exploited as a mechanism for absolution rather than genuine resolution. Section 65 of the Code embodies a clear legislative mandate that the insolvency resolution process shall not be invoked fraudulently or with malicious intent, or for any purpose other than resolution of insolvency.

Invoking its power under section 60(5) of the code CIRP of Alchemist Limited was terminated and recalled by the NCLT, in view of the fact that permitting the CIRP to continue would not only prejudice statutory proceedings under the PMLA but would also undermine the integrity of the insolvency regime itself. This Tribunal cannot be a silent spectator to such abuse.

QUICK GLANCE ON LATEST CIRCULAR BY IBBI

It has been observed that in certain cases under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC), the assets of the corporate debtor are under attachment by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) under the provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA). The restitution of such attached assets can significantly enhance the value of the Corporate Debtor thereby leading to higher realization.

Accordingly, it has been advised that in cases where assets of the corporate debtor are attached by the ED under the provisions under PMLA, the Insolvency Professional may file an application before the Special Court under sections 8(7) or 8(8) of the PMLA for restitution of such assets.

Further, with a view to facilitate the expeditious disposal of such applications by the Special Courts, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, in consultation with the ED, has formulated a standard undertaking to be furnished by the Insolvency Professional along with the application for restitution of assets.

CONCLUSION-

The law is settled—the Corporate Debtor and its Assets are granted a fresh start to ensure they remain productive economic units. However, the "reach" of the PMLA remains firmly fixed on the individuals responsible for the crime. This "Dual-Track" system ensures that while the business survives for the creditors and employees, the wrongdoers do not escape the consequences of their actions.
